questions.title: Classify a temperature reading
questions.promptHtml: A laboratory records a temperature of −7 °C. Which statement correctly classifies the number −7?
questions.hint: An integer can be negative. A rational number can be written as a fraction of two integers.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. −7 is an integer because it has no fractional part.
  2. −7 = −7/1, so it is also rational. It is not a natural number.

options.label: Integer and rational, but not natural
Neither an integer nor a rational number

questions.title: Calculate in the correct order
questions.promptHtml:
Calculate 72 ÷ (3 × 4) + 23 − 5.

Enter a whole number.
questions.hint: Complete the brackets and the power first. Then divide, and finally add and subtract.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Inside the brackets: 3 × 4 = 12. The power is 23 = 8.
  2. 72 ÷ 12 + 8 − 5 = 6 + 8 − 5 = 9.

questions.title: Prepare a laboratory mixture
questions.promptHtml:
A laboratory mixes liquids A and B in the ratio 3 : 5. It needs 640 mL in total.

How much of each liquid is needed? Enter whole numbers in mL.
questions.hint: There are 3 + 5 equal parts. Find the volume of one part first.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total parts = 3 + 5 = 8. One part = 640 ÷ 8 = 80 mL.
  2. Liquid A: 3 × 80 = 240 mL. Liquid B: 5 × 80 = 400 mL.
  3. The volumes sum to 640 mL and the ratio 240 : 400 simplifies to 3 : 5.

questions.title: A price rises, then returns
questions.promptHtml:
A textbook price rises from ¥240 to ¥276.

Find the percentage increase. Then find the percentage discount on ¥276 that would return the price to ¥240. Give both percentages to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Percentage change = change ÷ starting value × 100. The starting value is different in the second calculation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Price change = 276 − 240 = ¥36.
  2. Increase = (36 ÷ 240) × 100 = 15.00%.
  3. To return to ¥240, the discount uses ¥276 as its base: (36 ÷ 276) × 100 = 13.043478…%, or 13.04%.

questions.title: Model a delivery cost
questions.promptHtml:
A delivery cost is calculated using C = 18 + 2.4x, where C is the cost in yuan and x is the distance in kilometres.

Calculate C when x = 7.5. Then find x when C = 60. Give both answers to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: Substitute x = 7.5 for the first part. For the second, subtract 18 from both sides before dividing by 2.4.

questions.title: Convert measurements
questions.promptHtml:
Convert the following measurements:

  • 2.75 km to metres.
  • 960 mL to litres.
  • 90 km/h to metres per second.

Use whole numbers for metres and m/s, and 2 decimal places for litres.
questions.hint: 1 km = 1,000 m; 1 L = 1,000 mL; 1 hour = 3,600 seconds.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 2.75 × 1,000 = 2,750 m.
  2. 960 ÷ 1,000 = 0.96 L.
  3. 90 km/h = 90,000 m ÷ 3,600 s = 25 m/s.

questions.title: Arrange six display items
questions.promptHtml:
A shop places six different products in a single row. Each product is used once.

How many different arrangements are possible? Also give the value of 0!. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: For six different items in a row, multiply 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1. Remember the definition of 0!.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. There are 6 choices for the first position, then 5, then 4, and so on.
  2. 6! = 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 720 arrangements.
  3. By definition, 0! = 1. There is one way to arrange an empty selection.

questions.title: Assign three different roles
questions.promptHtml:
A team has 9 members. It must appoint a supervisor, an assistant and an inspector. One person cannot hold more than one role.

How many different assignments are possible? Enter a whole number.
questions.hint: The roles are different, so order matters. There are 9 choices, then 8, then 7.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The three roles are distinct: choosing the same three people for different roles creates a different assignment.
  2. P(9, 3) = 9! ÷ (9 − 3)! = 9 × 8 × 7 = 504 assignments.

questions.title: Choose a review committee
questions.promptHtml:
A team has 9 members. It selects a committee of 3 people. All committee members have the same role.

How many different committees can be formed? Enter a whole number.
questions.hint: The order of the three people does not matter. Divide the number of ordered selections by 3!.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Order does not matter because the committee has no separate roles.
  2. C(9, 3) = 9! ÷ (3! × 6!) = (9 × 8 × 7) ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 84 committees.

questions.title: A terminating decimal
questions.promptHtml: Which description fits 0.375?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. 0.375 = 375/1000 = 3/8, so it is rational; it has a non-zero fractional part.

questions.title: A square root
questions.promptHtml: Which description fits √49?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. √49 = 7. It is a positive whole number and can be written as 7/1.

questions.title: An irrational length
questions.promptHtml: Which number is irrational?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. √2 cannot be written as a ratio of integers. The other three numbers can.

questions.title: A repeating decimal
questions.promptHtml: The decimal 0.272727… repeats forever. How is it classified?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. A repeating decimal is rational: 0.272727… = 27/99 = 3/11.

questions.title: A negative fraction
questions.promptHtml: Which set contains −11/4?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. −11/4 is a ratio of two integers with a non-zero denominator, but equals −2.75 rather than an integer.

questions.title: Evaluate 18 − 3 × (2 + 1)^2
questions.promptHtml: Calculate 18 − 3 × (2 + 1)2.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.

questions.title: Evaluate (48 ÷ 6 + 2) × 1.5
questions.promptHtml: Calculate (48 ÷ 6 + 2) × 1.5.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.

questions.title: Evaluate −4^2 + (−4)^2
questions.promptHtml: Calculate −42 + (−4)2.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.

questions.title: Evaluate 36 ÷ 3 × 2 − 5
questions.promptHtml: Calculate 36 ÷ 3 × 2 − 5.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Division and multiplication have equal priority: work left to right.
  2. 36 ÷ 3 × 2 = 12 × 2 = 24; 24 − 5 = 19.

questions.title: Evaluate 2.4 + 3 × (5.5 − 1.5) ÷ 2
questions.promptHtml: Calculate 2.4 + 3 × (5.5 − 1.5) ÷ 2.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Brackets give 4.
  2. 3 × 4 ÷ 2 = 6; 2.4 + 6 = 8.4.

questions.title: Evaluate (7 + 5)! ÷ 11!
questions.promptHtml: Calculate (7 + 5)! ÷ 11!.
questions.hint: Brackets and powers come before multiplication or division; equal-priority operations go left to right.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. (7 + 5)! = 12! = 12 × 11!.
  2. Cancel 11! to obtain 12.

questions.title: Allocate a research budget
questions.promptHtml: A research budget is split between equipment and staffing in the ratio 3:7. The total is 8500. Find both shares.
questions.hint: Divide the total by the total number of ratio parts.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total parts = 10; one part = 8500 ÷ 10 = 850.
  2. First share = 2550; second share = 5950.

questions.title: Mix cleaning solution
questions.promptHtml: Concentrate and water are mixed in the ratio 2:9. The total is 825. Find both shares.
questions.hint: Divide the total by the total number of ratio parts.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total parts = 11; one part = 825 ÷ 11 = 75.
  2. First share = 150; second share = 675.

questions.title: Divide laboratory time
questions.promptHtml: Microscopy and sample preparation share the available hours in the ratio 5:3. The total is 14. Find both shares.
questions.hint: Divide the total by the total number of ratio parts.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total parts = 8; one part = 14 ÷ 8 = 1.75.
  2. First share = 8.75; second share = 5.25.

questions.title: Recover the total mixture
questions.promptHtml: A mixture has active ingredient to carrier in the ratio 2:7. It contains 175 mL of carrier. Find the active ingredient and total volume.
questions.hint: The 175 mL corresponds to seven parts, not nine.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. One part = 175/7 = 25 mL.
  2. Active ingredient = 2 × 25 = 50 mL; total = 225 mL.

questions.title: Scale a treatment batch
questions.promptHtml: A batch for 12 test samples uses 45 mL of reagent. At the same rate, how much is needed for 38 samples?
questions.hint: Find the amount per sample.

questions.title: Simplify a decimal ratio
questions.promptHtml: Simplify 1.2:0.45 to the smallest positive whole-number ratio.
questions.hint: Multiply both terms by 100, then divide by their greatest common factor.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 1.2:0.45 = 120:45.
  2. Divide both by 15 to obtain 8:3.

questions.title: More pumps, less time
questions.promptHtml: Four identical pumps empty a tank in 18 hours. How long do six such pumps take, assuming constant rates and no interference?
questions.hint: The total number of pump-hours stays constant.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 4 × 18 = 72 pump-hours.
  2. 72/6 = 12 hours.

questions.title: Clinic visits rise
questions.promptHtml: A recorded value changes from 240 to 294. Calculate the percentage change. Use a negative answer for a decrease.
questions.hint: Use the original value as the denominator.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Change = 54.
  2. Percentage change = (54/240) × 100 = 22.50%.

questions.title: Defect count falls
questions.promptHtml: A recorded value changes from 160 to 124. Calculate the percentage change. Use a negative answer for a decrease.
questions.hint: Use the original value as the denominator.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Change = -36.
  2. Percentage change = (-36/160) × 100 = -22.50%.

questions.title: Energy use changes
questions.promptHtml: A recorded value changes from 82.5 to 75.9. Calculate the percentage change. Use a negative answer for a decrease.
questions.hint: Use the original value as the denominator.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Change = -6.6.
  2. Percentage change = (-6.6/82.5) × 100 = -8.00%.

questions.title: Find the price before a discount
questions.promptHtml: After a 15% discount, equipment costs ¥714. What was its original price?
questions.hint: The sale price is 85% of the original.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 0.85 × original = 714.
  2. Original = 714/0.85 = ¥840.

questions.title: Two successive increases
questions.promptHtml: A laboratory fee of ¥500 rises by 10%, then by a further 8%. Find the final fee and the overall percentage increase.
questions.hint: Apply the second increase to the new fee.

questions.title: Recover after a fall
questions.promptHtml: Output falls from 250 units to 200 units. What percentage increase from 200 is needed to return to 250?
questions.hint: The recovery percentage uses 200 as its base.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Required increase = 50 units.
  2. 50/200 × 100 = 25%.

questions.title: Percentage points and relative change
questions.promptHtml: A response rate rises from 40% to 52%. Find the increase in percentage points and the relative percentage increase.
questions.hint: Subtract the rates for percentage points; divide that change by the original rate for relative change.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 52 − 40 = 12 percentage points.
  2. 12/40 × 100 = 30% relative increase.

questions.title: Discount followed by tax
questions.promptHtml: An item has a listed price of ¥1250. A 12% discount is applied, then 6% tax is charged on the discounted price. Find the amount paid.
questions.hint: Use one multiplier for the discount and another for the tax.

questions.title: Substitute a negative value
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate y = 3x² − 2x + 5 when x = −2.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.

questions.title: Solve a linear equation
questions.promptHtml: Solve 4x + 7 = 31.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Subtract 7: 4x = 24.
  2. Divide by 4: x = 6.

questions.title: Rearrange a cost model
questions.promptHtml: Total cost is C = 180 + 12q. Find q when C = 780.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.

questions.title: Use a rate formula
questions.promptHtml: Speed v = d/t. A sample travels 135 metres in 18 seconds. Calculate v in metres per second.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. v = 135/18.
  2. v = 7.5 metres per second.

questions.title: Solve with a bracket
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Divide by 2.5: x − 4 = 7.
  2. Add 4: x = 11.

questions.title: Evaluate a square-root formula
questions.promptHtml: Calculate z = (x − μ)/σ when x = 46, μ = 52 and σ = √9.
questions.hint: Substitute carefully, or undo the operations in reverse order.

questions.title: Convert a small volume
questions.promptHtml: Convert 0.085 litres to millilitres.
questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.

questions.title: Convert a dose mass
questions.promptHtml: Convert 750 micrograms to milligrams. Use 1000 micrograms = 1 milligram.
questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.

questions.title: Convert hours to minutes
questions.promptHtml: Convert 2.35 hours to minutes.
questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. 2.35 × 60 = 141 minutes. Decimal hours are not hours and minutes.

questions.title: Convert an imperial length
questions.promptHtml: Convert 7.5 inches to centimetres. Use 1 inch = 2.54 cm.
questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.

questions.title: Convert an area
questions.promptHtml: Convert 0.032 m² to cm². Use 1 m = 100 cm.
questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.

questions.title: Convert a speed
questions.promptHtml: Convert 54 km/h to m/s. Use 1 km = 1000 m and 1 h = 3600 s.
questions.hint: Write the conversion factor with units before calculating.

questions.title: Order five specimens
questions.promptHtml: Five distinct specimens are placed in a row. How many orders are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use factorial: 5!.
  2. The number of possibilities is 120.

questions.title: Order seven presentations
questions.promptHtml: Seven different presentations are scheduled in seven time slots. How many schedules are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use factorial: 7!.
  2. The number of possibilities is 5040.

questions.title: Assign two officers
questions.promptHtml: From nine staff, choose one chair and a different secretary. How many assignments are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use permutation: 9!/(7)!.
  2. The number of possibilities is 72.

questions.title: Rank three finalists
questions.promptHtml: Seven finalists compete for first, second and third place, with no ties. How many ordered results are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use permutation: 7!/(4)!.
  2. The number of possibilities is 210.

questions.title: Select three samples
questions.promptHtml: Choose three of eight distinct samples for testing. Order does not matter. How many selections are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use combination: 8!/(3! × 5!).
  2. The number of possibilities is 56.

questions.title: Select four representatives
questions.promptHtml: Choose a four-person committee from ten people, with no assigned roles. How many committees are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use combination: 10!/(4! × 6!).
  2. The number of possibilities is 210.

questions.title: Create a two-symbol label
questions.promptHtml: A label uses two different symbols chosen from six. Symbol order matters and repetition is forbidden. How many labels are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use permutation: 6!/(4)!.
  2. The number of possibilities is 30.

questions.title: Select a pair of clinics
questions.promptHtml: Choose two of nine clinics for a joint study. The clinics have equal roles. How many pairs are possible?
questions.hint: Decide whether order or distinct roles matter. All objects or people are distinct.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use combination: 9!/(2! × 7!).
  2. The number of possibilities is 36.

questions.title: A committee with a chair
questions.promptHtml: From eight staff, select a three-person committee, then choose one of its members as chair. How many outcomes are possible?
questions.hint: Choose the committee, then its chair.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. C(8,3) = 56 committees.
  2. Each has 3 possible chairs: 56 × 3 = 168 outcomes.

questions.title: Compare repetition rules
questions.promptHtml: A three-digit laboratory code uses digits 1–5. Find the number of codes (a) with repetition allowed and (b) with no repeated digit.
questions.hint: With repetition the options stay constant; without repetition they decrease.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. With repetition: 5³ = 125.
  2. Without repetition: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.

questions.title: Cancel factorials before calculating
questions.hint: Expand 8! only far enough to cancel 6!.

questions.title: Find the original group sizes
questions.promptHtml: The ratio of laboratory assistants to technicians is 3:5. There are 14 more technicians than assistants. Find the number in each group.
questions.hint: The difference of two ratio parts corresponds to 14 people.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 5 − 3 = 2 parts; one part = 14/2 = 7.
  2. Assistants = 3 × 7 = 21; technicians = 5 × 7 = 35.

questions.title: Recover the starting enrolment
questions.promptHtml: After increasing by 12.5%, course enrolment is 180 students. What was the enrolment before the increase?
questions.hint: 180 is 112.5% of the original enrolment.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Original × 1.125 = 180.
  2. Original = 180/1.125 = 160 students.

questions.title: Read membership and count distinct elements
questions.promptHtml:
A set is written as A = {2, 2, 4, 7, 9}. Repeating a value does not add a new element.

Choose the true membership statement and give n(A).
questions.hint: Count distinct values, then read ∈ as “is an element of”.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The distinct elements are 2, 4, 7 and 9. Therefore n(A) = 4.
  2. The statement 4 ∈ A is true because 4 appears in A.

questions.title: Find the common elements
questions.promptHtml: Let A = {1, 3, 5, 6} and B = {2, 3, 6, 8}. Select A ∩ B.
questions.hint: An intersection contains only elements that appear in both sets.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 3 and 6 occur in both A and B.
  2. Therefore A ∩ B = {3, 6}.

questions.title: Combine material options
questions.promptHtml:
A supplier offers material set A = {glass, steel, paper}. Another offers B = {paper, bamboo}.

Choose A ∪ B and give its number of elements.
questions.hint: A union includes every distinct element in either set. Count paper once.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Combine the options without repeating paper.
  2. A ∪ B = {glass, steel, paper, bamboo}, so n(A ∪ B) = 4.

questions.title: Use the universal set for a complement
questions.promptHtml:
The universal set of sample labels is U = {101, 102, 103, 104, 105, 106}. The inspected samples are I = {101, 103, 106}.

Which set is Ic, the samples in U that have not been inspected?
questions.hint: Start with U and remove every element in I.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Remove 101, 103 and 106 from U.
  2. The complement is Ic = {102, 104, 105}. Values outside U do not belong in this complement.

questions.title: Distinguish an empty set from a set containing zero
questions.promptHtml:
Let E = {2, 4, 6} and O = {1, 3, 5}.

Select E ∩ O and give n(E ∩ O).
questions.hint: No number in these lists is both even and odd. The empty set and {0} are different.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. There are no shared elements, so E ∩ O = ∅.
  2. An empty set has 0 elements. The set {0} would have one element, namely zero.

questions.title: Complete a two-group survey
questions.promptHtml:
Of 80 laboratory staff, 46 use software A, 39 use software B, and 17 use both. Each software total includes the staff who use both.

Find the numbers using A only, B only, at least one package, and neither. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: Place the 17 shared users first. Subtract them from each total before finding the union.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A only = 46 − 17 = 29. B only = 39 − 17 = 22.
  2. At least one = 29 + 17 + 22 = 68. Neither = 80 − 68 = 12.
  3. Check all four separate groups: 29 + 17 + 22 + 12 = 80.

questions.title: Recover a missing overlap
questions.promptHtml:
A survey of 120 students records 72 using the library (L), 65 using the study centre (S), and 18 using neither. Students can use both.

Find n(L ∪ S), n(L ∩ S), and the number using the library only.
questions.hint: First subtract neither from the total. The extra count in 72 + 65 is the overlap.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. At least one = 120 − 18 = 102.
  2. Both = 72 + 65 − 102 = 35.
  3. Library only = 72 − 35 = 37. For a check, study centre only = 65 − 35 = 30, and 37 + 35 + 30 + 18 = 120.

questions.title: Correct a double count
questions.promptHtml:
A group has 60 people. Of these, 44 speak language A, 32 speak language B and 20 speak both.

A student writes: “44 + 32 = 76, so 76 people speak at least one of the two languages.” Identify the error and give the correct number speaking at least one.
questions.hint: The 20 bilingual people appear in both totals.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Adding the totals counts every bilingual person twice.
  2. Subtract the overlap once: 44 + 32 − 20 = 56.
  3. The remaining 60 − 56 = 4 speak neither language.

options.label: People who speak both were counted twice.
People who speak both should be excluded entirely.
Every union must be divided by two.
The two language totals cannot overlap.

fields.label: Correct number speaking at least one

questions.title: Recognise a quadratic after simplifying
questions.promptHtml:
Which equation is quadratic after like terms have been simplified?

For the equation you select, give a, b and c in the form ax² + bx + c = 0.
questions.hint: Move all terms to one side. An equation is quadratic only if the resulting x² coefficient is non-zero.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. For 3x² + 2x = 7, standard form is 3x² + 2x − 7 = 0. Thus a = 3, b = 2, c = −7.
  2. In x² + 4x = x² + 9, the x² terms cancel, leaving a linear equation. The remaining options are linear and cubic.

questions.title: Solve a quadratic by factoring
questions.promptHtml: Solve x² − 7x + 12 = 0 by factoring. Enter the smaller root first and the larger root second.
questions.hint: Find two numbers whose product is 12 and whose sum is −7.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The numbers are −3 and −4, so x² − 7x + 12 = (x − 3)(x − 4).
  2. A product is zero when at least one factor is zero. The roots are 3 and 4.
  3. Check: 9 − 21 + 12 = 0 and 16 − 28 + 12 = 0.

questions.title: Find a negative and a positive root
questions.promptHtml: Solve x² + 2x − 15 = 0. Enter the smaller root first and the larger root second.
questions.hint: The two factor numbers must multiply to −15 and add to 2.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Factor: (x + 5)(x − 3) = 0.
  2. Set each bracket to zero: x + 5 = 0 or x − 3 = 0. The roots are −5 and 3.
  3. Both satisfy the original equation: 25 − 10 − 15 = 0 and 9 + 6 − 15 = 0.

questions.title: Use the quadratic formula with signed coefficients
questions.promptHtml:
Solve 2x² − x − 6 = 0 using the quadratic formula.

Give the smaller and larger roots to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: Use a = 2, b = −1 and c = −6. Keep their signs in b² − 4ac.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The discriminant is (−1)² − 4(2)(−6) = 1 + 48 = 49.
  2. x = [1 ± √49] / 4 = (1 ± 7) / 4.
  3. The roots are −1.5 and 2.0. Check: 2(−1.5)² − (−1.5) − 6 = 0, and 2(2)² − 2 − 6 = 0.

questions.title: Round roots only at the end
questions.promptHtml: Solve x² − 4x − 1 = 0. Give both roots to 3 decimal places, smaller first.
questions.hint: The discriminant is 20. Keep the square root unrounded until the final answers.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. a = 1, b = −4 and c = −1. Therefore x = [4 ± √(16 + 4)] / 2.
  2. This simplifies to x = 2 ± √5.
  3. The roots are −0.2360679… and 4.2360679…, giving −0.236 and 4.236 to 3 d.p.

questions.title: Find the root a student missed
questions.promptHtml:
A student solves x² = 49 and writes “x = 7, because √49 = 7.”

Which correction is needed? Enter both roots, smaller first.
questions.hint: The square-root symbol means the non-negative square root, but an equation involving x² can also have a negative solution.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Both 7² and (−7)² equal 49.
  2. The principal square root √49 is 7, while the equation x² = 49 has two roots: −7 and 7.

options.label: No correction: only the positive root is allowed.

questions.title: Choose a physically possible quadratic root
questions.promptHtml:
A rectangular label has width x cm and length (x + 3) cm. Its area is 54 cm².

Find the width and length, then explain why one mathematical root must be rejected.
questions.hint: Use area = width × length. After solving, both dimensions must be positive.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. x(x + 3) = 54, so x² + 3x − 54 = 0.
  2. Factor: (x + 9)(x − 6) = 0, giving x = −9 or x = 6.
  3. A width cannot be negative, so choose width 6 cm and length 9 cm. Their area is 6 × 9 = 54 cm².

options.label: It gives a negative physical width and length.
It does not solve the quadratic equation.
Negative numbers can never solve equations.
Always choose the largest root regardless of context.

questions.title: Simplify before substituting
questions.promptHtml: Simplify 4x − 3 + 2(x + 5) − x. Then find its value when x = −2.
questions.hint: Expand the bracket first, then collect x terms and constants separately.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Expand: 4x − 3 + 2x + 10 − x.
  2. Collect like terms: (4 + 2 − 1)x + (−3 + 10) = 5x + 7.
  3. At x = −2: 5(−2) + 7 = −3.

questions.title: Solve with a variable on both sides
questions.promptHtml: Solve 4(x − 2) + 3 = 2x + 9. Then give the common value of the left and right sides when you substitute your solution.
questions.hint: Expand the bracket, collect like terms and keep both sides balanced.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Expand and simplify: 4x − 8 + 3 = 2x + 9, so 4x − 5 = 2x + 9.
  2. Subtract 2x and add 5 to both sides: 2x = 14, giving x = 7.
  3. Check the original sides: 4(7 − 2) + 3 = 23 and 2(7) + 9 = 23.

questions.title: Repair an expansion sign error
questions.promptHtml:
A student expands −2(3x − 4) as −6x − 8.

Select the correct expansion and evaluate the original expression at x = 2.
questions.hint: Multiply −2 by each term inside the bracket, keeping the sign of each term.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. −2 × 3x = −6x and −2 × (−4) = +8.
  2. The correct expansion is −6x + 8.
  3. At x = 2: −6(2) + 8 = −4. Direct check: −2(6 − 4) = −4.

questions.title: Explain equal-priority operations
questions.promptHtml:
A student writes 30 ÷ 5 × 2 = 30 ÷ 10 = 3.

Select the rule that fixes the first incorrect step, then give the correct result.
questions.hint: Multiplication and division share the same priority. Read their sequence from left to right.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The first operation is 30 ÷ 5 = 6, followed by 6 × 2 = 12.
  2. The incorrect step treats multiplication as always preceding division. At equal priority, calculate from left to right.

options.label: Always complete every multiplication before any division.
Do multiplication and division from left to right.
Do multiplication and division from right to left.
Insert brackets around 5 × 2 whenever division appears.

questions.title: Explain why distinct roles change the count
questions.promptHtml:
A team chooses a chair and a different secretary from 7 members. A student gives C(7, 2) = 21.

Explain the error and give the correct number of appointments.
questions.hint: Swapping the chair and secretary changes the outcome.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The combination counts pairs without distinguishing their roles. Each pair has two assignments.
  2. There are 7 choices of chair and 6 remaining choices of secretary: 7 × 6 = 42.
  3. Equivalently, 21 pairs × 2 role assignments = 42.

options.label: The two roles are different, so swapping people creates another outcome.
The same person must hold both roles.
Selecting a secretary replaces the chair.

questions.title: Judge a load against a stated mass limit
questions.promptHtml:
For a mathematical planning check, a load has mass 1,900 kg and a handling system has a stated mass limit of 4,200 lb. Use 1 kg ≈ 2.205 lb.

Convert the load to pounds to 1 decimal place and decide whether it meets this mass limit. This question checks only the stated mass limit.
questions.hint: Convert the load and limit to the same unit before comparing.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Load ≈ 1,900 × 2.205 = 4,189.5 lb.
  2. The load is 4,200 − 4,189.5 = 10.5 lb below the stated limit. It meets this mass criterion.
  3. Expressing the load in pounds changes the number and unit, not the physical mass.

fields.label: Comparison with the stated mass limit

options.label: Cannot compare because 1,900 is smaller than 4,200.

questions.title: Repair a percentage-change denominator
questions.promptHtml:
A price falls from ¥250 to ¥200. A student calculates the decrease as (50 ÷ 200) × 100 = 25%.

Select the denominator required for the percentage decrease and calculate the correct percentage. Enter a positive percentage for the decrease.
questions.hint: Percentage change compares the amount of change with the starting value.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The decrease is ¥250 − ¥200 = ¥50. The starting price is ¥250.
  2. Percentage decrease = (50 ÷ 250) × 100 = 20%.
  3. The student’s 25% would describe the increase from ¥200 back to ¥250, which uses a different starting price.

questions.title: Connected case: bottle features and product choices
questions.promptHtml:
A bottle design team surveys 160 students. Of these, 96 request a reusable bottle, 88 request insulation, and 24 request neither. Each feature total includes people selecting both.

The team can offer one of 4 colours, one of 3 sizes and one of 2 lid types. Every combination is available.

Find the number requesting at least one feature, the number requesting both, the percentage of all respondents requesting both, and the number of product versions. Then select the conclusion supported by the survey. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: Recover the overlap from the survey totals. Count versions using one choice from each independent design category.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. At least one = 160 − 24 = 136.
  2. Both = 96 + 88 − 136 = 48. The other regions are reusable only 48 and insulation only 40. Their sum with both and neither is 160.
  3. Both as a percentage of all respondents = 48 ÷ 160 × 100 = 30%.
  4. Product versions = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24. This counts available combinations, not customer demand for each version.
  5. 136 ÷ 160 × 100 = 85% of the respondents requested at least one feature. The given counts do not establish the same percentage for all students.

fields.label: Respondents requesting at least one feature
Percentage of all respondents requesting both

options.label: 85% of the 160 respondents requested at least one feature.
85% of every student at the university requests at least one feature.
Each of the 24 versions will have equal demand.
Every surveyed student will buy a bottle.

extension.promptHtml: In two sentences, explain why the survey does not prove that 85% of all university students want at least one feature. Name one piece of information about survey selection you would need.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: The 85% describes the 160 respondents. Before making a claim about all university students, we need to know how those respondents were selected and whether important groups were excluded.
rubric: Identify the 160 respondents as the group directly described.
Explain that wider generalisation needs evidence about selection.
Name a relevant check, such as who could be selected or how selection occurred.

questions.title: Connected case: production inputs and paid orders
questions.promptHtml:
A workshop plans 300 laboratory trays, each containing 720 g of accepted material. Production loses 10% of the input mass. The input mixture contains recycled and new material in the ratio 3 : 2, and the loss affects both materials proportionally.

Recycled material is sold in complete 20 kg sacks. The workshop has 200 confirmed paid orders. Each ordered tray has list price ¥45 and a 12% discount.

Calculate the total accepted mass, required input mass, recycled and new input masses, minimum number of recycled-material sacks, selling price and revenue from the confirmed orders. Use kg for masses, whole sacks, and 2 decimal places for money.
questions.hint: Convert grams to kilograms, work backwards through the 10% loss, then divide the input in the ratio 3:2. Revenue uses the confirmed orders.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Accepted mass = 300 × 720 ÷ 1,000 = 216 kg.
  2. 90% of the input survives. Required input = 216 ÷ 0.90 = 240 kg.
  3. There are 5 ratio parts. Recycled input = (3/5) × 240 = 144 kg; new input = (2/5) × 240 = 96 kg.
  4. 144 ÷ 20 = 7.2 sacks. Buy 8 complete sacks, providing 160 kg. Only 144 kg enters this batch.
  5. Selling price = 45 × 0.88 = ¥39.60. Revenue from 200 paid orders = 200 × 39.60 = ¥7,920.00.
  6. The revenue calculation covers the 200 paid orders. It does not establish that the other 100 planned trays will sell.

fields.label: Minimum whole sacks of recycled material

options.label: The 200 confirmed paid orders produce ¥7,920 of revenue under the stated pricing rule.
All 300 planned trays will sell at the same price.
Profit is ¥7,920 because revenue and profit are the same.
Every future batch will produce exactly the same revenue.

questions.title: Choose a clearly defined set
questions.promptHtml: A researcher needs a set whose membership can be decided using a clear rule. Which description meets that requirement?
questions.hint: A rule is well-defined when two people using the same information can agree who belongs.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. “Students registered for Statistics on 1 October 2026” has a course and a fixed date that can be checked against a registration list.
  2. Descriptions such as interesting, good and popular require an unstated judgement.

options.label: Students registered for Statistics on 1 October 2026

questions.title: Read a statement containing zero
questions.promptHtml: Let A = {0, 1, 4}. Which statement is true?
questions.hint: Zero is an element if it is explicitly listed. Cardinality counts elements, not their sum.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The set contains three distinct elements: 0, 1 and 4. Thus n(A) = 3.
  2. Zero belongs to A, and 3 does not belong to A. The value n(A) does not have to be an element of A.

questions.title: Compare sets written in different orders
questions.promptHtml:
Set A is {red, blue, green}. Set B is {green, red, blue, red}.

Choose the correct relationship and give n(B).
questions.hint: Ordering and repetition do not change a set’s distinct members.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Both sets contain exactly red, blue and green, so A = B.
  2. The repeated red does not add another distinct element. Therefore n(B) = 3.

options.label: A and B are equal sets.
B has one more element than A.
A and B are different because the order differs.

questions.title: Identify values outside two sets
questions.promptHtml:
Use U = {1, 2, …, 12}. A contains the multiples of 3 in U. B contains the even numbers in U.

Choose the values in neither A nor B, then give n(A ∪ B).
questions.hint: List A and B, combine their distinct values, then compare that union with U.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A = {3, 6, 9, 12}; B = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12}.
  2. Their union is {2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12}, with 8 elements.
  3. The values in neither set are {1, 5, 7, 11}.

questions.title: Distinguish exactly one from at least one
questions.promptHtml:
In a training group, 23 people attend workshop A and 19 attend workshop B. Eight attend both.

How many attend exactly one workshop? Which description matches this group?
questions.hint: Remove the eight shared attendees from each workshop total.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A only = 23 − 8 = 15 and B only = 19 − 8 = 11.
  2. Exactly one = 15 + 11 = 26.
  3. This group contains A-only and B-only attendees. It excludes both and neither. At least one would include the eight who attend both.

options.label: A only or B only, excluding both.

questions.title: Change the universal set
questions.promptHtml:
Originally U = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} and A = {2, 4, 6}. The universal set is then changed to U = {1, 2, …, 8}, while A stays the same.

Choose the new complement Ac and give its size.
questions.hint: A complement depends on the stated universe. Include every new universe element that is not in A.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The original complement was {1, 3, 5}.
  2. After the universe expands, 7 and 8 also lie outside A. The new complement is {1, 3, 5, 7, 8}, containing 5 elements.

questions.title: Check whether survey totals are possible
questions.promptHtml:
A report says that among 50 people, 37 use service A, 29 use service B and 12 use both.

Calculate the implied number using at least one. Is the report internally consistent? What is the smallest possible overlap if the totals 37, 29 and 50 are correct?
questions.hint: The union cannot exceed the whole group. Work backwards from that limit to find the minimum overlap.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The implied union is 37 + 29 − 12 = 54, greater than the total of 50. The counts are inconsistent.
  2. To keep the union at most 50, the overlap must be at least 37 + 29 − 50 = 16.
  3. An overlap of 16 would make the union exactly 50. Larger valid overlaps would leave some people using neither.

fields.label: Implied number using at least one

options.label: Yes, because the feature totals can overlap.
No, the implied union exceeds the group size.

questions.title: Recover totals from separate Venn regions
questions.promptHtml:
A survey table lists mutually exclusive regions:

RegionCount
A only14
Both A and B9
B only17
Neither6

Find n(A), n(B), n(A ∪ B) and the total surveyed.
questions.hint: A set total includes its shared region. The whole-group total includes all four separate regions.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. n(A) = 14 + 9 = 23; n(B) = 17 + 9 = 26.
  2. n(A ∪ B) = 14 + 9 + 17 = 40.
  3. Total = 14 + 9 + 17 + 6 = 46.

questions.title: Relate a set to its complement
questions.promptHtml:
A universal set U contains a set A and its complement Ac. There are 28 elements in A and 11 in Ac.

Find n(U), then identify A ∩ Ac.
questions.hint: Every element of U is either in A or outside A, and cannot be both.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A and its complement are disjoint and together cover U. Therefore n(U) = 28 + 11 = 39.
  2. No element can be both in and outside A, so A ∩ Ac = ∅.

questions.title: Count optional kit choices
questions.promptHtml:
A field kit contains one of 3 sensors and one of 4 cable types. It is sold either with a case or without a case. Every combination is available.

How many kit versions are possible? Explain how the optional case affects the count.
questions.hint: An optional yes/no feature creates two choices for every sensor-and-cable combination.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. There are 3 × 4 = 12 sensor-and-cable combinations.
  2. Each has two case options, giving 12 × 2 = 24 versions.

options.label: It adds just one version to the total.
An optional feature never changes the count.
It triples the count because a case is a third item.

questions.title: Count alternative travel routes
questions.promptHtml:
There are 3 direct bus services from campus to the museum. Alternatively, a student can choose one of 2 buses to Central Station and then one of 4 connecting buses to the museum. All eight two-bus connections are possible.

Count the possible service choices. A direct service and a two-bus connection count as different routes.
questions.hint: Multiply choices within a two-stage route, then add mutually exclusive route types.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Two-bus choices: 2 × 4 = 8.
  2. Add the 3 direct services: 3 + 8 = 11 choices.

questions.title: Select one sample from each category
questions.promptHtml:
A study requires one of 5 water samples and one of 7 soil samples. All samples are distinct.

Count the possible pairs and choose the correct method.
questions.hint: Each water sample can be paired with every soil sample.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. There are 5 × 7 = 35 pairs.
  2. Choosing any two from all 12 would wrongly include two-water and two-soil pairs.

questions.title: Schedule a fixed opening presentation
questions.promptHtml:
Six different presentations fill six time slots. The safety presentation must be first.

How many schedules meet the restriction?
questions.hint: The fixed first slot has only one choice. Arrange the remaining presentations.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. After fixing the safety presentation first, five different presentations remain.
  2. They can be arranged in 5! = 120 ways.

questions.title: Arrange displays with fixed ends
questions.promptHtml:
Eight distinct display objects stand in a row. A named calibration object must be at the far left and a named control object must be at the far right.

How many arrangements are possible?
questions.hint: Both end positions are fixed, leaving six objects to arrange in six positions.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Fixing the two named objects leaves 8 − 2 = 6 freely ordered objects.
  2. The number of arrangements is 6! = 720.

questions.title: Keep two posters together
questions.promptHtml:
Five different posters are arranged in a row. Posters A and B must be next to each other. They may appear as AB or BA.

How many arrangements meet this rule?
questions.hint: Treat the adjacent pair as one block, then consider the two orders inside the block.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The AB block and the other three posters form four objects, giving 4! orders.
  2. The block has two internal orders, AB and BA. Total = 4! × 2 = 48.

fields.label: Arrangements with A and B adjacent

questions.title: Keep incompatible containers apart
questions.promptHtml:
Six different labelled containers are placed in a row. Containers A and B must not be next to each other.

How many arrangements satisfy this mathematical placement rule?
questions.hint: Count all arrangements, then subtract those in which A and B form one adjacent block.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Unrestricted arrangements: 6! = 720.
  2. Adjacent arrangements: treat A and B as a block, giving 5! × 2 = 240.
  3. Permitted arrangements = 720 − 240 = 480.

fields.label: Arrangements with A and B separated

questions.title: Include one required committee member
questions.promptHtml:
A three-person committee is selected from eight staff. Dr Lin must be included. All three members have equal roles.

How many different committees can be formed?
questions.hint: One place is fixed. Choose the remaining two members from the other seven.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Include Dr Lin, then choose two of the seven other staff.
  2. C(7, 2) = (7 × 6) ÷ 2 = 21 committees.

questions.title: Exclude unavailable candidates
questions.promptHtml:
Nine students volunteer for a three-person panel. Two named students are unavailable and cannot be selected. Panel members have equal roles.

How many panels are possible?
questions.hint: First determine the eligible group, then choose without assigning roles.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. There are 9 − 2 = 7 eligible volunteers.
  2. C(7, 3) = 7 × 6 × 5 ÷ (3 × 2 × 1) = 35 panels.

questions.title: Select a team with a required composition
questions.promptHtml:
A three-person team must contain two of 5 chemistry students and one of 4 physics students. Students are distinct and no individual roles are assigned.

How many teams meet the requirement?
questions.hint: Choose the chemistry pair, choose the physics student, then combine those choices.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Chemistry pairs: C(5, 2) = 10. Physics choices: C(4, 1) = 4.
  2. Total = 10 × 4 = 40 teams.

questions.title: Restrict eligibility for one role
questions.promptHtml:
Seven volunteers can serve as reporter, but only three of them are qualified to lead. Choose one qualified leader and a different reporter.

Count the possible appointments.
questions.hint: After choosing a leader, any of the six remaining volunteers may report.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. There are 3 choices of qualified leader.
  2. For each leader, 6 other volunteers remain eligible as reporter. Total = 3 × 6 = 18.

questions.title: Count letters and digits under different rules
questions.promptHtml:
A sample code has two letters followed by one digit. Each letter is chosen from A, B or C and letters may repeat. The digit is chosen from 1, 2, 3 or 4.

How many codes are available?
questions.hint: The three positions have 3, 3 and 4 independent choices.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. There are 3 × 3 = 9 letter pairs, including AA, BB and CC.
  2. Each letter pair has 4 digit endings. Total = 9 × 4 = 36.

questions.title: Handle zero at the start of a number
questions.promptHtml:
A three-digit whole number is formed from digits 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, with no repeated digit. The first digit cannot be zero.

How many such numbers exist?
questions.hint: There are four possible first digits. Zero remains available for a later position.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. First digit: 4 choices, namely 1, 2, 3 or 4.
  2. Second digit: 4 remaining choices, including zero. Third digit: 3 choices.
  3. Total = 4 × 4 × 3 = 48 numbers.

questions.title: Recover the size of a group from role counts
questions.promptHtml:
A club can appoint a chair and a different secretary in 42 ways. Every member is eligible for either role.

How many members are in the club?
questions.hint: For n members, the role count is n(n − 1). Find consecutive whole numbers with product 42.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. With n members, there are n choices for chair and n − 1 for secretary.
  2. Since 7 × 6 = 42, the club has 7 members.

questions.title: Correct the divisor for unordered groups
questions.promptHtml:
Six distinct volunteers can fill three different roles in 120 ways. A student wants three-person groups with no roles and divides 120 by 3, obtaining 40.

What should the divisor be, and how many groups are there?
questions.hint: Count all ways to assign three roles within one selected group.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Each three-person group has 3! = 6 assignments of the roles.
  2. Divide the 120 ordered assignments by 6, giving 20 groups. Dividing by 3 removes only part of the repeated counting.

questions.title: Count the excluded people instead
questions.promptHtml:
A seven-person equal-role group is selected from ten people.

Which alternative count gives the same result? Calculate the number of groups.
questions.hint: Each selected group corresponds to exactly one set of people left out.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Selecting seven people uniquely determines the three excluded people, and vice versa.
  2. Therefore C(10, 7) = C(10, 3) = 120.

options.label: Choose the 3 people excluded from the group.
Assign 7 different roles from the 10 people.
Choose 7 excluded people after selecting 7 people.

questions.title: Simplify a square root of a fraction
questions.promptHtml: Simplify √(81/16) and choose its most precise description among the options.
questions.hint: For these positive numbers, take the square root of the numerator and denominator.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. √(81/16) = 9/4 = 2.25.
  2. It is a ratio of integers but not itself an integer, so it is rational but not an integer.

questions.title: Classify after simplifying a radical quotient
questions.promptHtml: Consider √50 ÷ √2. Simplify it and choose the correct classification.
questions.hint: Combine the positive radicands in the quotient before classifying.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. √50 ÷ √2 = √(50/2) = √25 = 5.
  2. Five is a natural number, an integer and a rational number. The original radical symbols do not by themselves make the result irrational.

questions.title: Add an integer to an irrational number
questions.promptHtml: Which statement correctly describes 3 + √2?
questions.hint: If the sum were rational, subtracting the rational number 3 would make √2 rational too.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. √2 is irrational. Adding 3 cannot turn it into a rational number.
  2. If 3 + √2 were rational, subtracting 3 would make √2 rational, a contradiction. Thus the sum is irrational.

options.label: It is an integer because 3 is an integer.
It is rational because any sum is rational.
It is irrational; subtracting 3 cannot remove its irrationality.
It is undefined because integers and roots cannot be added.

questions.title: Test a claim about products of irrational numbers
questions.promptHtml: A student says: “Multiplying two irrational numbers always gives an irrational result.” Test the claim using √2 × √8.
questions.hint: For positive radicands, multiply inside the square root.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. √2 × √8 = √16 = 4, which is rational.
  2. Both factors are irrational, so this example disproves the word “always”. Some products of irrational numbers are rational.

fields.label: Does the example support the student’s claim?

options.label: No; the product is rational, so the claim is false.
Yes; any expression containing roots is irrational.
Classification is impossible without a decimal approximation.

questions.title: State the natural-number convention
questions.promptHtml:
For this question, define natural numbers as N = {1, 2, 3, …} and whole numbers as {0, 1, 2, 3, …}.

Which description of 0 is correct under these definitions?
questions.hint: Use the definitions supplied here rather than a different textbook convention.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Zero belongs to the stated whole-number set and to the integers.
  2. It is rational because 0 = 0/1. Under this question’s definition it is not natural.

options.label: Whole, integer and rational, but not natural here.
Irrational because division by zero is impossible.
Neither an integer nor a rational number.

questions.title: Distinguish a value from its rounded approximation
questions.promptHtml:
A measurement calculation uses π. A report displays the rounded approximation 3.142.

Which statement correctly classifies π and the exact written decimal 3.142?
questions.hint: A finite decimal is rational. Rounding a number produces a different, approximate value.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. π is irrational. The finite decimal 3.142 equals 3142/1000 = 1571/500, so it is rational.
  2. The rational rounded approximation does not change the classification of the exact value π.

options.label: π is irrational; the written decimal 3.142 is rational.
Both are irrational because the decimal approximates π.
Both are rational because π can be rounded.
3.142 is an integer because it has finitely many digits.

questions.title: Separate a leading minus from a negative base
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate −24 + (−2)3.
questions.hint: In −2⁴, the power acts on 2 before the leading minus. The cubed negative base remains negative.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. −2⁴ = −(2⁴) = −16.
  2. (−2)³ = −8. Therefore the result is −16 − 8 = −24.

questions.title: Respect the grouping in a fraction
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate (18 − 6) ÷ (2 + 4) + 3².
questions.hint: Complete both bracketed parts and the power before adding.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The numerator is 12, the denominator is 6 and the power is 9.
  2. 12 ÷ 6 + 9 = 2 + 9 = 11.

questions.title: Apply a root to the entire bracket
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate √(49 + 15) − 2³. The square root covers all of 49 + 15.
questions.hint: Add inside the root first. A square root does not distribute over addition.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 49 + 15 = 64, so √(49 + 15) = √64 = 8.
  2. 2³ = 8. The result is 8 − 8 = 0.

questions.title: Translate a one-time fee into an expression
questions.promptHtml:
A service charges one setup fee of ¥12 plus ¥7.50 for each of 3 visits.

Choose the correct expression and calculate the total to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The setup fee is paid once. Only the visit charge is repeated three times.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The correct expression is 12 + 3 × 7.50.
  2. Multiply first: 3 × 7.50 = 22.50. Total = 12 + 22.50 = ¥34.50.

questions.title: Repair an addition-and-subtraction step
questions.promptHtml:
A student writes 22 − 7 + 4 = 22 − 11 = 11.

Identify the rule that was broken and calculate the correct result.
questions.hint: Addition and subtraction share priority, so proceed from left to right.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The first operation should be 22 − 7 = 15, followed by 15 + 4.
  2. The correct result is 19. Adding 7 and 4 first incorrectly changes which terms are subtracted.

options.label: Perform addition and subtraction from left to right.
Subtract the sum of all later numbers.
Always begin at the right end.

questions.title: Choose brackets that make the target value
questions.promptHtml: Which expression equals 5?
questions.hint: Evaluate each pair of brackets before division or addition.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 18 ÷ (3 + 3) + 2 = 18 ÷ 6 + 2 = 3 + 2 = 5.
  2. The alternatives evaluate to 11, 2.25 and 12, respectively.

questions.title: Work through nested decimal brackets
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate 40 − {2.5 × [6 − (1.2 + 0.8)]}.
questions.hint: Work from the innermost brackets outwards before the final subtraction.

questions.title: Identify the coefficient after combining terms
questions.promptHtml: Simplify 8y − 5y + 2. In the simplified expression, give the coefficient of y and the constant term.
questions.hint: Only terms containing the same variable to the same power can be combined.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 8y − 5y = 3y, so the expression simplifies to 3y + 2.
  2. The coefficient is 3, and the constant is 2.

questions.title: Distinguish an expression from an equation
questions.promptHtml:
Compare 2p + 7 with 2p + 7 = 19.

Which is an equation? Solve that equation for p.
questions.hint: An equation states that two expressions are equal. Solve by keeping the two sides balanced.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Only 2p + 7 = 19 contains an equality and is an equation.
  2. Subtract 7 from both sides: 2p = 12. Divide by 2: p = 6.

questions.title: Undo a fraction in a linear equation
questions.promptHtml: Solve (3x − 2) / 4 = 7. Give x, then the value of 3x − 2 at your solution.
questions.hint: Multiply both sides by 4 before undoing the subtraction and multiplication in the numerator.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Multiplying by 4 gives 3x − 2 = 28.
  2. Add 2: 3x = 30. Divide by 3: x = 10.
  3. The numerator is 3(10) − 2 = 28, and 28/4 = 7 checks the equation.

questions.title: Balance decimal coefficients
questions.promptHtml: Solve 0.6x + 1.8 = 0.2x + 5. Give x to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: Subtract 0.2x and 1.8 from both sides before dividing by the remaining coefficient.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 0.6x − 0.2x = 5 − 1.8 gives 0.4x = 3.2.
  2. Therefore x = 8.0. Check: both original sides equal 6.6.

questions.title: Check a proposed solution with a negative coefficient
questions.promptHtml:
A student solves 12 − 3t = 27 and gives t = 5.

Find the correct t and select the check that reveals the error in t = 5.
questions.hint: Substituting a proposed value into the original equation is a direct check.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Subtract 12: −3t = 15. Divide by −3: t = −5.
  2. At t = 5 the left side is 12 − 15 = −3, which is not 27.
  3. At t = −5, the left side is 12 + 15 = 27.

options.label: A positive solution never needs checking.
A negative coefficient makes an equation impossible.

questions.title: Substitute two signed values
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate V = 2ab + a² when a = −1.5 and b = 4. Give V to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Put the negative value in brackets wherever it is substituted.

questions.title: Keep unlike powers separate
questions.promptHtml: Simplify 3x² + 4x − x² + 2x, then evaluate it at x = 2.
questions.hint: The x² terms combine with one another; the x terms form a separate group.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 3x² − x² = 2x² and 4x + 2x = 6x. The simplified expression is 2x² + 6x.
  2. At x = 2: 2(2²) + 6(2) = 8 + 12 = 20.

questions.title: Rearrange before substituting into a rate model
questions.promptHtml:
A model gives t = (v − u) / a, where a ≠ 0.

Select the rearrangement for v, then find v when u = 8, a = 2.5 and t = 6.
questions.hint: Multiply both sides by a, then add u to both sides.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. at = v − u, so v = u + at.
  2. Substitution gives v = 8 + 2.5(6) = 23.

questions.title: Expand two brackets in one equation
questions.promptHtml: Solve 3(2x + 1) − 2(x − 4) = 22. Give x to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Distribute each outside coefficient, including the negative coefficient on the second bracket.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Expand: 6x + 3 − 2x + 8 = 22.
  2. Collect terms: 4x + 11 = 22, so 4x = 11.
  3. x = 2.75. Checking gives 3(6.5) − 2(−1.25) = 19.5 + 2.5 = 22.

questions.title: Interpret cancellation of all variable terms
questions.promptHtml:
Simplify each equation and decide how many real values of x solve it:

A: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6
B: 2(x + 3) = 2x + 7
questions.hint: After expanding, subtract 2x from both sides and compare what remains.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Equation A becomes 2x + 6 = 2x + 6, then 6 = 6. This is true for every real x.
  2. Equation B becomes 2x + 6 = 2x + 7, then 6 = 7. This is false, so it has no solution.
  3. A variable disappearing does not always mean that x = 0.

questions.title: Recognise a repeated quadratic root
questions.promptHtml: Solve x² − 10x + 25 = 0. Give the root and the number of distinct real roots.
questions.hint: Look for a square of one bracket. Repeating the same root does not create two distinct values.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. x² − 10x + 25 = (x − 5)².
  2. The equation holds when x = 5. The two factors are identical, so there is 1 distinct real root.

questions.title: Decide whether a real root exists
questions.promptHtml: How many real roots does x² + 9 = 0 have? Select the reason.
questions.hint: For a real x, x² is non-negative.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The equation would require x² = −9.
  2. A real square cannot be negative. Therefore there are no real roots. This question considers real numbers only.

options.label: No real roots, because x² cannot equal −9.
Every real x is a root.

questions.title: Avoid losing the zero root
questions.promptHtml:
A student solves x² − 6x = 0 by dividing both sides by x and concludes x = 6.

Give all roots, smaller first, and explain what went wrong.
questions.hint: Factor out x. Dividing by x assumes x is not zero.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Factor: x(x − 6) = 0, so x = 0 or x = 6.
  2. Both values satisfy the original equation.
  3. Dividing by x silently excludes x = 0, so it loses a valid root.

options.label: Dividing by x excludes the possible root x = 0.
Every quadratic has exactly one real root.

questions.title: Solve a quadratic with two negative roots
questions.promptHtml: Solve 3x² + 11x + 6 = 0. Give the smaller root first and the larger root second, to 3 decimal places.
questions.hint: Try factors (3x + 2)(x + 3), or use the quadratic formula.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 3x² + 11x + 6 = (3x + 2)(x + 3).
  2. The roots are x = −2/3 and x = −3.
  3. In increasing order, the answers are −3.000 and −0.667.

questions.title: Check factor signs before finding roots
questions.promptHtml: Which factorisation of x² − 9x + 20 is correct? Then solve x² − 9x + 20 = 0, smaller root first.
questions.hint: The two constant terms in the factors must multiply to +20 and add to −9.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The constants are −4 and −5, giving (x − 4)(x − 5).
  2. Setting either bracket to zero gives x = 4 or x = 5.
  3. Positive constants +4 and +5 would produce +9x, so their signs would be wrong here.

questions.title: Keep minus b separate from b
questions.promptHtml: For 2x² − 7x + 3 = 0, choose the correct quadratic-formula substitution. Then give both roots, smaller first, to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: b is −7, so −b is +7. The denominator is 2a = 4.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. a = 2, b = −7 and c = 3. The discriminant is 49 − 24 = 25.
  2. The correct substitution is x = [7 ± √25] / 4.
  3. The roots are (7 − 5)/4 = 0.5 and (7 + 5)/4 = 3.0.

questions.title: Build a quadratic from its roots
questions.promptHtml:
A quadratic in the form x² + bx + c = 0 has roots −2 and 5.

Find b and c.
questions.hint: A root of −2 gives factor (x + 2), and a root of 5 gives factor (x − 5).
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The equation is (x + 2)(x − 5) = 0.
  2. Expanding gives x² − 3x − 10 = 0. Therefore b = −3 and c = −10.

questions.title: Convert cubic metres to litres
questions.promptHtml:
A reservoir model has volume 0.018 m³. Use 1 m³ = 1,000 L.

Give its volume in litres, then in millilitres using 1 L = 1,000 mL.
questions.hint: Apply the two volume conversion factors in sequence.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 0.018 × 1,000 = 18 L.
  2. 18 × 1,000 = 18,000 mL.

questions.title: Correct a square-unit conversion
questions.promptHtml:
A student converts 0.45 m² to 45 cm² by multiplying by 100.

Use 1 m = 100 cm. Give the correct area in cm² and explain the error.
questions.hint: An area has two length dimensions, so the conversion factor must be squared.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 1 m² = 100 cm × 100 cm = 10,000 cm².
  2. 0.45 × 10,000 = 4,500 cm².
  3. The student converted only one dimension; an area needs the factor 100².

options.label: The area conversion needs the square of the length factor.

questions.title: Combine masses before checking a limit
questions.promptHtml:
A parcel contains equipment of mass 1.25 kg and packaging of mass 780 g. The stated parcel mass limit is 2.00 kg.

Find the total mass and select the correct comparison. Give the mass to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Convert packaging to kilograms before adding it to the equipment.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 780 g = 0.78 kg. Total = 1.25 + 0.78 = 2.03 kg.
  2. The parcel exceeds the 2.00 kg limit by 0.03 kg.

options.label: Below the limit because 780 is less than 2,000.

questions.title: Distinguish minutes from decimal hours
questions.promptHtml:
A session lasts 2 hours 18 minutes. A student records this as 2.18 hours.

Give the correct duration in decimal hours to 2 decimal places and select the reason.
questions.hint: An hour contains 60 minutes, not 100.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 18 minutes = 18/60 = 0.30 hour.
  2. Total = 2 + 0.30 = 2.30 hours.
  3. The digits after a decimal point represent fractions of an hour; they are not a minutes field.

options.label: Eighteen minutes is 18/60 of an hour, not 18/100.
Durations must always be whole numbers.

questions.title: Specify which gallon is being used
questions.promptHtml:
Tank A contains 3 US gallons; tank B contains 3 Imperial gallons. Use 1 US gallon ≈ 3.785 L and 1 Imperial gallon ≈ 4.546 L.

Find each volume and the difference B − A in litres, to 3 decimal places.
questions.hint: Identical numbers with different gallon definitions do not represent the same volume.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A ≈ 3 × 3.785 = 11.355 L. B ≈ 3 × 4.546 = 13.638 L.
  2. Difference ≈ 13.638 − 11.355 = 2.283 L.
  3. The type of gallon must be stated because the unit definitions differ.

questions.title: Convert a scaled map distance
questions.promptHtml:
A map uses the scale 1 cm represents 250 m. A straight route measures 3.6 cm on the map.

Find the represented distance in metres and in kilometres. Give kilometres to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: First apply the scale, then use 1 km = 1,000 m.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Distance = 3.6 × 250 = 900 m.
  2. 900 ÷ 1,000 = 0.90 km.

questions.title: Convert a rate into kilometres per hour
questions.promptHtml:
A model vehicle moves at a constant 7.2 m/s. Use 1 hour = 3,600 seconds and 1 km = 1,000 m.

Convert the speed to km/h to 2 decimal places, then interpret it.
questions.hint: Multiply by seconds per hour, then divide metres by 1,000 to obtain kilometres.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 7.2 m/s × 3,600 s/h ÷ 1,000 m/km = 25.92 km/h.
  2. At that constant speed for one hour, the vehicle would travel 25.92 km.

options.label: At this constant speed, it travels 25.92 km in one hour.
It travels 25.92 km in one second.
It travels 25.92 metres in one hour.
It takes exactly 25.92 hours for every trip.

questions.title: Compare lengths without rounding too early
questions.promptHtml:
An opening is 32 inches wide. A rigid box is 82 cm wide. The box must pass with this width aligned to the opening, without tilting. Use 1 inch = 2.54 cm.

Find the opening width and the amount by which the box is wider, to 2 decimal places. Then decide whether the widths allow it to pass.
questions.hint: Convert the opening to centimetres, then compare the unrounded measurements.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Opening width = 32 × 2.54 = 81.28 cm.
  2. The box is 82 − 81.28 = 0.72 cm wider.
  3. It does not pass under the stated alignment condition.

options.label: The box is too wide under the stated condition.

questions.title: Identify the whole in a percentage calculation
questions.promptHtml:
A university orders 375 laboratory notebooks. It assigns 48% of this order to the science programme.

How many notebooks go to science, and which value is the whole in this calculation?
questions.hint: The percentage describes a share of the complete notebook order.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The whole is 375 notebooks.
  2. Science allocation = 0.48 × 375 = 180 notebooks.

questions.title: Distinguish a completed share from a remaining share
questions.promptHtml:
A team has checked 52 of 80 reports.

Calculate the percentage checked and the percentage still unchecked. Enter whole percentages.
questions.hint: Both percentages use all 80 reports as their denominator.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Checked = 52/80 × 100 = 65%.
  2. Unchecked reports = 80 − 52 = 28, giving 28/80 × 100 = 35%.
  3. The shares total 100%.

questions.title: Compare a part with another part and with the whole
questions.promptHtml:
In a mixture, ingredient A and ingredient B are in the ratio 5 : 7. Together they form the entire mixture.

Express A as a percentage of B, then as a percentage of the total. Give both to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The first denominator is seven parts. The second denominator is all twelve parts.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A as a percentage of B = 5/7 × 100 = 71.43% to 2 d.p.
  2. A as a percentage of the whole = 5/(5 + 7) × 100 = 41.67%.
  3. Different comparisons require different denominators.

fields.label: A as a percentage of B (2 d.p.)
A as a percentage of total (2 d.p.)

questions.title: Combine two linked ratios
questions.promptHtml:
Research funding satisfies A : B = 2 : 3 and B : C = 4 : 5. The total funding is ¥350,000.

Find the amounts for A, B and C. Enter whole yuan.
questions.hint: Make the B parts equal in the two ratios before combining them.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Scale 2:3 by 4 to get A:B = 8:12. Scale 4:5 by 3 to get B:C = 12:15.
  2. Thus A:B:C = 8:12:15, with 35 parts. One part = 350,000/35 = ¥10,000.
  3. A = ¥80,000, B = ¥120,000, C = ¥150,000.

questions.title: Change a mixture ratio by adding one component
questions.promptHtml:
A 500 mL mixture has concentrate:water = 1 : 4. More water is added without removing any liquid. Volumes are additive.

How much water must be added to make concentrate:water = 1 : 7? Give the final mixture volume too.
questions.hint: The concentrate amount stays fixed. Use it to find the new required water amount.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Initially concentrate = 500/5 = 100 mL and water = 400 mL.
  2. At 1:7, the 100 mL concentrate requires 700 mL water. Add 700 − 400 = 300 mL.
  3. Final volume = 100 + 700 = 800 mL.

questions.title: Combine two concentrations
questions.promptHtml:
A technician mixes 200 mL of a 10% solution with 300 mL of a 20% solution. Percentages are volumes of dissolved ingredient per total solution volume. Assume volumes add and no ingredient is lost.

Find the total ingredient volume and the final concentration percentage.
questions.hint: Find the amount of ingredient in each solution, add those amounts, then divide by total solution volume.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Ingredient volumes: 0.10 × 200 = 20 mL and 0.20 × 300 = 60 mL.
  2. Total ingredient = 80 mL; total solution = 500 mL.
  3. Concentration = 80/500 × 100 = 16%. A simple average of 10% and 20% would ignore the unequal solution volumes.

questions.title: Recover input through two stages of loss
questions.promptHtml:
A process loses 4% of its input mass in stage 1 and then 10% of the remaining mass in stage 2. The accepted output is 172.8 kg.

Find the original input mass and the overall percentage lost. Give the percentage to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: The retained fractions multiply: 0.96 × 0.90. Work backwards from the accepted output.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Retained fraction = 0.96 × 0.90 = 0.864.
  2. Input = 172.8/0.864 = 200 kg.
  3. Overall loss = 100% − 86.4% = 13.6%. The second loss uses a smaller starting mass, so the rates are not added.

questions.title: Compare two discount offers
questions.promptHtml:
An item has list price ¥500. Offer A applies a 20% discount followed by another 10% discount on the reduced price. Offer B applies one 30% discount.

Find both final prices and select the cheaper offer.
questions.hint: Successive discounts multiply the retained fractions.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Offer A: 500 × 0.80 × 0.90 = ¥360.
  2. Offer B: 500 × 0.70 = ¥350.
  3. Offer B is ¥10 cheaper. Offer A’s combined discount is 28%, not 30%.

questions.title: Compare two percentage bases for the same difference
questions.promptHtml:
A workshop makes a product for ¥80 and sells it for ¥100. Define markup as (selling price − cost) / cost × 100. Define gross margin here as (selling price − cost) / selling price × 100.

Calculate the markup and gross margin using these definitions.
questions.hint: The difference is the same, but the definitions specify different denominators.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Price minus cost = 100 − 80 = ¥20.
  2. Markup = 20/80 × 100 = 25%.
  3. Gross margin = 20/100 × 100 = 20%. These percentages answer different questions.

questions.title: Correct a report that confuses percentage points
questions.promptHtml:
A report says: “The response rate increased from 20% to 40%, which is a 20% relative increase.”

Give the change in percentage points and the correct relative percentage increase.
questions.hint: Subtract the rates for percentage points, then divide that change by the original rate for relative change.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Change in percentage points = 40 − 20 = 20 percentage points.
  2. Relative increase = (40 − 20)/20 × 100 = 100%.
  3. The response rate doubled. The report has confused percentage points with relative percentage change.

questions.title: Recognise a zero starting value
questions.promptHtml:
A new laboratory recorded 0 bookings in its first week and 12 bookings in its second week.

Give the absolute increase and decide whether the usual percentage-change formula gives a defined percentage.
questions.hint: The usual formula divides by the starting value.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Absolute increase = 12 − 0 = 12 bookings.
  2. The usual percentage calculation would divide 12 by 0, which is undefined.
  3. Report the increase in bookings rather than claiming a finite percentage increase from zero.

options.label: Undefined because the starting value is zero

questions.title: State the assumption behind proportional scaling
questions.promptHtml:
Together, two operators produce 15 test kits per hour. A manager predicts the output with four operators by direct proportion.

What output does this model predict, and which assumption is needed?
questions.hint: Direct proportion assumes the output per operator remains unchanged.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Four operators are twice as many as two, so the model predicts 30 kits per hour.
  2. The prediction assumes unchanged productivity per operator, including enough equipment and no new interference. It is a model assumption, not a guarantee.

options.label: Every increase in staff always doubles output.
Output per operator stays the same with enough resources.
Each operator works half as long.
The extra operators must change the quality standard.

questions.title: Allocate a total among three activities
questions.promptHtml:
A research assistant divides 120 hours among planning, data collection and analysis in the ratio 2 : 3 : 7.

Find the hours for each activity.
questions.hint: There are 12 equal parts across the three activities.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. One part = 120/(2 + 3 + 7) = 10 hours.
  2. Planning = 20 hours, collection = 30 hours and analysis = 70 hours.
  3. The allocations sum to 120 hours.

questions.title: Put ratio quantities into matching units
questions.promptHtml: Two cables have lengths 240 cm and 1.5 m. Find the ratio of the first length to the second in its smallest whole-number form.
questions.hint: Convert both lengths into the same unit before simplifying.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 1.5 m = 150 cm, so the ratio is 240:150.
  2. Divide both terms by 30 to obtain 8:5.

questions.title: Recalculate a ratio after the group changes
questions.promptHtml:
A class initially has boys:girls = 2 : 3 and contains 30 girls. Six boys then join, while the number of girls stays unchanged.

Give the new boys:girls ratio in its smallest whole-number form and the new total class size.
questions.hint: Recover the original boys count from the ratio, add six boys, then simplify the new counts.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Three parts correspond to 30 girls, so one part is 10. Initially there are 20 boys.
  2. After six boys join, the counts are 26 boys and 30 girls. The ratio is 13:15.
  3. New total = 26 + 30 = 56 students.

questions.title: Apply a discount before a fixed delivery charge
questions.promptHtml:
A purchase has a ¥120 subtotal. A 15% discount applies to the subtotal only. Delivery then adds a fixed ¥8. The budget is ¥112.

Find the amount paid and the amount of budget remaining.
questions.hint: Apply the percentage to the subtotal, then add the fixed charge.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Discounted subtotal = 120 × 0.85 = ¥102.
  2. Amount paid = 102 + 8 = ¥110.
  3. Budget remaining = 112 − 110 = ¥2. Applying the discount to delivery would contradict the stated rule.

questions.title: Test whether equal percentage changes cancel
questions.promptHtml:
A fee of ¥800 increases by 15%, then decreases by 15% of the increased fee.

Find the final fee and its percentage decrease relative to the original ¥800, to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The second percentage uses the new, larger fee.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. After the increase: 800 × 1.15 = ¥920.
  2. After the decrease: 920 × 0.85 = ¥782.
  3. Overall decrease = (800 − 782)/800 × 100 = 2.25%. Equal percentage rates applied to different bases do not cancel.

questions.title: Separate delivery from the discounted item price
questions.promptHtml:
An item has list price ¥240. A customer pays ¥198 in total, including a fixed ¥18 delivery fee. The discount applies only to the item.

Find the discounted item price and the discount percentage.
questions.hint: Remove delivery from the total before comparing the item’s prices.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Discounted item price = 198 − 18 = ¥180.
  2. Discount amount = 240 − 180 = ¥60.
  3. Discount percentage = 60/240 × 100 = 25%.

questions.title: Recover a total from the rejected share
questions.promptHtml:
In a completed inspection, 4 out of every 7 items passed. Exactly 27 items failed, and every item either passed or failed.

Find the total inspected and the number that passed.
questions.hint: The failed items represent three of the seven ratio parts.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Failure corresponds to 7 − 4 = 3 parts. One part = 27/3 = 9 items.
  2. Total = 7 × 9 = 63; passed = 4 × 9 = 36.
  3. Check: 36 + 27 = 63, and 36/63 = 4/7.

questions.title: Check an exact percentage against a whole-person count
questions.promptHtml:
A report claims that exactly 37.5% of 42 students chose option A. Each student made exactly one choice.

What student count would that exact percentage imply? Can the claim be exact?
questions.hint: An exact percentage of a headcount must produce a whole-number count.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 37.5% of 42 = 0.375 × 42 = 15.75 students.
  2. A count of students cannot be 15.75. Therefore the percentage cannot be exact for this group size.
  3. A rounded or approximate percentage would need to be labelled as such and checked against the actual count.

fields.label: Count implied by the exact percentage
Can the stated percentage be exact?

options.label: Yes, fractional students are allowed in a count.
No, it implies a non-whole student count.
Yes, simply round the student count and keep “exactly”.
Every percentage is exact by definition.

questions.title: Explain why adding equal amounts does not preserve a ratio
questions.promptHtml:
A student writes: “3:5 is equivalent to 5:7 because I added 2 to both terms.”

Select an equivalent ratio to 3:5 and the valid rule for generating it.
questions.hint: Equivalent ratios multiply or divide every term by the same non-zero factor.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Multiplying each term by 2 gives 6:10, which is equivalent to 3:5.
  2. Adding 2 gives 5:7, but 3/5 = 0.6 while 5/7 ≈ 0.714. The proportions differ.

options.label: Add the same non-zero number to both terms.
Multiply both terms by the same positive factor.
Swap the terms in every ratio.

questions.title: Model a packed shipment using one bottle mass
questions.promptHtml:
A carton containing six identical bottles has total mass 3.60 kg. The empty carton weighs 0.24 kg.

A shipment contains 32 bottles. Each carton holds at most six bottles, and every carton used weighs 0.24 kg even when partly full.

Find one bottle’s mass in grams, the minimum number of cartons, and the complete shipment mass in kilograms to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Form an equation for one full carton. Convert the bottle mass to grams, and round the number of cartons up.
questions.solutionHtml:
