1. Let x be one bottle’s mass in kg. Then 6x + 0.24 = 3.60, so x = (3.60 − 0.24)/6 = 0.56 kg = 560 g.
  2. 32/6 = 5 remainder 2. The partly filled final carton is needed, giving 6 cartons.
  3. Shipment mass = 32(0.56) + 6(0.24) = 17.92 + 1.44 = 19.36 kg.

questions.title: Form a quadratic from a rectangular panel
questions.promptHtml:
A rectangular panel has width x cm and length (2x + 1) cm. Its area is 45 cm².

Select the equation for its area, find the physical width and length to 1 decimal place, and explain which mathematical root is unsuitable.
questions.hint: Multiply width by length. After solving, check whether each root gives positive dimensions.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The area equation is x(2x + 1) = 45, giving 2x² + x − 45 = 0.
  2. Factoring gives (2x − 9)(x + 5) = 0. The mathematical roots are x = 4.5 and x = −5.
  3. The negative root gives negative physical dimensions. Use width 4.5 cm and length 10.0 cm. Check: 4.5 × 10 = 45 cm².

options.label: It does not solve the equation.
A root below 10 is always invalid.
A decimal root cannot describe a measurement.

questions.title: Find a border width and reject an impossible layout
questions.promptHtml:
A card is 20 cm by 16 cm. A border of uniform width x cm runs inside all four edges. The remaining printed area is 192 cm².

Find both mathematical roots of the area equation, smaller first. Then give the physically valid border width and the printed dimensions, longer side first.
questions.hint: The border removes x from both ends of each dimension, so the printed dimensions are 20 − 2x and 16 − 2x.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. (20 − 2x)(16 − 2x) = 192 gives 4x² − 72x + 128 = 0.
  2. Divide by 4: x² − 18x + 32 = 0 = (x − 2)(x − 16). Roots are 2 and 16.
  3. A valid printed width requires 16 − 2x > 0, so x < 8. Thus x = 2 cm is valid.
  4. Printed dimensions are 16 cm by 12 cm, and their product is 192 cm². The root 16 would give negative printed dimensions.

questions.title: Find where two delivery cost models agree
questions.promptHtml:
For a non-negative distance d in kilometres, two delivery services use these prices in yuan:

A = 18 + 2.5d
B = 30 + 1.7d

Find the distance where their costs agree and that common cost. Then decide which service is cheaper at 20 km and give the difference in cost.
questions.hint: Set the two cost expressions equal to find the crossing distance. Compare both models again at 20 km.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 18 + 2.5d = 30 + 1.7d gives 0.8d = 12, so d = 15 km.
  2. Common cost = 18 + 2.5(15) = ¥55.50.
  3. At 20 km, A = ¥68 and B = ¥64. Service B is cheaper by ¥4.

questions.title: Repair a filling equation with mixed units
questions.promptHtml:
A tank initially contains 5 L. A pump adds 250 mL per minute at a constant rate, with no losses. The target is 12 L.

A student writes 5 + 250t = 12, with t in minutes. Select a valid corrected equation, find the time to reach the target, and find the volume after 10 minutes in litres to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: Convert every volume to the same unit before building the equation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. In millilitres, the equation is 5,000 + 250t = 12,000. The student mixed litres with millilitres.
  2. 250t = 7,000 gives t = 28 minutes.
  3. After 10 minutes: 5,000 + 250(10) = 7,500 mL = 7.5 L.

questions.title: Use a quadratic and unit conversion to check a fit
questions.promptHtml:
A rectangular component has width x cm, length (x + 2) cm, and area 35 cm².

An opening is 60 mm wide and 80 mm long. The corresponding edges stay parallel, and the component has negligible thickness.

Find the component’s positive dimensions, convert the opening dimensions to cm, and decide whether the component fits under these conditions.
questions.hint: Solve x(x + 2) = 35, then put the component and opening dimensions in the same unit.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. x² + 2x − 35 = 0 gives (x + 7)(x − 5) = 0. Reject the negative width −7.
  2. The component is 5 cm wide and 7 cm long.
  3. The opening is 6 cm wide and 8 cm long. Since 5 < 6 and 7 < 8, it fits under the stated conditions.

options.label: Both dimensions fit with the corresponding edges parallel.

questions.title: Model a path surrounding a square garden
questions.promptHtml:
A square garden has side length 10 m. A path of uniform width x m surrounds it outside all four sides. The combined outer square has area 144 m².

Choose the equation, find the positive path width and outer side length, and calculate the area of the path alone.
questions.hint: A path adds its width on both ends of each side, giving outer side 10 + 2x.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The correct equation is (10 + 2x)² = 144.
  2. The positive physical outer side is √144 = 12 m. Thus 10 + 2x = 12 and x = 1 m.
  3. The other algebraic branch would give outer side −12 m and x = −11 m, which is physically invalid.
  4. Garden area = 10² = 100 m². Path area = 144 − 100 = 44 m².

questions.title: Solve for a radius after converting volume units
questions.promptHtml:
An ideal cylinder has height 12 cm and volume 1.5 L. Its radius r in cm satisfies V = πr²h. Use 1 L = 1,000 cm³ and your calculator’s π value.

Convert the volume to cm³, find the physical radius to 2 decimal places, and explain why the negative algebraic root is rejected.
questions.hint: Use cubic centimetres with the height in centimetres. Rearrange to r² = V/(πh) before taking the square root.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Volume = 1.5 × 1,000 = 1,500 cm³.
  2. 1,500 = 12πr², so r² = 125/π. The algebraic roots are r = ±√(125/π).
  3. The physical radius is positive: r = 6.307831… cm, or 6.31 cm to 2 d.p.
  4. A negative radius is not a possible physical length even though its square satisfies the equation.

options.label: A negative number cannot be squared.
It does not satisfy the volume equation.
A radius is a physical length and must be positive here.
Negative roots can never be rounded.

questions.title: Study student travel times
questions.promptHtml:
A university has 6,000 students. Researchers randomly select 120 students and find that their mean daily travel time is 43.5 minutes.

Identify the population, the sample and the type of numerical summary reported.
questions.hint: The population is the whole group of interest. A statistic summarises a sample; a parameter summarises the whole population.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The population is all 6,000 university students.
  2. The sample is the 120 selected students.
  3. 43.5 minutes is a statistic because it was calculated from the sample. The mean for all 6,000 students would be a population parameter.

fields.label: The sample mean of 43.5 minutes is a…

questions.title: Classify factory variables
questions.promptHtml:
A factory records each employee’s department, the number of defective items in a batch, and the mass of an item in grams.

Classify each variable. Treat mass as a measurement, even if the instrument rounds its display.
questions.hint: Categories name groups. Counts are usually discrete; measurements are usually continuous.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Department is qualitative: it describes a category, such as Sales or Production.
  2. Number of defective items is quantitative and discrete: the count takes whole-number values.
  3. Mass is quantitative and continuous: in principle it can take any value within a measurement range.

questions.title: Match four sampling plans
questions.promptHtml:
Identify the method used in each plan:

  1. A computer randomly selects 60 different IDs from the full student list.
  2. After a random start, a researcher selects every 20th student on a list.
  3. A researcher randomly selects 20 students from each year group.
  4. A researcher randomly selects three classes and surveys every student in those classes.
questions.hint: Stratified sampling takes some people from every group. Cluster sampling takes everyone from selected groups.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Plan 1 uses simple random sampling: the IDs are selected randomly from the complete list.
  2. Plan 2 uses systematic sampling: it follows a fixed interval after a random start.
  3. Plan 3 uses stratified sampling: each year group contributes a random sample.
  4. Plan 4 uses cluster sampling: whole selected classes are surveyed.

questions.title: Select records systematically
questions.promptHtml:
A clinic has a list of 1,000 patient records, numbered 1 to 1,000. It needs a systematic sample of 50 records.

The random starting record is 13. Find the sampling interval, the second selected record and the final selected record. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: Use k = N ÷ n. The selected records are 13, 13 + k, 13 + 2k, and so on.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sampling interval: k = 1,000 ÷ 50 = 20.
  2. The second selected record is 13 + 20 = 33.
  3. The 50th and final selected record is 13 + 49(20) = 993.

questions.title: Review a satisfaction survey
questions.promptHtml:
A university posts a survey link on its website. Students decide for themselves whether to respond. The university uses the replies to estimate satisfaction among all students.

Identify the main sampling problem and choose the best improvement.
questions.hint: Think about whether students who feel strongly might be more likely to respond.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The survey is vulnerable to voluntary response bias: students who choose to reply may differ from other students.
  2. A better starting design is to randomly select students from the complete student list and follow up with selected nonrespondents.
  3. A larger self-selected sample alone does not remove this bias. Random selection and follow-up improve coverage, although nonresponse can still require attention.

options.label: No possible bias because everyone can access the link
The population mean is too large
Keep the link open longer and assume the bias disappears
Randomly select students from the full list and follow up with nonrespondents
Collect more volunteer responses and ignore who responds

questions.title: Define the target population
questions.promptHtml: A university wants the mean commute time of all 2400 enrolled students. It surveys 120 students. What is the target population?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The target population is the full group the conclusion is intended to describe.

questions.title: Identify a sample
questions.promptHtml: A factory tests 35 batteries from today’s production of 700 batteries. Which group is the sample?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The sample consists of the units actually selected for study.

questions.title: A hospital-wide mean
questions.promptHtml: The mean age is calculated using every nurse currently employed by one hospital. For that hospital’s nurses, this mean is a:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. A numerical summary of the entire defined population is a parameter.

questions.title: An estimate from selected records
questions.promptHtml: A random sample of 80 customer records has a mean expenditure of ¥215. For all customers, ¥215 is a:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The mean comes from a sample, so it is a statistic used to estimate a population parameter.

questions.title: Recognise a census
questions.promptHtml: Which plan is a census of a company’s current employees?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. A census includes every member of the defined population.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: Collect data from every current employee

options.value: Collect data from every current employee
options.label: Collect data from every current employee

questions.title: An incomplete student list
questions.promptHtml: A study targets all enrolled students, but its list contains only students living in university accommodation. What is the main problem?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Students living elsewhere have no chance of selection: the frame undercovers the target population.

options.value: The sample must be too large
options.label: The sample must be too large

questions.title: Count missed appointments
questions.promptHtml: The number of missed appointments per patient in a year is:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. This is a numerical count with whole-number values.

questions.title: Measure a sample mass
questions.promptHtml: The true mass of a specimen, measured in grams, is:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Mass can vary continuously even if the measuring instrument rounds the display.

questions.title: Numbers used as labels
questions.promptHtml: Hospital patient identification numbers are:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The numbers identify people; their arithmetic differences do not measure an amount.

questions.title: Rank service ratings
questions.promptHtml: A single survey item has responses poor, fair, good and excellent. These categories are:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The categories have a natural order, but the gaps are not measured equal intervals.

questions.title: Record a blood group
questions.promptHtml: A patient’s blood group is recorded as A, B, AB or O. This is:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Blood-group categories have no natural ranking.

questions.title: Rounded measurements
questions.promptHtml: A scale reports weight to the nearest kilogram. The underlying variable, weight, is:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Rounding a measurement does not change the continuous nature of the underlying variable.

options.value: Ordinal because people can be ranked

options.value: Discrete because all displays are integers
options.label: Discrete because all displays are integers

questions.title: Draw employee IDs
questions.promptHtml: A computer selects 50 different IDs from a complete employee list so that every possible group of 50 is equally likely. Which method is used?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Equal probability for every possible sample of the given size defines simple random sampling.

questions.title: Use every twentieth record
questions.promptHtml: A researcher randomly chooses one of the first 20 records, then selects every twentieth record. Which method is used?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. A random start followed by a fixed interval is systematic sampling.

questions.title: Represent every department
questions.promptHtml: Employees are divided by department. A random sample is taken within every department. Which method is used?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. All strata contribute selected members; department membership defines the strata.

questions.title: Select whole classes
questions.promptHtml: Five classes are randomly selected from 40 classes. Every student in those five classes is surveyed. Which method is used?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Whole groups are selected, then all members in those selected groups are included.

options.value: Simple random sampling of individual students
options.label: Simple random sampling of individual students

questions.title: Select schools, then pupils
questions.promptHtml: A team randomly selects schools, then randomly samples pupils inside each selected school. Which description is most precise?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Selection occurs at two levels: schools first, pupils second.

options.value: One-stage cluster sampling with every pupil included

questions.title: Survey nearby colleagues
questions.promptHtml: A lecturer surveys the colleagues sitting beside them because they are easy to reach. This is:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Ease of access, rather than a probability selection procedure, determines participation.

questions.title: An open website poll
questions.promptHtml: A newspaper posts a poll that any reader may choose to answer. This is:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. People self-select into the sample; highly motivated readers may be overrepresented.

questions.title: Fixed quotas without random selection
questions.promptHtml: An interviewer must recruit 20 men and 20 women but chooses whichever passers-by are easiest to approach. This is:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Group quotas do not make selection random. Within-group convenience selection distinguishes this from stratified random sampling.

questions.title: Missing night-shift workers
questions.promptHtml: A staff survey is conducted only at 10 a.m.; night-shift staff are absent. What is the clearest risk?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. A defined part of the target population is systematically missed.

questions.title: Selected people do not reply
questions.promptHtml: A random sample of 500 patients is invited, but only 90 respond. Respondents may differ systematically from nonrespondents. Which bias is the concern?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Nonresponse can distort results when responding is related to the outcome of interest.

questions.title: A leading question
questions.promptHtml: A survey asks: “Don’t you agree our excellent new service is much better?” What is the main problem?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Positive language and an expected answer can push respondents toward agreement.

options.value: The sample interval is too large
options.label: The sample interval is too large

questions.title: A sensitive question in public
questions.promptHtml: Employees report rule-breaking while their manager watches. Which problem is most likely?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Respondents may give answers they think are acceptable rather than truthful.

options.value: A larger sample eliminates all bias
options.label: A larger sample eliminates all bias

questions.title: A faulty measuring device
questions.promptHtml: A thermometer reads 1.5 °C too high for every patient. What is the main issue?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The instrument consistently shifts recorded values upward; changing the sample alone will not fix it.

questions.title: A large biased poll
questions.promptHtml: An online poll has 100000 volunteer responses. Does its size guarantee an unbiased estimate of all residents’ views?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. A larger sample can reduce random error, but does not automatically correct systematic self-selection.

options.value: Yes; any sample above 1000 is unbiased
options.label: Yes; any sample above 1000 is unbiased

options.value: Yes; size makes it a census
options.label: Yes; size makes it a census

options.value: No; large samples are always worse
options.label: No; large samples are always worse

questions.title: Periodicity in a list
questions.promptHtml: Records repeat in a day–evening–night shift order. A random start followed by every third record samples only one shift. What is the risk?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Periodicity aligned with the interval can produce a poorly representative sample.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: The sampling interval matches a repeating pattern

options.value: Systematic sampling always includes every shift
options.label: Systematic sampling always includes every shift

options.value: The sampling interval matches a repeating pattern
options.label: The sampling interval matches a repeating pattern

questions.title: Improve a department comparison
questions.promptHtml: You need reliable results for each of four departments, including a small department. Which plan is most suitable?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Stratification ensures each department contributes observations for comparison.

options.value: Select one department and survey everyone there
options.label: Select one department and survey everyone there

options.value: Take volunteers from the largest department
options.label: Take volunteers from the largest department

questions.title: Reduce travel costs
questions.promptHtml: Residents live in 200 widely scattered villages. Which probability plan can reduce travel by concentrating fieldwork?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Randomly selected geographic clusters concentrate travel while retaining probability selection.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: Randomly select villages and survey all households in those villages

options.value: Choose only villages recommended by friends
options.label: Choose only villages recommended by friends

options.value: Randomly select villages and survey all households in those villages
options.label: Randomly select villages and survey all households in those villages

options.label: Survey only the nearest village without random selection

questions.title: Improve an online-only survey
questions.promptHtml: A council wants views from all adult residents, including residents without internet. Which change most directly reduces undercoverage?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. An offline route helps include people who cannot access the online survey.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: Offer accessible offline response routes within the sampling plan

questions.title: Separate chance from bias
questions.promptHtml: Two properly drawn random samples give slightly different mean ages. Does that alone prove either sample was biased?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Sample estimates vary by chance. A difference alone does not establish systematic bias.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: No; random sampling variability can produce differences

options.value: Yes; sample means must match exactly
options.label: Yes; sample means must match exactly

options.value: Yes; the smaller sample is always biased
options.label: Yes; the smaller sample is always biased

options.value: No; samples can never be biased
options.label: No; samples can never be biased

options.value: No; random sampling variability can produce differences
options.label: No; random sampling variability can produce differences

questions.title: Clusters and representation
questions.promptHtml: A study randomly selects two schools and surveys every pupil in them. Why might its estimate be imprecise?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Within-cluster similarity can reduce the information gained per pupil. This is not proof that cluster sampling is inherently biased.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: Pupils within a school may be similar, and two schools may not reflect between-school variation

options.label: Cluster sampling always causes selection bias

options.label: Pupils within a school may be similar, and two schools may not reflect between-school variation

options.label: Random selection makes all pupils identical

questions.title: Avoid a double question
questions.promptHtml: A survey asks: “Are the library’s opening hours and internet service satisfactory?” What is the best improvement?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. A respondent may be satisfied with one service but not the other; separate items allow distinct answers.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: Ask separate questions about hours and internet

options.value: Ask separate questions about hours and internet
options.label: Ask separate questions about hours and internet

options.label: Replace both with an ID number

questions.title: Random selection versus assignment
questions.promptHtml: Researchers randomly select patients for a survey. Does this mean patients were randomly assigned to treatments?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Random selection concerns who enters a study; random assignment concerns which treatment participants receive.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: No; selection and treatment assignment are different processes

options.value: No; selection and treatment assignment are different processes
options.label: No; selection and treatment assignment are different processes

options.label: Yes; these terms mean the same thing

questions.title: Systematic plan for 1800 records
questions.promptHtml: A list has 1800 records. Select 90 records systematically with starting position 7. Find the interval and the positions of the second and last selected records.
questions.hint: k = N/n; selected positions are start, start + k, start + 2k, …

questions.title: Systematic plan for 960 records
questions.promptHtml: A list has 960 records. Select 60 records systematically with starting position 11. Find the interval and the positions of the second and last selected records.
questions.hint: k = N/n; selected positions are start, start + k, start + 2k, …

questions.title: Systematic plan for 2520 records
questions.promptHtml: A list has 2520 records. Select 120 records systematically with starting position 4. Find the interval and the positions of the second and last selected records.
questions.hint: k = N/n; selected positions are start, start + k, start + 2k, …

questions.title: Allocate a sample across faculties
questions.promptHtml: Three faculties contain 600, 300 and 100 people. Allocate a sample of 80 proportionally. Give the three allocations in the same order.
questions.hint: Each allocation equals group size / total population × total sample.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total population = 1000.
  2. Allocations: 600/1000 × 80 = 48, 300/1000 × 80 = 24, 100/1000 × 80 = 8.
  3. The allocations sum to 80.

questions.title: Allocate a sample across departments
questions.promptHtml: Three departments contain 240, 360 and 600 people. Allocate a sample of 100 proportionally. Give the three allocations in the same order.
questions.hint: Each allocation equals group size / total population × total sample.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total population = 1200.
  2. Allocations: 240/1200 × 100 = 20, 360/1200 × 100 = 30, 600/1200 × 100 = 50.
  3. The allocations sum to 100.

questions.title: Allocate a sample across districts
questions.promptHtml: Three districts contain 150, 250 and 600 people. Allocate a sample of 60 proportionally. Give the three allocations in the same order.
questions.hint: Each allocation equals group size / total population × total sample.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total population = 1000.
  2. Allocations: 150/1000 × 60 = 9, 250/1000 × 60 = 15, 600/1000 × 60 = 36.
  3. The allocations sum to 60.

questions.title: A fraction and an interval
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 1,440 students. Researchers select 72 of them systematically. Calculate the sampling fraction as a decimal and a percentage, and find the interval.

Give the decimal to two decimal places. Enter the percentage as a number such as 5 for 5%.
questions.hint: The fraction is n/N. The interval is N/n. They answer different questions.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sampling fraction = 72/1,440 = 0.05.
  2. Percentage selected = 0.05 × 100 = 5%.
  3. Interval = 1,440/72 = 20, so select every twentieth position after a random start from 1–20.

questions.title: Finish a random selection procedure
questions.promptHtml:
A complete employee list contains unique IDs 1–480. A team needs a simple random sample of 30 different employees. Its generator produces equally likely IDs but may repeat them.

Choose a valid way to finish the selection.
questions.hint: A repeated ID does not identify an additional employee. Keep using the same random mechanism until there are 30 distinct IDs.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Keep each new random ID and reject duplicates until there are 30 distinct IDs.
  2. Each draw must treat all 480 IDs equally. Sampling distinct IDs this way gives a simple random sample of 30.
  3. Choosing friends or the next name after a duplicate changes the selection rule.

options.label: Replace repeated IDs with the next name on the list
Ask the manager to choose replacements
Reject repeated IDs and keep drawing uniformly until 30 distinct IDs have been obtained
Count a repeated ID as another employee

questions.title: Equal chances do not guarantee a simple random sample
questions.promptHtml:
Six people are labelled A, B, C, D, E and F. A computer selects one of three fixed pairs: AB, CD or EF, each with probability 1/3.

Every person has a 1/3 chance of selection. Is this a simple random sample of two people?
questions.hint: Simple random sampling concerns the chance of each possible sample, not only each individual.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. No. Only AB, CD and EF are possible under this rule.
  2. A simple random sample of two would give all 15 possible pairs the same chance, including AC and BD.
  3. Equal individual chances alone are insufficient.

options.label: No: simple random samples can never contain two people
No: other pairs such as AC have no chance of selection
Yes: each person has an equal chance, which is the complete SRS requirement
Yes: the computer automatically makes any procedure SRS

questions.title: Work backwards through a systematic sample
questions.promptHtml: A complete list contains 1,680 records. A systematic sample uses every 24th record. The sixth selected record is 137. Find the starting ID and the total number selected. Also decide whether the listed IDs prove that the start was chosen randomly.
questions.hint: Five intervals come before the sixth selection. A sequence shows what was selected, but not how its start was chosen.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Starting ID = 137 − 5 × 24 = 17.
  2. There are 1,680/24 = 70 selected records, from 17 to 1,673.
  3. The IDs alone do not prove a random start. Check that the start was chosen uniformly from 1–24.

fields.label: Does the sequence establish a random start?

options.label: No: check the recorded procedure for choosing a start from 1–24
Yes: every systematic sequence has a random start
No: a random process cannot produce 17

questions.title: Round a stratified allocation without losing places
questions.promptHtml:
Three departments have 125, 215 and 360 employees. Allocate 53 invitations proportionally.

Use the largest-remainder rule: round all allocations down, then give the remaining places to the largest decimal remainders. Choose how to select employees within each department.
questions.hint: Total population = 700. Multiply each department’s fraction by 53. The whole-number allocations must total 53.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Ideal allocations: 125/700 × 53 = 9.4643; 215/700 × 53 = 16.2786; 360/700 × 53 = 27.2571.
  2. Rounding down gives 9 + 16 + 27 = 52. The largest remainder is 0.4643, so the first department receives the final place.
  3. Allocate 10, 16 and 27. Randomly select those numbers of distinct IDs from the complete department lists.

options.label: Select the required number of distinct IDs randomly from its complete list
Take the first names on the list
Accept volunteers until the allocation is filled
Ask the manager to nominate their preferred employees

questions.title: Equal group samples from unequal groups
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 300 Business students and 900 Engineering students. A researcher randomly selects 30 from each programme.

Identify the design and calculate each student’s selection chance as a percentage.
questions.hint: Stratified means random selection within every group. Proportional means preserving the population shares.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The design is stratified but not proportional.
  2. Business selection chance = 30/300 × 100 = 10%.
  3. Engineering selection chance = 30/900 × 100 = 3.33%.
  4. Business students have three times the selection chance. Equal sample counts from unequal populations are not proportional.

options.label: Simple random sampling of 60 from the college

questions.title: Invited, replied and supported
questions.promptHtml:
A clinic randomly invites 280 patients to a survey. 175 reply, and 119 of the respondents support Saturday appointments.

Calculate the response rate and the support percentage among respondents. Give percentages to two decimal places.
questions.hint: Response rate uses invitations as the denominator. Support among respondents uses replies.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Response rate = 175/280 × 100 = 62.50%.
  2. Support among respondents = 119/175 × 100 = 68.00%.
  3. The 105 missing replies mean that 68% does not establish support among all invitees or all patients.

questions.title: Repair the denominator in a report
questions.promptHtml:
A report says: “We invited 360 residents, received 216 replies, and counted 135 supporters. Therefore, 37.5% of respondents support the plan.”

Correct the support percentage among respondents and identify what the reported 37.5% actually measures.
questions.hint: The numerator 135 is correct. Decide which group the denominator describes.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Respondent support = 135/216 × 100 = 62.50%.
  2. 135/360 × 100 = 37.5% is the percentage of all invitees who are known supporters.
  3. It is not the support rate among respondents, and it does not establish total support among all invitees because missing views are unknown.

options.label: The exact percentage supporting across the whole city
Known supporters as a percentage of all invitees

questions.title: Could missing replies change a majority?
questions.promptHtml:
Of 240 invited students, 150 reply. Exactly 96 respondents support a proposal. All other respondents do not support it. No views are known for the nonrespondents.

Find the lowest and highest possible support percentages among the 240 invitees. Does this evidence establish support from more than half of the invitees?
questions.hint: There are 90 missing replies. For the lower bound none support; for the upper bound all support. Both bounds use 240.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Missing replies = 240 − 150 = 90.
  2. Minimum = 96/240 × 100 = 40%.
  3. Maximum = (96 + 90)/240 × 100 = 77.5%.
  4. A majority is not established: the possible range crosses 50%. These bounds concern the invitees only.

fields.label: Is a majority among invitees established?

options.label: Yes: every missing reply must support
No: possible support lies both below and above 50%

questions.title: A majority that missing replies cannot remove
questions.promptHtml:
A researcher invites 200 members of a club. 160 reply, including 112 supporters. The other 48 respondents do not support the plan.

Find the minimum and maximum possible support percentages among all invitees. Decide what can be concluded before the other 40 members reply.
questions.hint: Compare the number of confirmed supporters with half of all invitees.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Minimum support = 112/200 × 100 = 56%.
  2. Maximum support = (112 + 40)/200 × 100 = 76%.
  3. A majority of the 200 invitees is established because confirmed supporters already exceed 100. This alone makes no claim about any wider population.

options.label: A majority cannot ever be established unless everyone replies
At least 56% of every club in the city supports
More than half of the 200 invitees support, even if all missing replies oppose

questions.title: Consistent estimates can still miss the truth
questions.promptHtml:
A simulation has a known population percentage of 50%. Repeated samples from three procedures produce these percentages:

  • A: 59, 60, 61
  • B: 40, 50, 60
  • C: 49, 50, 51

Judge precision from the spread and accuracy here from closeness to the known value.
questions.hint: A and C have the same narrow spread. Only one also stays close to 50%.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A and C are equally precise here: each has a range of 2 percentage points. B has a range of 20.
  2. C combines narrow spread with a centre at 50%.
  3. A is consistent but centred 10 percentage points too high. Consistency alone does not guarantee accuracy.

fields.label: Most precise procedures in this illustration
Procedure that is precise and centred on the truth

questions.title: More decimal places in a weak survey
questions.promptHtml:
An open website poll reports 72.438% support for a town policy. The analyst says: “Three decimal places prove that our estimate is accurate.”

Choose the best response.
questions.hint: The number of printed digits does not tell us who participated or who was missing.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The claim confuses numerical reporting detail with evidence about accuracy.
  2. Self-selection and coverage can still distort an open poll. More digits do not repair those problems.
  3. We need the selection process, target population and response information before assessing the wider claim.

options.label: Extra decimal places do not establish accurate sampling or remove bias
Three decimals guarantee accuracy within 0.001 percentage points
Rounding to a whole number would automatically remove bias

questions.title: Compare sampling costs and limitations
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 60 centres with 30 trainees each. Both plans select 180 trainees, and everyone takes part.

  • Plan A: simple random selection of individual IDs. This draw covers 45 centres.
  • Plan B: randomly select six whole centres and include all 30 trainees at each.

Fieldwork costs ¥80 per centre visited plus ¥12 per trainee. Calculate each cost and identify Plan B’s main statistical limitation.
questions.hint: Total cost = centres × 80 + trainees × 12. Consider similarity among trainees at the same centre.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A costs 45 × 80 + 180 × 12 = ¥5,760.
  2. B costs 6 × 80 + 180 × 12 = ¥2,640.
  3. B uses cluster sampling. Similar trainees in a few centres can lead to greater variation between samples. Random clusters are not automatically biased.

options.label: Plan B surveys every trainee in the college
Equal sample sizes force identical precision
Similar trainees within only six centres may reduce precision
Cluster sampling is always biased even with random selection

questions.title: Follow up the selected nonrespondents
questions.promptHtml:
A researcher randomly selects 180 patients. Only 108 reply. To fill the gap, an assistant suggests recruiting 72 volunteers from a social-media page.

Choose the best next step for the original random-sample survey.
questions.hint: The original selection process chose particular people. New volunteers do not provide those missing people’s answers.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Follow up the 72 originally selected nonrespondents using reminders and accessible response methods.
  2. Volunteers enter through a different process, so replacing missing respondents with volunteers does not preserve the original design.
  3. Follow-up helps, but it does not guarantee that all remaining nonresponse bias disappears.

options.label: Recruit any 72 volunteers and call the sample unchanged
Delete 72 existing replies so every count matches
Assume every nonrespondent has the same view as the respondents
Contact the 72 originally selected nonrespondents and offer accessible ways to reply

questions.title: Repair a measurement problem
questions.promptHtml:
A laboratory balance records every specimen as 0.24 g too heavy. The team proposes measuring twice as many specimens to solve the problem.

Choose the repair that addresses the cause.
questions.hint: Collecting more observations does not remove an error built into every measurement.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Check the balance against suitable reference masses, correct its calibration and verify it before further measurements.
  2. Doubling the sample preserves the +0.24 g shift in each new reading.
  3. Existing records need an appropriate correction or remeasurement after confirming the nature of the fault.

options.label: Round every faulty reading to more decimal places
Check and calibrate the balance against reference masses, then verify it
Double the sample while using the same faulty balance
Randomly choose a different list of specimen IDs

questions.title: Ask about the actual proposal
questions.promptHtml:
A canteen proposes adding a smaller meal option while keeping its usual portion. An initial question asks, “Don’t you agree we should remove wasteful large meals?”

Choose the best replacement question and response options.
questions.hint: A neutral question must describe adding a choice accurately, without praising or criticising it.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The replacement should ask about adding a smaller option while keeping the usual portion.
  2. Support / Oppose / Unsure permits balanced responses.
  3. The original wording both leads respondents and changes the proposal from adding an option to removing one.

options.label: Why do you oppose our excellent smaller option?
Do you agree smaller portions are better and healthier? Agree / Strongly agree
Would you support adding a smaller meal option alongside the usual portion? Support / Oppose / Unsure
Would you support replacing all usual portions with small meals? Yes / No

questions.title: An estimate is not a confirmed count
questions.promptHtml:
A simple random sample of 160 students is drawn from 3,200 students. All respond, and 58 use the university shuttle.

Use the sample proportion to estimate the number of shuttle users in the college. Then choose how to describe that result.
questions.hint: Multiply 58/160 by 3,200. Sampling does not inspect every person in the population.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Estimated count = 58/160 × 3,200 = 1,160.
  2. This is a sample-based estimate, not an established exact count.
  3. Another valid random sample could give a different estimate.

options.label: An estimate of the population count from a sample
The exact count proved by a census
The size of the selected sample
A guarantee that any other random sample gives the same result

questions.title: A comparison does not establish a cause
questions.promptHtml:
A canteen records 12 kg of leftovers on Monday using usual portions and 9 kg on Tuesday using smaller portions. The number of meals served is equal, but menus and customers differ between the days.

Calculate the percentage decrease in recorded leftovers, then choose the conclusion supported by this comparison.
questions.hint: Use Monday as the original amount. A numerical change alone cannot isolate which difference caused it.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Decrease = (12 − 9)/12 × 100 = 25%.
  2. The study recorded 25% less waste on Tuesday.
  3. It cannot attribute that decrease solely to smaller portions because the menu and customers also changed.

options.label: Recorded leftovers were 25% lower, but this comparison alone does not establish that smaller portions caused the reduction
Smaller portions are proved to reduce waste by exactly 25%
The data show no numerical change at all
Randomly counting leftovers would remove all day-to-day differences

questions.title: An imbalanced draw and a biased procedure
questions.promptHtml:
A college is 40% Engineering students. Researchers randomly select four whole classes using an equal-chance generator. In this particular draw, only 20% of selected students study Engineering.

What does this outcome establish?
questions.hint: Judge the actual sample composition separately from whether the process systematically favours a group.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Engineering is underrepresented in this draw.
  2. One imbalanced random draw does not prove that the procedure systematically favours other programmes.
  3. If both programme groups must be represented in chosen numbers, stratified selection is a suitable design for a future study.

options.label: The sample is imbalanced, but this one draw does not prove a systematically biased selection procedure
The random generator must be faulty
Every random sample must match all population percentages exactly
Cluster sampling always creates selection bias

questions.title: Library survey: from allocation to replies
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 900 Business and 600 Engineering students. It proportionally allocates 150 invitations and randomly selects distinct students within each programme.

There are 72 Business replies and 24 Engineering replies. Among all replies, 60 support longer library hours.

Find the invitation allocations, Engineering’s response rate, support among all respondents, and the most appropriate next step.
questions.hint: Keep the denominator tied to the group: allocations use 1,500; Engineering response uses Engineering invitations; overall respondent support uses 96 replies.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Business invitations = 900/1,500 × 150 = 90. Engineering invitations = 60.
  2. Engineering response rate = 24/60 × 100 = 40%.
  3. Total replies = 72 + 24 = 96. Respondent support = 60/96 × 100 = 62.50%.
  4. Follow up originally selected nonrespondents, prioritising Engineering’s lower response rate. Different response rates raise concern but do not themselves establish opinion bias.

options.label: Follow up selected nonrespondents, prioritising Engineering, with accessible ways to reply
Replace missing Engineering replies with Business volunteers
Declare that proportional invitations guarantee proportional responses
Report 62.5% as the exact college-wide support

extension.promptHtml: Optional: write two sentences describing the result and its limitation.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: Among the 96 respondents, 62.5% supported longer library hours. Engineering’s response rate was 40%, so we should follow up originally selected nonrespondents and investigate whether missing students have different views before making a college-wide claim.
rubric: State 62.5% with respondents as the reference group.
Identify the lower Engineering response rate without claiming that it proves bias.
Recommend follow-up of originally selected nonrespondents.

questions.title: Canteen survey: audit the headline
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 2,400 students. A survey invites 200 environmental-club members. 120 reply, and 84 support adding a smaller meal option.

The canteen headline reads: “70% of college students want smaller portions.” The actual proposal would keep the usual portion available.

Calculate the response rate, support among respondents, and the lowest possible support among all invitees. Then choose a defensible headline and one design repair.
questions.hint: Different percentages describe different groups. A club-only frame cannot establish a college-wide result.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Response rate = 120/200 × 100 = 60%.
  2. Respondent support = 84/120 × 100 = 70%.
  3. Minimum among invitees = 84/200 × 100 = 42% if none of the missing 80 supports.
  4. A defensible headline says: 70% of the 120 club respondents supported adding a smaller option.
  5. Use complete college lists with appropriate random selection and follow-up. More replies from only the club would not fix the original coverage problem.

options.label: 70% of all invitees certainly support the option
The survey proves smaller portions reduce food waste
70% of the 120 club respondents supported adding a smaller portion option
70% of all 2,400 students support smaller portions

fields.label: Best design repair for a college-wide opinion survey

options.label: Remove respondents who oppose smaller portions
Sample randomly from complete college lists and follow up selected nonrespondents

extension.promptHtml: Optional: write a brief corrected report about support. State one further type of evidence needed to assess whether smaller portions reduce waste.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: Among 120 environmental-club respondents, 70% supported adding a smaller option, but college-wide support remains unknown. A college-wide random survey with follow-up is needed. The waste claim requires actual leftover measurements under suitably comparable conditions; opinions about the option do not measure waste.
rubric: Limit the 70% figure to the 120 club respondents.
Identify club-only coverage or nonresponse as a limitation.
Keep opinion evidence separate from measurements of food waste.

questions.title: The research population changes
questions.promptHtml:
A researcher surveys every one of the 80 nurses in Hospital A. Their mean travel time is 32 minutes.

First the research concerns Hospital A’s nurses only. Later the same result is used to discuss all nurses employed by the city’s eight hospitals. Classify the same mean in each research question.
questions.hint: The data do not change. The target population does.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. For Hospital A’s nurses, 32 minutes is a parameter, because all members of that population were measured.
  2. For nurses across all eight hospitals, the same 32 minutes is a statistic from only part of the wider population.
  3. A complete survey of one hospital does not establish the city-wide mean.

questions.title: What a low response rate can establish
questions.promptHtml:
A simple random sample receives 300 invitations, and 60 people reply. No further information about nonrespondents is available.

A student writes: “The 20% response rate proves the estimated satisfaction level is biased downward.” Choose the best correction.
questions.hint: A low response rate raises a question about missing people. It does not reveal their opinions or the direction of any bias.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The response rate is correctly calculated: 60/300 × 100 = 20%.
  2. Low response raises concern, but bias depends on whether responding relates to satisfaction.
  3. The information does not establish that bias exists or predict its direction. Investigate and follow up missing respondents.

options.label: Low response raises concern, but neither bias nor its direction is established without relevant information about nonrespondents
Any response rate below 50% proves downward bias
Random invitation guarantees no nonresponse bias
A 20% response rate means exactly 80% are dissatisfied

questions.title: What is missing behind the percentage?
questions.promptHtml:
A university headline says: “81% support weekend teaching.” No other details appear.

Which information is most useful for assessing whether this supports a claim about all university students?
questions.hint: Look for who was eligible, how they were chosen, who replied, and what they were asked.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. We need the target population, selection method, invitation and response counts, and exact question with response options.
  2. These help assess coverage, nonresponse and wording.
  3. The percentage alone cannot establish a representative or accurate population estimate.

options.label: Only the number of decimal places in 81%
Only confirmation that the percentages add to 100%
Target population, selection procedure, invitation/reply counts, and exact wording/options
The chart colour and the report font

questions.title: Define a population with a place and a period
questions.promptHtml:
A transport office wants the mean delay of all bus departures from East Station during September. It randomly checks 48 of those departures.

Identify the target population and the selected sample.
questions.hint: The research question specifies a location, a time period and a unit: one bus departure.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The population is every bus departure from East Station during September.
  2. The sample is the 48 checked departures.
  3. The population does not include other stations or all months, and it is not a group of passengers.

options.label: All bus departures in every month
All bus departures from East Station during September
All passengers living in the city

questions.title: Inviting everyone and obtaining everyone’s data
questions.promptHtml:
A company has 420 current employees. It invites every employee to answer a questionnaire, but only 315 reply. The analyst calls the completed dataset a census of all current employees.

Assess the description and calculate how many employees did not reply.
questions.hint: A plan can attempt a census while the resulting data remain incomplete.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The company attempted a census by inviting all 420 employees.
  2. The completed dataset contains data from only 315 respondents, so it is not a complete census of all employees.
  3. The remaining 105 employees are still members of the target population.

options.label: A complete census because more than half replied
An attempted census with responses from only part of the population
A complete census because everyone was invited

questions.title: Population, contact list and respondents
questions.promptHtml:
A study concerns all 2,100 adults in a district. Its contact list contains 1,650 adults. Researchers randomly choose 100 people from that list and receive 74 replies.

Identify the target population and the observed respondents. Does the contact list itself contain the whole population?
questions.hint: The target group, the available list and the people whose data arrive are three different groups.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The target population is all 2,100 adults.
  2. The observed respondents are the 74 who replied.
  3. The contact list contains only 1,650 adults, so it leaves 450 members of the target population out.

fields.label: Population members absent from the contact list

questions.title: One patient can make several visits
questions.promptHtml:
A clinic asks: “What is the mean waiting time per appointment for all 900 appointments in June?” Some patients attend more than once. The clinic randomly selects 90 appointment records and checks the waiting time for each.

Choose the correct population and sampling unit.
questions.hint: Read whether the quantity is per patient or per appointment.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The population consists of the 900 June appointments.
  2. The sampling unit is one appointment. A patient with three appointments contributes three units to this appointment population.
  3. A study of mean waiting time per patient would be a different research question.

options.label: All people who have ever attended the clinic
One unique patient regardless of appointment count

questions.title: Two percentages in an audit
questions.promptHtml:
A warehouse contains 800 sealed boxes. A completed inventory records that exactly 40 of all 800 boxes have damaged labels. An inspector later randomly selects 50 boxes and finds 4 with damaged labels.

Classify the inventory percentage and the sample percentage for this warehouse’s current boxes.
questions.hint: A parameter describes the complete defined population. A statistic is calculated from a sample.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The inventory gives 40/800 × 100 = 5%, a parameter.
  2. The sample gives 4/50 × 100 = 8%, a statistic.
  3. The difference does not change the labels: their source groups determine the classification.

questions.title: A very large sample is still a sample
questions.promptHtml:
A researcher measures 980 of a university’s 1,000 laboratory instruments. The mean calibration error for the measured instruments is 0.06 units. The research concerns all 1,000 instruments.

Does measuring 98% of the population turn the reported sample mean into a population parameter?
questions.hint: The distinction depends on whether every population member is included, not on a high percentage cutoff.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. No. The 0.06-unit mean is a statistic because it uses only 980 instruments.
  2. The unmeasured 20 instruments could change the mean for all 1,000.
  3. A large sampling fraction may help estimation, but it does not make a sample mean a known population parameter.

options.label: It becomes a parameter whenever at least 90% are measured
It becomes a parameter because 0.06 has decimal places
The labels depend only on whether the mean is accurate
It remains a statistic because 20 population members were not measured

questions.title: An estimate can equal the population value
questions.promptHtml:
The known mean mass of a complete batch of 600 packages is 2.40 kg. A random sample of 30 packages also has a mean of 2.40 kg.

How should the two means be labelled?
questions.hint: Equal numerical values do not mean the numbers were calculated from the same group.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The mean calculated from all 600 packages is a parameter.
  2. The mean calculated from 30 packages is a statistic, even though its value happens to match the parameter.
  3. Classification is about which observations produced the number.

options.label: Both are parameters because the numbers agree
Both are statistics because both are averages
Full-batch mean: statistic; sample mean: parameter
Full-batch mean: parameter; sample mean: statistic

questions.title: Elapsed age and completed years
questions.promptHtml:
A research form records two different variables for each tree:

  • X: elapsed age measured in years, which could be 12.6 years.
  • Y: the number of complete years since planting, such as 12.

Classify X and Y.
questions.hint: An elapsed measurement and a count of completed units are different variable definitions.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. X is quantitative continuous: elapsed age is measured on a time scale.
  2. Y is quantitative discrete: the number of complete years can take only whole-number values.
  3. This differs from merely displaying a rounded continuous age.

questions.title: Measurements converted into bands
questions.promptHtml:
A sensor measures exact journey time. A report then stores only a band: under 10 minutes, 10–under 20 minutes, or 20 minutes or more.

Classify the original measurement and the stored band.
questions.hint: Classify what each column actually records. A category containing numbers is still a category.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Exact journey time is quantitative continuous.
  2. The stored band is an ordered categorical variable.
  3. The band identifies a range, not the exact journey time.

questions.title: An ordered response code
questions.promptHtml:
A survey codes safety ratings as 1 = very unsafe, 2 = unsafe, 3 = safe, and 4 = very safe.

Choose the most accurate description of the recorded ratings.
questions.hint: The code numbers identify ordered response labels. Their gaps are not measured amounts of safety.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The ratings are ordered categorical data.
  2. The code 4 represents a higher category than 2, but it does not establish that a respondent feels twice as safe.
  3. Writing numbers for category labels does not make their differences measured quantities.

options.label: Measurements showing that code 4 means twice the safety of code 2
Ordered categories whose numerical codes do not establish equal measured gaps

questions.title: A pharmacy record has three variables
questions.promptHtml:
A pharmacy records packaging type (bottle or blister pack), number of tablets in a pack, and measured mass of the filled pack.

Classify each recorded variable.
questions.hint: Separate a label, a count and a measurement.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Packaging type is categorical.
  2. Number of tablets is quantitative discrete.
  3. Measured mass is quantitative continuous, even if a display rounds the value.

questions.title: A player’s shirt and match record
questions.promptHtml:
A sports file records a player’s shirt number 18 and the number of goals scored, 3.

A student says both columns are quantitative because both contain whole numbers. Assess the columns.
questions.hint: Ask whether arithmetic differences represent an amount or merely a difference between labels.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The shirt number is a categorical identifier.
  2. The goal count is quantitative discrete.
  3. A player wearing 18 has not scored six times as many goals as someone wearing 3; shirt numbers do not measure performance.

questions.title: A continuous variable can include zero
questions.promptHtml:
A rain gauge measures rainfall depth in millimetres. It records 0.0 mm on dry days and values such as 2.7 mm on wet days.

Does the presence of zeros change rainfall depth into a categorical or discrete variable?
questions.hint: The kind of quantity being measured determines its type. One possible recorded value does not change it.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Rainfall depth remains quantitative continuous.
  2. Zero describes no measured rainfall, while positive depths can vary continuously.
  3. A separate variable such as “rain / no rain” would be categorical.

options.label: Quantitative continuous, including when a value is zero
Categorical because some days are dry
Discrete because zero is a whole number

questions.title: A measurement and a pass/fail decision
questions.promptHtml:
A quality test records the percentage of moisture in a grain sample, then labels it pass or fail using a fixed moisture limit.

Classify the moisture measurement and the decision label.
questions.hint: A decision based on a measurement is a different variable from the measurement itself.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The underlying moisture percentage is quantitative continuous.
  2. Pass/fail is categorical.
  3. Knowing only pass/fail does not reveal the exact moisture measurement.

questions.title: A uniformly shuffled list
questions.promptHtml:
A complete list contains 360 unique staff IDs. Software produces a random permutation in which every ordering is equally likely. Researchers take the first 24 IDs from that shuffled list.

Does this give a simple random sample of 24 staff members?
questions.hint: Taking the first entries of a uniformly shuffled complete list differs from taking the first entries of a fixed list.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Yes. Every group of 24 IDs is equally likely to occupy the first 24 positions.
  2. The complete list and uniform shuffle provide the random selection.
  3. No ID appears twice because the list is a permutation of unique IDs.

options.label: Yes: every group of 24 has the same chance after a uniform shuffle
No: taking the first entries can never be random
Yes: any alphabetical ordering is equivalent to a random shuffle
No: an SRS must include half the population

questions.title: Make a paper lottery valid
questions.promptHtml:
A small laboratory has 32 technicians and needs an SRS of 8 different technicians. It will use paper slips.

Choose the procedure that gives every group of eight an equal chance, assuming the mixing and drawing work fairly.
questions.hint: Each technician needs exactly one equally selectable slip, and the same person should not be selected twice.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Place one identical folded slip for each of the 32 unique IDs in a container, mix thoroughly, then draw eight without replacement.
  2. Drawing blindly prevents choosing by name or appearance.
  3. Equal treatment of the slips gives every group of eight the same chance under the stated assumptions.

options.label: Let the manager read the slips and choose eight
Return each selected slip and count repeated names as different technicians
Use one identical folded slip per technician, mix thoroughly, and blindly draw eight without replacement
Use two slips for supervisors and one for other technicians

questions.title: A generator with the wrong range
questions.promptHtml:
A student list has IDs 1–750. A research assistant uses a uniform generator set to 1–700 and draws 50 distinct IDs.

Explain why this is not an SRS of all 750 students, then choose a precise repair before contacting anyone.
questions.hint: Every possible sample from the defined population must have a chance. Check the generator’s endpoints.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Students with IDs 701–750 have zero chance under the proposed generator range.
  2. Reset the range to 1–750 and redraw all 50 distinct IDs uniformly.
  3. Adding a few hand-picked omitted students would not turn the existing selection into an SRS.

fields.label: Students with no chance under the proposed rule

options.label: Redraw 50 distinct IDs uniformly from the full range 1–750
Keep the draw and add the last five IDs
Use the same 1–700 range but draw 100 IDs

questions.title: Choose from the complete range of starts
questions.promptHtml:
A register has 1,056 students. Researchers need a systematic sample of 88. They will first choose a start uniformly from a consecutive range of valid positions.

Find the interval and select the correct range.
questions.hint: For this exact division, k = N/n. There are k possible starting positions: 1 through k inclusive.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. k = 1,056/88 = 12.
  2. The start must be selected uniformly from 1–12 inclusive.
  3. Using 1–11 would exclude one of the possible systematic sequences.

questions.title: Infer a sample from its fraction
questions.promptHtml:
A systematic survey selects 4% of 1,800 records, using a fixed interval and a random start. The population size is an exact multiple of the interval.

Find the sample size and interval.
questions.hint: First convert 4% to 0.04 and find n. Then calculate N/n.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sample size = 0.04 × 1,800 = 72.
  2. Interval = 1,800/72 = 25.
  3. Selecting one in every 25 records gives a fraction of 1/25 = 4%.

questions.title: The final position has one fewer jump
questions.promptHtml:
A list contains 960 records. A systematic sample of 80 uses start 9 and interval 12. A student computes the final ID as 9 + 80 × 12 = 969.

Correct the final ID and identify the error.
questions.hint: The starting ID already counts as the first selected record.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The 80th selection comes after 79 jumps.
  2. Final ID = 9 + 79 × 12 = 957.
  3. The student added 80 jumps, which would move to the 81st selection and past this list’s end.

options.label: The interval must always be one
The sample size should be added to the population size
Using 80 jumps instead of 79 after counting the start as the first selection

questions.title: A repeating ward pattern
questions.promptHtml:
A hospital list repeats in blocks of four records: Ward A, Ward B, Ward C, Ward D. Researchers choose a start uniformly from 1–8 and then take every eighth record.

With start 3, which ward appears in the sample? Which change directly breaks the list pattern while keeping systematic selection?
questions.hint: Adding eight moves forward by two full blocks of four, leaving the within-block position unchanged.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Positions 3, 11, 19, … all belong to Ward C.
  2. A uniform random shuffle of the complete record list before systematic selection breaks the fixed ward pattern.
  3. A random start alone still leaves each draw confined to one ward in this arrangement.

fields.label: Keep systematic selection but repair the pattern

options.label: Select a start of 11 although starts should be 1–8
Uniformly shuffle the complete list before choosing the random start and fixed interval
Collect more records using the unchanged repeating sequence

questions.title: What an incomplete selection record tells us
questions.promptHtml:
A report states: “We selected every 17th record, and the fourth selected ID was 61.” The total number of records is not reported.

Find the start and decide whether the exact sample size can be determined.
questions.hint: Three jumps precede the fourth selected record. The end of the list is a separate piece of information.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Start = 61 − 3 × 17 = 10.
  2. The exact sample size cannot be determined without the stopping rule or total list length.
  3. We know that at least four records were selected, but not how many later IDs were included.

fields.label: Can the exact sample size be determined?

options.label: Yes: a fourth selection proves there were exactly four
No: the list length or stopping point is missing

questions.title: Recover the interval from two selected positions
questions.promptHtml:
In a systematic sample, the third selected ID is 41 and the eighth selected ID is 131. The complete list contains 1,440 records, and selection continues to its end.

Find the interval, starting ID and sample size.
questions.hint: There are five equal jumps from the third to the eighth selection. Then work back two jumps to the start.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Interval = (131 − 41)/(8 − 3) = 90/5 = 18.
  2. Start = 41 − 2 × 18 = 5.
  3. The list contains 1,440/18 = 80 selected records. The final ID is 5 + 79 × 18 = 1,427.

questions.title: Is a particular ID in the sample?
questions.promptHtml:
A systematic sample starts at ID 14 and selects every 23rd record. The list contains 1,150 records.

Decide whether ID 336 is selected. If it is, give its position in the selected sample. Also decide whether ID 337 is selected.
questions.hint: Subtract the start. A selected ID differs from 14 by a whole-number multiple of 23. Sample position is one more than the number of jumps.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. (336 − 14)/23 = 322/23 = 14 whole jumps, so ID 336 is selected.
  2. It is the 15th selected record.
  3. (337 − 14)/23 is not a whole number, so 337 is not selected.

fields.label: Position of ID 336 in the sample

options.label: It depends on the respondent’s opinion

questions.title: Random systematic selection is not simple random selection
questions.promptHtml:
A list has 12 students. Choose a start uniformly from 1–3 and select every third position to obtain four students. The possible samples are:

  • 1, 4, 7, 10
  • 2, 5, 8, 11
  • 3, 6, 9, 12

How many different samples can this rule produce, and why is it not an SRS of four students?
questions.hint: The method can be random without allowing every group of four students.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The rule permits three samples, one for each start.
  2. A group such as 1, 2, 3, 4 can never occur.
  3. Thus the rule is systematic random sampling, but not an SRS of four individuals.

fields.label: Number of possible samples under this rule

options.label: Some groups of four have zero chance under the fixed-interval rule
The starting position was selected randomly
The sample includes more than one student

questions.title: Allocate across four shifts
questions.promptHtml:
A factory has 320 morning, 240 afternoon, 160 evening, and 80 night-shift employees. Select 100 employees proportionally across the four shifts.

Give each allocation. Use random selection within every complete shift list.
questions.hint: The total population is 800. Apply each shift’s share to the sample of 100.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Morning: 320/800 × 100 = 40.
  2. Afternoon: 240/800 × 100 = 30.
  3. Evening: 160/800 × 100 = 20.
  4. Night: 80/800 × 100 = 10. The four allocations sum to 100.

questions.title: Include enough members of a small programme
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 960 Business and 240 Engineering students. Researchers have 100 invitations and need at least 30 Engineering students selected for a programme comparison.

Would proportional allocation meet that minimum? Choose a valid stratified plan that uses all 100 invitations and meets the minimum.
questions.hint: First work out Engineering’s proportional allocation. A stratified sample can deliberately use a different allocation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Proportional Engineering allocation = 240/1,200 × 100 = 20, below the minimum of 30.
  2. Select 30 Engineering and 70 Business students, randomly and without replacement within the complete programme lists.
  3. This is stratified but not proportional. Overall estimates must account for the unequal population shares and selection probabilities.

options.label: Randomly select 20 Engineers and 80 Business students
Accept the first 30 Engineering volunteers and call it random stratified sampling
Randomly select one whole class without checking the programme requirement
Randomly select 30 distinct Engineers and 70 distinct Business students from their separate lists

questions.title: Round down, then distribute the remaining places
questions.promptHtml:
Three departments contain 170, 260 and 370 employees. Allocate a sample of 37 proportionally.

Round all ideal allocations down, then assign remaining places in order of the largest decimal remainders.
questions.hint: Calculate each group’s size divided by 800, multiplied by 37. The final integers must sum to 37.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Ideal allocations are 7.8625, 12.0250 and 17.1125.
  2. Rounding down gives 7 + 12 + 17 = 36.
  3. The first department has the largest remainder, 0.8625, so it receives the remaining place.
  4. The allocations are 8, 12 and 17, summing to 37.

questions.title: Check whether allocations are proportional
questions.promptHtml:
Three faculties contain 450, 750 and 300 students. Researchers randomly select 36, 60 and 24 respectively from their complete faculty lists.

Calculate the selection percentage in each faculty and decide whether this allocation is proportional.
questions.hint: Proportional allocation produces the same sampling fraction in every faculty.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 36/450 × 100 = 8%.
  2. 60/750 × 100 = 8%.
  3. 24/300 × 100 = 8%.
  4. The equal fractions confirm a proportional allocation: 120 students are selected from 1,500.

options.label: No: a proportion cannot be below 10%
Yes: every faculty has the same 8% selection fraction
No: proportional allocations must give equal numbers

questions.title: Correct totals do not make random selection
questions.promptHtml:
A company correctly allocates 48 invitations to Production and 32 to Sales in proportion to department sizes. The assistant then takes the first 48 names and first 32 names on fixed alphabetical lists.

What must change to make this a proportional stratified random sample?
questions.hint: Allocation decides how many. A separate step determines which people are selected.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Keep the correct allocations of 48 and 32.
  2. Number each complete department list and select the required number of distinct IDs uniformly at random within that department.
  3. Taking fixed early names systematically favours them, even when the group totals are correct.

options.label: Keep the allocations but randomly select 48 and 32 distinct IDs within the complete department lists
Increase both totals but continue taking the first names
Call the alphabetical lists random because no one volunteered

questions.title: Hospitals can define strata or clusters
questions.promptHtml:
Each nurse works at exactly one of 12 hospitals. Complete nurse lists are available.

  • Plan A: randomly select 10 different nurses within every hospital.
  • Plan B: randomly select three hospitals, then survey every nurse at those hospitals.

Classify both plans.
questions.hint: Look at whether every group contributes some people or only selected groups contribute everyone.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A is stratified random sampling: every hospital contributes selected nurses.
  2. B is cluster sampling: only selected hospitals contribute, and every nurse within each selected hospital is included.
  3. The name of the grouping variable does not determine the method; the selection procedure does.

options.label: Simple random selection of individual nurses

questions.title: The same sample size, different designs
questions.promptHtml:
A college has 30 classes of 20 students. Each student belongs to one class.

  • P: select 60 distinct IDs uniformly from the complete student list.
  • Q: randomly select three classes and include every student in them.

A student says both plans must be the same method because each selects 60 students. Assess the claim.
questions.hint: Sample size describes how many are selected. The method describes how they are selected.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. P is an SRS of individuals because every group of 60 IDs has the same chance.
  2. Q is cluster sampling: 3 × 20 = 60 students in whole selected classes.
  3. Equal sample sizes do not make the selection procedures equivalent.

questions.title: Small numbers from every village
questions.promptHtml:
A district has 18 villages. Within every village, a computer uniformly selects six different household IDs from that village’s complete list. The selected households are combined into one sample.

Name the design and calculate the selected sample size.
questions.hint: Using villages as groups does not automatically mean cluster sampling. Check which villages contribute and how households are chosen.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The villages act as strata, because random household selection occurs in every village.
  2. Sample size = 18 × 6 = 108 households.
  3. Without village population sizes, we cannot tell whether equal allocations are proportional.

options.label: Cluster sampling of selected whole villages
Simple random sampling from one complete district list
No: the village population sizes are not given
Yes: all equal allocations are proportional
No: stratified sampling can never be proportional

questions.title: An outdated contact list
questions.promptHtml:
A college wants current students’ views on transport. It randomly selects names from last year’s register, which includes graduates and omits newly enrolled students.

Choose the main design repair.
questions.hint: Random selection cannot repair a list that does not match the current target population.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Update and verify the register against the current enrolled-student population before drawing the sample.
  2. The old list both excludes new students and includes people outside the current target population.
  3. A larger draw from the same incorrect list would retain those coverage problems.

options.label: Build and verify a current register, then draw the random sample from it
Draw more names from last year’s list
Keep graduates because they are easier to contact
Delete replies from new students if they find the survey

questions.title: Choose a survey time that covers the target
questions.promptHtml:
A gym wants opinions from all current members. Staff invite only members entering between 10 a.m. and noon on weekdays, before any questionnaire is answered.

What is the main problem at this selection stage?
questions.hint: Ask who has no opportunity to be invited under the stated rule.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Members who attend only evenings or weekends are excluded from invitations.
