  2. This is a selection/coverage problem, not merely a failure of selected people to reply.
  3. Randomly select from the full current membership list, with accessible ways to respond.

options.label: Time of day cannot affect who is selected
The rule excludes members who attend outside those times
Nonresponse by all invited members is proved
Every invitation becomes a measurement error

questions.title: Duplicate names in a supposedly fair list
questions.promptHtml:
A staff list has 100 people. Ninety have one entry each, but ten managers accidentally have two entries each. One of the 110 rows is selected uniformly for an interview.

Compare a manager’s selection chance with an ordinary employee’s, then choose the repair.
questions.hint: The generator chooses rows. Two rows for one person give that person two chances.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. An ordinary employee has chance 1/110.
  2. Each duplicated manager has chance 2/110, which is two times the ordinary employee’s chance.
  3. Deduplicate the verified person list so that every eligible employee has exactly one unique entry, then draw again.

options.label: Keep duplicates because row selection is random
Remove duplicate person entries and randomly select from the verified unique list
Add more copies of all managers

questions.title: Who is more likely to return a travel survey?
questions.promptHtml:
A university randomly invites commuters to a survey. Suppose students with short journeys are more likely to reply than students with long journeys, with other relevant factors unchanged.

What bias risk does this create for mean journey time among replies?
questions.hint: The invited sample can be random while the responding group favours one kind of commuter.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. This creates a nonresponse bias risk.
  2. Short journeys are overrepresented among replies, so the respondent mean tends to be too low relative to the invited group’s mean under the stated condition.
  3. Follow-up should seek replies from originally selected nonrespondents.

options.label: A guarantee of no bias because invitations were random

fields.label: Likely direction under the stated condition

options.label: The direction must be upward and downward at the same time

questions.title: Strong opinions in a volunteer poll
questions.promptHtml:
A local website invites voluntary comments on a transport plan. People with strong opinions are more likely to contribute. The report does not say whether strong supporters or strong opponents contribute more often.

Identify the concern and decide whether the direction of support bias is known.
questions.hint: Knowing that participation depends on opinion does not necessarily tell you which side is overrepresented.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Self-selection creates a voluntary response bias concern.
  2. The given facts do not establish whether reported support is too high or too low.
  3. Both the participation pattern and its connection to support matter when judging direction.

options.label: Not determined from the information given

questions.title: Privacy and neutral wording solve different problems
questions.promptHtml:
A manager asks named staff, while watching them, “Our excellent new rota is fair, isn’t it?” Staff must answer aloud.

Select the pair of changes that directly addresses both leading wording and pressure to please the manager.
questions.hint: One problem is the question’s wording. Another is the way answers are collected.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Use a neutral question such as “How fair or unfair is the new rota?” with balanced options.
  2. Collect responses privately through a confidential process that does not expose individual answers to the manager.
  3. Changing only the number of respondents would not address either source of response bias.

options.label: Use neutral, balanced wording and collect answers privately without the manager watching
Keep the wording but print it in larger letters
Ask twice as many staff aloud

questions.title: Sampling and calibration address separate faults
questions.promptHtml:
A team selects fruit boxes by a valid random procedure. Its scale then adds 35 g to every mass reading.

Which statement correctly describes the remaining problem?
questions.hint: A fair selection procedure does not guarantee an accurate measurement instrument.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The scale introduces systematic measurement error despite the valid random selection.
  2. Check and calibrate the scale before using its readings as accurate masses.
  3. Choosing a new random sample alone would reproduce the same scale error.

options.label: More decimal places remove the 35 g error
The measurements remain systematically too high even though selection was random
Random selection automatically cancels a faulty scale
The scale fault changes the method to cluster sampling

questions.title: Zero spending is a valid response
questions.promptHtml:
A spending survey has 145 valid replies. Among them, 22 respondents report zero spending on a service. The analyst removes those replies because “zero means there is no useful information.”

How many valid records should remain, and what is the effect of removing genuine zeros on the reported mean when some remaining amounts are positive?
questions.hint: A valid zero is a measured amount. Compare the same positive total divided by a smaller number of respondents.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Keep all 145 valid replies, including the 22 zeros.
  2. Removing zeros leaves the same total spending but reduces the divisor from 145 to 123.
  3. With some positive spending, the resulting mean is higher. It no longer describes all valid respondents.

fields.label: Effect of deleting the genuine zeros

options.label: It decreases the reported mean spending
It increases the reported mean spending

questions.title: Make a recall question easier to answer accurately
questions.promptHtml:
A food survey asks students to recall exactly how many meals they skipped over the previous twelve months. Many respondents say they cannot remember.

Which change most directly addresses the measurement problem?
questions.hint: The issue concerns how accurately people can report the requested information, not just how they were selected.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A shorter, clearly defined recall period or a prospective meal diary reduces reliance on distant memory.
  2. The revised variable must be reported for its actual period, such as meals skipped during the next seven days.
  3. A larger sample answering the same difficult recall question would not automatically improve each answer’s accuracy.

options.label: Use a clearly defined short period with a meal diary, and report that period explicitly
Ask more students to guess the twelve-month total
Remove every student who is uncertain
Tell students to give a high number when unsure

questions.title: Random invitations but an inaccessible questionnaire
questions.promptHtml:
A survey randomly invites current employees from complete staff lists. The questionnaire is offered only in a language that one third of the selected staff cannot read.

What is the best repair for the invited survey?
questions.hint: Inclusion in the invitation list is not the same as being able to understand and answer the questionnaire.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Provide accurately translated, equivalent versions and accessible instructions to the originally selected staff.
  2. Language barriers may cause nonresponse or inaccurate answers related to staff group.
  3. Replacing selected staff with easy-to-reach speakers would change the selection process.

options.label: Remove staff who cannot read the questionnaire from the target population after selection
Recruit only volunteers who speak the questionnaire language
Assume random invitations guarantee understandable questions
Provide equivalent translations and support so the originally selected staff can respond

questions.title: Response categories that do not cover everyone
questions.promptHtml:
A survey asks for a student’s main transport mode but offers only car and bus. Students who walk or cycle must choose one of those two options to submit.

Identify the problem and choose a repair.
questions.hint: Respondents need an option that describes their actual situation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The response categories omit valid transport modes and force incorrect answers.
  2. Add relevant categories such as walking and cycling, with a suitable “other” option if needed.
  3. Sampling more students would not repair the forced misclassification.

options.label: Incomplete answer options create inaccurate recorded categories
The survey is necessarily an SRS
The sample interval is too short
All travel variables must be continuous
Keep the choices and collect more forced answers
Offer relevant transport categories and an appropriate other option

questions.title: One protocol for all observers
questions.promptHtml:
Two researchers record patient waiting time. Researcher A starts timing at reception check-in. Researcher B starts when the patient sits in the waiting room. Both stop when the consultation begins.

What change most directly makes their measurements comparable?
questions.hint: The observers are using different operational definitions of the same named variable.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Agree one precise start event and end event, train both observers, and use that definition consistently.
  2. Different start events create measurements of different time intervals.
  3. Randomly sampling patients does not make inconsistent measurement definitions equivalent.

options.label: Use larger sample sizes while keeping different definitions
Ask each researcher to use whichever definition is easiest
Define and use the same start and end events for every observation
Average the two researchers’ instructions without changing them

questions.title: A selected person is unavailable on the first visit
questions.promptHtml:
A household survey randomly selects addresses. Interviewers visit on a weekday morning. If nobody answers, they immediately substitute the neighbouring address and never return.

Choose the best correction to retain the original selection plan.
questions.hint: Availability at one visit may be related to household characteristics. A neighbour is not the originally selected household.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Attempt the originally selected addresses again at different times, such as evenings or weekends, using accessible contact options.
  2. Immediate neighbour substitution changes which households enter the responding group.
  3. Document remaining nonresponse rather than assuming the substituted households are equivalent.

options.label: Always choose whichever neighbouring household is home
Visit only addresses known to have retired residents
Count a locked door as a negative survey answer
Return to the originally selected addresses at varied times and document nonresponse

questions.title: A unit error in otherwise careful measurements
questions.promptHtml:
A lab correctly measures temperatures, but one device exports degrees Fahrenheit while another exports degrees Celsius. The spreadsheet combines them as if every entry were Celsius.

What should be repaired before analysis?
questions.hint: The observations need a consistent unit and a verified record of their source.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Identify the source unit for each record and convert all valid readings to one common unit using the correct conversion.
  2. Check the export settings and retain unit labels to prevent recurrence.
  3. Averaging the unconverted numbers would combine different measurement scales.

options.label: Randomly delete half the Fahrenheit records
Add more measurements in both units without labels
Treat every numerical entry as directly comparable
Verify each source unit and convert all readings correctly to one common unit

questions.title: Selection and nonresponse can both matter
questions.promptHtml:
A survey aims to describe library satisfaction among all currently enrolled college students, but invites only library users. Among those invited, students unhappy with the library are much more likely to reply.

Identify the problem at each stage.
questions.hint: First ask who can be invited. Then ask who replies among the invitees.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Restricting invitations to library users creates a selection/coverage problem for a claim about all students.
  2. Different response likelihoods linked to satisfaction create nonresponse bias among invitees.
  3. A repair should broaden the sampling frame and follow up the originally selected nonrespondents.

options.label: Coverage excludes students who do not use the library

questions.title: A question has fewer answers than the questionnaire
questions.promptHtml:
A survey invites 400 people. 250 return questionnaires, but only 200 answer the support question. Among those 200, 132 support the proposal.

Calculate the questionnaire response rate and support among people who answered the support question. Give percentages to two decimal places.
questions.hint: A returned questionnaire and an answered item are different denominators. Use 200 for the stated support percentage.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Questionnaire response rate = 250/400 × 100 = 62.50%.
  2. Support among item respondents = 132/200 × 100 = 66.00%.
  3. The missing support answers from 50 returned questionnaires cannot be assumed to mean opposition or support.

questions.title: Combine response counts before calculating a rate
questions.promptHtml:
A survey sends 120 invitations to Department A and gets 90 replies. It sends 80 invitations to Department B and gets 40 replies.

Calculate each response rate and the combined response rate. Is the combined rate simply the unweighted mean of the two department rates?
questions.hint: For the combined rate, add replies and divide by all invitations. The department invitation counts differ.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A: 90/120 × 100 = 75%.
  2. B: 40/80 × 100 = 50%.
  3. Combined: (90 + 40)/(120 + 80) × 100 = 65%.
  4. The unweighted mean is 62.5%, which gives equal importance to departments with unequal invitation counts.

options.label: Total replies divided by total invitations
Always take the unweighted average of subgroup rates
Divide total invitations by total replies

questions.title: Even the highest possible support is below half
questions.promptHtml:
Of 300 invitees, 240 reply. Exactly 75 respondents support a plan, and the other respondents do not support it.

Find the minimum and maximum possible support percentages among all invitees. Could more than half of the invitees support the plan?
questions.hint: There are 60 missing views. Add all 60 to the known supporters for the maximum.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Minimum = 75/300 × 100 = 25%.
  2. Maximum = (75 + 60)/300 × 100 = 45%.
  3. Even if every nonrespondent supports, support reaches only 45%. A majority among these 300 invitees is therefore ruled out.
  4. These are logical bounds for invitees, not a confidence interval for a wider population.

fields.label: Could more than half of the invitees support?

options.label: Yes: every respondent must be a supporter
No: even the maximum is only 45%
Yes: any missing replies make a majority possible

questions.title: Recover the invitation count
questions.promptHtml:
A report says the survey received 156 replies, giving an exact 65% response rate. Of the respondents, 117 supported the proposal.

Find how many people were invited and calculate support among respondents.
questions.hint: If 156 is 65% of the invitation total, divide by 0.65. The support denominator is still the 156 replies.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Invitations = 156/0.65 = 240.
  2. Respondent support = 117/156 × 100 = 75%.
  3. The 65% and 75% rates describe different stages of the survey.

questions.title: Higher response and higher support are different claims
questions.promptHtml:
Two branches survey their own customers:

  • A: 180 invited, 126 replied, 63 supported.
  • B: 150 invited, 90 replied, 63 supported.

Find each response rate and each support percentage among respondents. Which branch has the higher respondent-support percentage?
questions.hint: Both branches have 63 supporters, but they have different numbers of respondents.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A response = 126/180 × 100 = 70%; A support = 63/126 × 100 = 50%.
  2. B response = 90/150 × 100 = 60%; B support = 63/90 × 100 = 70%.
  3. B has the higher support percentage among respondents, despite the lower response rate.

options.label: The two must be equal because supporter counts match

questions.title: Same centre, different spread
questions.promptHtml:
In a repeated-sampling simulation, the known population percentage is 40%.

  • Procedure P produces 39%, 40%, 41%.
  • Procedure Q produces 32%, 40%, 48%.

Which procedure is more precise in this illustration? Do the listed results show a shift in either procedure’s centre away from 40%?
questions.hint: Compare spread separately from the location of the centre.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. P has the smaller spread, so it is more precise in the illustration.
  2. Both sets are centred at 40%, so neither shows a shifted centre here.
  3. Precision concerns consistency, while closeness to the true value concerns accuracy. A few illustrative results alone do not prove an underlying method is unbiased.

options.label: Both are at the known 40% value

questions.title: A consistent offset from the truth
questions.promptHtml:
A device measures a reference object whose true length is 100.0 mm. Repeated readings are 104.9, 105.0 and 105.1 mm.

Choose the best description of these readings and the most useful next step.
questions.hint: A very small spread can coexist with a substantial distance from a known reference value.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The readings are precise but inaccurate in this illustration: they cluster closely around 105.0 mm rather than 100.0 mm.
  2. Check the device’s calibration against the known reference.
  3. Taking many more readings with the same offset would not remove that systematic discrepancy.

options.label: Precise but inaccurate relative to the reference
Check and correct calibration against the reference
Print the same readings with extra decimal places
Assume consistency proves the reference is 105.0 mm

questions.title: When the true value is not known
questions.promptHtml:
Two procedures estimate an unknown population mean. Repeated estimates from P are 28, 29, 30, while those from Q are 24, 29, 34. No trustworthy population value is available.

What comparison can be made directly from these results?
questions.hint: Spread can be compared without knowing the truth. Accuracy requires information about the target value.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. P has the narrower spread and is more precise in the listed results.
  2. Both illustrated centres are 29, but the true population mean is unknown.
  3. We cannot determine their closeness to the truth from these results alone.

options.label: P is more precise here, but closeness to the true value cannot be established
P is certainly accurate because its range is smaller
Q must be accurate because its range is larger
The true population mean must equal 29

questions.title: More clusters with the same number of people
questions.promptHtml:
A study can sample 200 people in either of two ways. It uses random selection at the relevant stages.

  • Plan A: 20 people from each of 10 selected neighbourhoods.
  • Plan B: 100 people from each of two selected neighbourhoods.

Suppose people within a neighbourhood have very similar views, while neighbourhoods differ substantially. Which plan is likely to provide more information about between-neighbourhood differences?
questions.hint: The number of people is the same, but the number of distinct neighbourhoods is not.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Plan A covers 10 neighbourhoods, compared with two for B.
  2. Under the stated similarity pattern, the wider spread across neighbourhoods is likely to improve information and precision.
  3. This is a reasoned comparison under the stated conditions, not a guarantee of a perfectly representative draw.

fields.label: More informative about neighbourhood differences under these conditions

options.label: The designs must be equally precise because both contain 200 people

questions.title: A method that fits available lists
questions.promptHtml:
A field team has a complete list of 80 villages and can obtain complete household lists for villages it visits. It cannot afford to visit more than four villages, and it does not have a single district-wide list of households.

Choose a feasible probability design and its main limitation.
questions.hint: Choose a random procedure using the list that exists, while respecting the travel constraint.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Randomly select four distinct villages from all 80 and attempt every household in those villages using their complete lists.
  2. This is a feasible cluster design under the four-village constraint.
  3. Only four villages may provide limited information about differences across villages, reducing precision when households within villages are similar.

options.label: Randomly select four distinct villages and attempt every listed household in each
Choose the nearest four villages without randomness
Claim an SRS of all households without any way to list or select them
Survey only village leaders as if they were every household
Visiting fewer villages guarantees exact population values
Four selected villages may capture limited between-village variation
Cluster sampling is automatically biased under any random selection

questions.title: Increase sample size or repair bias?
questions.promptHtml:
Plan X uses a valid random sample and an accurate instrument. Plan Y uses a larger sample but an instrument that consistently overstates each measurement.

Which statement correctly separates the effects of sample size and measurement bias?
questions.hint: More observations can reduce chance variation under suitable sampling conditions. They do not calibrate an instrument.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Increasing the size of an otherwise comparable valid random sample generally improves precision by reducing random sampling variation.
  2. Plan Y’s systematic measurement error remains unless the instrument is repaired or appropriately corrected.
  3. Therefore, larger sample size alone is not a guarantee of greater accuracy.

options.label: A larger valid random sample can improve precision, but does not by itself remove systematic measurement error
Any larger sample is automatically more accurate
Sample size and calibration are the same concept
A faulty instrument becomes accurate once 1,000 readings are taken

questions.title: Budget and a sampling trade-off
questions.promptHtml:
Two random survey plans each interview 160 trainees.

  • Plan A visits 32 centres.
  • Plan B visits eight centres, with more trainees interviewed per centre.

Cost is ¥75 per visited centre plus ¥15 per trainee. The budget is ¥3,500.

Calculate each cost and select the defensible decision from the options. Assume trainees within the same centre may have similar views.
questions.hint: Add the visit cost and interview cost. A feasible plan still has statistical limitations.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A costs 32 × 75 + 160 × 15 = ¥4,800, over budget.
  2. B costs 8 × 75 + 160 × 15 = ¥3,000, within budget.
  3. B is feasible, while acknowledging that concentration in fewer centres may reduce precision because of within-centre similarity.

options.label: A fits the budget and has no possible limitations
B guarantees exact population opinions because it is cheaper
Both plans must give identical results because they interview 160 trainees
B fits the budget, but fewer centres may reduce precision

questions.title: A regional result used for a national headline
questions.promptHtml:
A survey randomly samples residents from one coastal city. All selected residents respond, and 64% support a ferry expansion. The headline says, “64% of the country supports the ferry expansion.”

What is the main unsupported step in the headline?
questions.hint: A well-run survey can still answer only the research question its sampling population supports.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The survey’s random selection covered one city, not the country.
  2. Complete response in that city does not establish national support.
  3. A defensible description identifies the surveyed city and sample, with population estimation limited to an appropriate target and design.

options.label: Using random selection within the city
Extending one city’s survey result to the whole country without national sampling evidence

questions.title: A statement justified by complete sample response
questions.promptHtml:
A researcher selects an SRS of 200 students from a complete college register. Every selected student responds. Exactly 146 support a proposal.

Which statement accurately describes what was observed and its relationship to the college?
questions.hint: Complete response removes missing replies within this selected sample, but it does not make the sample a census.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Observed support = 146/200 × 100 = 73%.
  2. This is the exact percentage among the 200 respondents.
  3. It can estimate college support under the stated design, but random sampling variation means the college percentage is not proved to equal exactly 73%.

options.label: The result is unusable because samples never inform populations
73% of sampled students supported; this estimates college support without proving an exact population value
Exactly 73% of all college students support, with no uncertainty
The sample is a census because response was complete

questions.title: Association in a patient survey
questions.promptHtml:
A survey finds that patients who use a clinic’s reminder app report fewer missed appointments than patients who do not use it. Patients chose whether to use the app, and the survey did not control for other differences between the groups.

Which conclusion is justified?
questions.hint: Groups formed by personal choice may differ for reasons other than the app.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The survey shows an association between app use and reported missed appointments.
  2. It does not isolate a causal app effect, because app users and non-users may differ in organisation, schedules or other relevant characteristics.
  3. A causal claim requires a design and evidence that address these alternative explanations.

options.label: An association proves that the app has no effect
App users reported fewer missed appointments, but the survey alone does not establish that the app caused the difference
The app is proved to prevent missed appointments
The groups must be identical because both are clinic patients

questions.title: Equal samples from unequal programmes
questions.promptHtml:
A college is 80% Business and 20% Engineering. A survey randomly selects 50 students within each programme, and all reply. Support is 90% among the Business respondents and 30% among the Engineering respondents.

The analyst reports the unweighted combined sample support, 60%, as an estimate of college-wide support. What should be considered?
questions.hint: The sample gives both programmes half the observations, even though their population shares are unequal.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The unweighted sample has equal programme shares, unlike the college.
  2. An overall estimate should account for the 80% and 20% population shares under this stratified design.
  3. For illustration, 0.80 × 90% + 0.20 × 30% = 78%, a population-share-weighted estimate. It is still an estimate, not an exact census result.

options.label: Equal group sample sizes always preserve population shares
The 60% must be exact because each group was randomly sampled
Remove the smaller population group entirely
Account for unequal population shares before using the equal-group sample as an overall estimate

questions.title: The largest category is not necessarily a majority
questions.promptHtml:
All 150 survey respondents choose exactly one preferred opening time. 63 choose 7 a.m., 51 choose 8 a.m., and 36 choose 9 a.m.

A report says, “A majority of respondents prefer 7 a.m.” Calculate the 7 a.m. percentage and choose a corrected statement.
questions.hint: A majority means more than half. The largest category need not pass 50%.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 7 a.m. support = 63/150 × 100 = 42%.
  2. It is the largest category, but not a majority of respondents.
  3. A corrected statement is: 7 a.m. was the most commonly selected option among the respondents, at 42%.

options.label: A majority preferred 7 a.m. because 63 is the largest count
All students in the population prefer 7 a.m.
7 a.m. was the most selected option among respondents, but fewer than half chose it

questions.title: An opinion question cannot measure an outcome
questions.promptHtml:
Among 180 respondents, 126 say they expect a proposed recycling campaign to reduce waste. The organiser writes, “The survey proves waste will fall by 70%.” No waste amounts have been measured.

Identify what the 70% actually describes and what evidence the outcome claim needs.
questions.hint: The percentage of people expecting a change is not the percentage change in the amount of waste.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 126/180 × 100 = 70% describes the respondents who expect a reduction.
  2. It is not a measured or proved 70% reduction in waste.
  3. Assessing the outcome requires waste measurements under a suitable comparison design that addresses other influences.

options.label: Respondents who expect the campaign to reduce waste
The guaranteed reduction in waste mass
The share of all city residents who recycle
The response rate, regardless of invitation count

fields.label: Needed evidence for a waste-reduction claim

options.label: Measurements of waste under a suitable comparison design
More opinions alone, treated as measured waste
A more colourful chart of the same opinions
Changing the question wording to require agreement

questions.title: Summarise daily service requests
questions.promptHtml:
A help desk receives the following numbers of service requests over six days:

12, 14, 14, 15, 17, 18

Find the mean, median and mode. Give the mean and median to 1 decimal place; give the mode as a whole number.
questions.hint: The data are already ordered. With six values, the median is the average of the third and fourth values.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total = 12 + 14 + 14 + 15 + 17 + 18 = 90. Mean = 90 ÷ 6 = 15.0 requests.
  2. Median = (14 + 15) ÷ 2 = 14.5 requests.
  3. 14 occurs twice, more often than any other value, so the mode is 14 requests.

questions.title: Reduce the effect of extreme waiting times
questions.promptHtml:
Ten waiting times, in minutes, are:

8, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 20, 44

Calculate the trimmed mean after removing 20% of the observations from each end. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: 20% of 10 is 2. Remove the two smallest and the two largest observations, then average what remains.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Remove 8 and 11 from the lower end, and 20 and 44 from the upper end.
  2. The remaining six values are 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 and 17. Their sum is 87.
  3. Trimmed mean = 87 ÷ 6 = 14.5 minutes. This reduces the influence of the extreme 44-minute wait.

questions.title: Describe the spread of delivery times
questions.promptHtml:
Eight delivery times, in minutes, are already ordered:

10, 12, 15, 18, 20, 24, 28, 34

Use the n + 1 method: Q1 is at position 0.25(n + 1), and Q3 at position 0.75(n + 1). Interpolate between neighbouring values.

Find the range, Q1, Q3 and IQR. Give all answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: For n = 8, the quartile positions are 2.25 and 6.75. A fractional position tells you how far to move between two values.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Range = 34 − 10 = 24.00 minutes.
  2. Q1 position = 0.25(8 + 1) = 2.25. Q1 = 12 + 0.25(15 − 12) = 12.75 minutes.
  3. Q3 position = 0.75(8 + 1) = 6.75. Q3 = 24 + 0.75(28 − 24) = 27.00 minutes.
  4. IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 27 − 12.75 = 14.25 minutes. This describes the spread of the middle 50% of the observations.

questions.title: Find a waiting-time percentile
questions.promptHtml:
Nine waiting times, in minutes, are:

5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 17, 19, 24

Find the 65th percentile using position (65/100)(n + 1), with linear interpolation. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: The percentile position is 6.5. Find the value halfway between the sixth and seventh observations.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Position = 0.65(9 + 1) = 6.5.
  2. The sixth value is 14 and the seventh is 17.
  3. P65 = 14 + 0.5(17 − 14) = 15.5 minutes using the specified percentile convention.

questions.title: Measure variation across all batches
questions.promptHtml:
A factory produced exactly four batches today. Their defect counts were:

4, 6, 8, 10

Treat these four batches as the entire population for today. Calculate the population variance σ² and population standard deviation σ. Give both to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Find the mean, square each deviation from it, and divide the sum of squared deviations by N = 4.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Population mean μ = (4 + 6 + 8 + 10) ÷ 4 = 7.
  2. Squared deviations: (4 − 7)² + (6 − 7)² + (8 − 7)² + (10 − 7)² = 9 + 1 + 1 + 9 = 20.
  3. Population variance σ² = 20 ÷ 4 = 5.00 defects².
  4. Population standard deviation σ = √5 = 2.236067… = 2.24 defects. Standard deviation is expressed in the original units.

questions.title: Estimate variation in battery life
questions.promptHtml:
A random sample of five batteries has operating times, in hours, of:

8, 10, 12, 14, 16

Calculate the sample variance s² and sample standard deviation s. Give both to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: These batteries are a sample. Divide the sum of squared deviations by n − 1, not by n.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sample mean x̄ = (8 + 10 + 12 + 14 + 16) ÷ 5 = 12 hours.
  2. Sum of squared deviations = (−4)² + (−2)² + 0² + 2² + 4² = 16 + 4 + 0 + 4 + 16 = 40.
  3. Sample variance s² = 40 ÷ (5 − 1) = 10.00 hours².
  4. Sample standard deviation s = √10 = 3.162277… = 3.16 hours. The n − 1 denominator is used because we are estimating population variance from a sample.

questions.title: Compare relative consistency
questions.promptHtml:
Two production lines have the following daily output summaries:

Daily output in units
LineMeanStandard deviation
A504
B808

Calculate CV = (standard deviation ÷ mean) × 100 for each line. Give percentages to 1 decimal place, then identify the line with less variation relative to its mean.
questions.hint: Compare the coefficients of variation, not just the standard deviations. The smaller CV means less relative variation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Line A: CV = (4 ÷ 50) × 100 = 8.0%.
  2. Line B: CV = (8 ÷ 80) × 100 = 10.0%.
  3. Line A is more consistent relative to its mean because its CV is smaller.

questions.title: Recognise a long tail
questions.promptHtml:
Seven customer service times, in minutes, are:

8, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 40

Which direction of skewness does this pattern suggest, and which statement about the mean and median is correct?
questions.hint: The unusually large value pulls the mean towards the high end, but it has little effect on the middle observation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Most observations lie between 8 and 12, while 40 creates a long tail to the right: the data suggest positive (right) skewness.
  2. The median is the fourth value, 10 minutes. The mean is 100 ÷ 7 = 14.2857… minutes.
  3. Therefore, the mean is greater than the median for this dataset.

questions.title: Interpret a kurtosis measure
questions.promptHtml:
A report gives a distribution’s Pearson kurtosis as 5.4. Under this convention, a normal distribution has kurtosis 3.

Calculate excess kurtosis to 1 decimal place and choose the appropriate description.
questions.hint: Excess kurtosis = Pearson kurtosis − 3. Positive excess kurtosis is described as leptokurtic.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Excess kurtosis = 5.4 − 3 = 2.4.
  2. It is positive, so the distribution is called leptokurtic relative to the normal benchmark.
  3. Kurtosis describes the influence of extreme deviations from the mean; it should not be interpreted simply as the height of the central peak.

fields.label: Description relative to the normal benchmark

questions.title: Read a box plot
questions.promptHtml:
The box plot shows delivery times. The labelled values are in minutes.

Read the median, calculate the upper outlier fence Q3 + 1.5 × IQR, and decide whether 47 minutes is an outlier by this rule. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: The line inside the box is the median. The box extends from Q₁ = 14 to Q₃ = 26.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The central line gives a median of 20 minutes.
  2. IQR = 26 − 14 = 12 minutes. Upper fence = 26 + 1.5(12) = 44 minutes.
  3. 47 is greater than 44, so 47 minutes is an upper outlier. The whisker ends at 38, the largest observed value that is not an outlier.

questions.title: Quartiles using the n + 1 rule (1)
questions.promptHtml: Ordered values: 3, 5, 8, 12, 14, 18, 23. Find the range, Q1, Q3 and IQR. Use positions (n + 1)/4 and 3(n + 1)/4, with linear interpolation between adjacent values.
questions.hint: A fractional position tells you how far to move between the two adjacent observations.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Range = 23 − 3 = 20.
  2. Q1 position = 0.25 × (7 + 1) = 2. This is observation 2, giving Q1 = 5.
  3. Q3 position = 0.75 × (7 + 1) = 6. This is observation 6, giving Q3 = 18.
  4. IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 18 − 5 = 13.

questions.title: Quartiles using the n + 1 rule (2)

questions.solutionHtml:

  2. Q1 position = 0.25 × (8 + 1) = 2.25. Between observations 2 and 3: Q1 = 4 + 0.25 × (6 − 4) = 4.5.
  3. Q3 position = 0.75 × (8 + 1) = 6.75. Between observations 6 and 7: Q3 = 13 + 0.75 × (17 − 13) = 16.

questions.title: Apply the 1.5 × IQR rule (3)
questions.promptHtml: Q1 = 5 and Q3 = 9. Find the lower and upper outlier fences. Which of the observations -2 and 14 lie strictly outside those fences?
questions.hint: Fences are Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Equality with a fence is not outside.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. IQR = 4; 1.5 × IQR = 6.0.
  2. Lower fence = -1.0; upper fence = 15.0.
  3. Classification: -2.

questions.title: Apply the 1.5 × IQR rule (4)
questions.promptHtml: Q1 = 100 and Q3 = 120. Find the lower and upper outlier fences. Which of the observations 69 and 151 lie strictly outside those fences?
questions.hint: Fences are Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. Equality with a fence is not outside.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. IQR = 20; 1.5 × IQR = 30.0.
  2. Lower fence = 70.0; upper fence = 150.0.
  3. Classification: Both listed observations.

questions.title: A very high income
questions.promptHtml: Most incomes are around ¥5000, but one income is ¥200000. Which measure usually better describes a typical person’s income?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The median is resistant to an extreme high value; the mean is pulled upward.

questions.title: A long right tail
questions.promptHtml: Waiting times have many low values and a few very large values. The distribution has:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The tail extends toward the larger values, so the skew is positive.

questions.title: A long left tail
questions.promptHtml: Most exam scores are high, with a few unusually low scores. The distribution is most plausibly:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The few low scores extend the left tail.

questions.title: Mean compared with median
questions.promptHtml: In a typical strongly right-skewed distribution, which relationship is commonly expected?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Large observations in the right tail tend to pull the mean above the median; this is a typical pattern, not a universal theorem.

questions.title: Zero standard deviation
questions.promptHtml: A dataset has standard deviation zero. What follows?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Zero squared deviations mean every observation equals the mean; that common value need not be zero.

questions.title: Units of variance
questions.promptHtml: Mass is measured in grams. What are the units of variance and standard deviation?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Variance squares the deviations; taking its square root restores the original units.

questions.title: A more extreme maximum
questions.promptHtml: Only the largest observation is increased substantially, and Q1 and Q3 remain unchanged. What happens?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Range uses the maximum; IQR uses Q3 − Q1, which is unchanged here.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: Range increases; IQR stays the same

options.value: Range increases; IQR stays the same
options.label: Range increases; IQR stays the same

questions.title: Specify the convention
questions.promptHtml: Using Pearson kurtosis (normal distribution = 3), a distribution has kurtosis 5. Its excess kurtosis is:
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Excess kurtosis equals Pearson kurtosis minus 3: 5 − 3 = 2.

questions.title: Interpret excess kurtosis
questions.promptHtml: A distribution has positive excess kurtosis. Which statement is most appropriate?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Kurtosis concerns standardized fourth-moment/tail behaviour, not the direction of skew or sign of the mean.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: Its kurtosis exceeds the normal benchmark, commonly associated with heavier tails

options.value: Its kurtosis exceeds the normal benchmark, commonly associated with heavier tails
options.label: Its kurtosis exceeds the normal benchmark, commonly associated with heavier tails

questions.title: Read the middle half
questions.promptHtml: A box plot has Q1 = 14 and Q3 = 26. Which interval represents the middle 50% of the distribution?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. The box runs from the 25th to the 75th percentile.

questions.title: A mean of zero
questions.promptHtml: A variable has mean 0 and SD 4. Can CV = SD/mean × 100 be calculated?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. CV is undefined at a zero mean; it is not appropriate for all measurement scales.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: No; the expression divides by zero

options.value: No; the expression divides by zero
options.label: No; the expression divides by zero

questions.title: A constant calibration shift
questions.promptHtml: Every measurement is increased by 5. What happens to the mean and SD?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Adding a constant shifts both data and mean equally, leaving all deviations unchanged.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: Mean rises by 5; SD is unchanged

options.value: Mean rises by 5; SD is unchanged
options.label: Mean rises by 5; SD is unchanged

options.value: Mean is unchanged; SD rises by 5
options.label: Mean is unchanged; SD rises by 5

questions.title: Change the measurement scale
questions.promptHtml: Every measurement is multiplied by 3. What happens to SD and variance?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Deviations triple, their squares multiply by 9, and the square root gives an SD multiplier of 3.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: SD is multiplied by 3; variance by 9

options.value: SD is multiplied by 3; variance by 9
options.label: SD is multiplied by 3; variance by 9

questions.title: Combine unequal groups
questions.promptHtml: One group has 10 observations with mean 20; another has 30 with mean 40. What is the combined mean?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. Combined total = 10 × 20 + 30 × 40 = 1400; divide by 40 observations to get 35.

questions.title: Choose the denominator
questions.promptHtml: Six randomly selected patients are used to estimate variation in a large patient population. Which denominator belongs in the sample variance formula?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. For sample variance, divide the sum of squared deviations by n − 1 = 5.

questions.title: Same mean, different spread
questions.promptHtml: Two wards have the same mean waiting time. Ward A has SD 2 minutes and B has SD 9 minutes. Which conclusion is supported?
questions.hint: Identify the definition that fits the information given.
questions.solutionHtml: 1. SD describes dispersion; it does not establish the order of every individual observation or sample sizes.

fields.label: Choose the best answer
fields.answer: A has less variation around its mean

options.value: A has less variation around its mean
options.label: A has less variation around its mean

options.value: Every A patient waits less than every B patient
options.label: Every A patient waits less than every B patient

options.value: B has exactly 4.5 times as many patients
options.label: B has exactly 4.5 times as many patients

questions.title: Recover a missing observation
questions.promptHtml: Five readings have mean 12. Four readings are 8, 10, 13 and 14. Find the missing reading.
questions.hint: Find the required total and subtract the known values.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Required total = 5 × 12 = 60.
  2. Known total = 45; missing reading = 60 − 45 = 15.

questions.title: Correct a data-entry error
questions.promptHtml: The reported mean of 10 readings is 18. One value was entered as 42 instead of 24. Find the corrected mean.
questions.hint: Correct the total; the number of readings stays the same.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Reported total = 10 × 18 = 180.
  2. Corrected total = 180 − 42 + 24 = 162; mean = 162/10 = 16.2.

questions.title: Use a sum of squared deviations
questions.promptHtml: For a sample of 9 readings, the sum of squared deviations from the sample mean is 128. Find the sample variance and SD.
questions.hint: Use n − 1 in the denominator.

questions.title: Fence versus whisker
questions.promptHtml: A modified box plot uses Q1 = 10, Q3 = 18, and whiskers at the most extreme non-outlier observations. The upper fence is 30. Observed values above Q3 are 20, 24, 29 and 35. Where does the upper whisker end?
questions.hint: The whisker ends at an observed value within the fence, not necessarily at the fence itself.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Upper fence = 18 + 1.5 × 8 = 30.
  2. 35 is an outlier. The largest observed value within the fence is 29, so the whisker ends at 29.

questions.title: The same records, two different targets
questions.promptHtml:
A clinic records the waiting times of all 12 patients in one morning. The sum of squared deviations from their mean is 132 min².

First describe only those 12 patients. Then use these records as a sample to estimate variation among all patients this month. Select the variance divisor for each purpose. Assume the sampling limitations are considered separately.
questions.hint: Ask which group the question is trying to describe. The number of records alone does not decide the method.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. For the 12 patients in that morning, the complete target group is observed: divide by N = 12.
  2. For the larger monthly population, the 12 records form a sample: divide by n − 1 = 11.
  3. The second calculation does not make one morning representative of the whole month; that is a separate design question.

questions.title: What is missing from the SD question?
questions.promptHtml:
A question says only: “Find the standard deviation of 4, 6, 8, 10.” It does not state whether these values are the entire target population or a sample from a larger group.

What is the best response before choosing a formula?
questions.hint: A short list of numbers can describe a whole small population or a sample of a larger one.
questions.solutionHtml: Ask which target group is intended, or explicitly state the convention you are using. The population SD is √5 ≈ 2.24, whereas the sample SD is √(20/3) ≈ 2.58. Neither formula is implied merely by having four numbers.

options.label: Always use sample SD because there are fewer than 30 values
Always use population SD because all listed values are available
Clarify the target group or state an explicit assumption
Either formula gives the same answer

questions.title: Repair the sample variance denominator
questions.promptHtml:
Five randomly selected batteries are used to estimate variation in a larger production run. Their sum of squared deviations is 40 hours². A student divides by 5 and reports variance 8 hours².

Find the correct sample variance and sample SD, to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: For sample variance, the divisor is one less than the sample size.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The five batteries are a sample from the production run, so use 5 − 1 = 4.
  2. s² = 40/4 = 10.00 hours².
  3. s = √10 = 3.16 hours. Dividing by 5 would describe the variance of these five observed values as a complete population.

questions.title: Zero total deviation is not zero variation
questions.promptHtml:
Three measured waits are 8, 10 and 12 minutes. Their mean is 10 minutes. A student adds the deviations −2, 0 and +2 and says: “The total is zero, so there is no variation.”

Find the sum of squared deviations, then correct the conclusion.
questions.hint: Opposite signed deviations cancel. Squaring stops positive and negative deviations cancelling.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Squared deviations are 4, 0 and 4, giving a total of 8 min².
  2. The observations differ, so there is variation. A zero sum of signed deviations from the mean does not imply zero SD.

options.label: All three observations must be equal
The signed deviations cancel, but the data still vary
The SD is negative because a deviation is negative

questions.title: Do not subtract the mean twice
questions.promptHtml:
For the complete population of five customers, the mean wait is 10 minutes and Σ(x − μ)² = 32 min². A student writes population variance = (32 − 10)/5.

Correct the calculation and find the population SD. Give both to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The supplied squared-deviation total already contains the subtraction of the mean from each observation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Do not subtract 10 again: 32 is already the sum of squared deviations.
  2. σ² = 32/5 = 6.40 min².
  3. σ = √6.4 = 2.53 minutes.

questions.title: What does an SD of three minutes mean?
questions.promptHtml:
A ward has mean waiting time 12 minutes and SD 3 minutes. A manager says: “Every patient waited exactly 9 or 15 minutes.”

Which correction is justified by the two summary values?
questions.hint: SD summarises spread across a dataset. It is not the deviation of every individual observation.
questions.solutionHtml: The mean and SD describe the average and overall spread; they do not fix every individual wait. Individual deviations can differ, and SD alone does not guarantee that all waits lie between 9 and 15 minutes.

options.label: SD summarises spread; individual waits can be different distances from 12
Every wait is guaranteed to lie between 9 and 15
Some patients must have waited −3 minutes

questions.title: Classify three kurtosis reports
questions.promptHtml:
Three distributions have ordinary (Pearson) kurtosis values A = 1.8, B = 3.0 and C = 5.6. The normal reference is 3.

Classify each supplied value. You do not need to calculate kurtosis from data.
questions.hint: Compare each value with 3: below, equal to or above the normal reference.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A: 1.8 < 3, so platykurtic.
  2. B: 3.0 = 3, so mesokurtic.
  3. C: 5.6 > 3, so leptokurtic.
  4. These comparisons concern the influence of extreme deviations relative to spread; peak height alone is insufficient.

questions.title: Equal SDs can hide different shapes
questions.promptHtml:
Two complete populations of eight recorded values are:

A: 8, 8, 8, 8, 12, 12, 12, 12
B: 6, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 10, 14

Each population has mean 10. Calculate each population SD, then judge the claim: “Equal means and SDs imply identical distribution shapes.”
questions.hint: For each set, square the deviations from 10, add them and divide by 8. Then compare where the observations occur.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A has eight squared deviations of 4: total 32. σ = √(32/8) = 2.00.
  2. B has squared deviations 16, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 16: total 32. Its σ is also 2.00.
  3. The claim is false: A has two groups away from the mean; B has six observations at the mean plus two farther extremes. Equal SDs do not determine the full shape.

options.label: True: equal SDs force the same shape
False: the locations of the observations differ despite equal SDs

questions.title: Choose typical wait and central spread
questions.promptHtml:
Most outpatient waits are between 5 and 15 minutes, but a few are over 90 minutes. You need to report a typical patient’s wait and the spread of the middle half of the waits.

Which pair is most suitable?
questions.hint: Choose a resistant measure of centre and a measure that specifically describes the middle 50%.
questions.solutionHtml: Median and IQR match both purposes. The median is less influenced by the few very long waits, and IQR measures the spread from Q₁ to Q₃. The long right tail suggests positive skewness.

questions.title: Quartile position is not the measured value
questions.promptHtml:
There are 14 ordered measurements. The 3rd is 8 cm and the 4th is 12 cm. Using the n + 1 method, a student reports “Q₁ = 3.75 cm.”

Give the correct Q₁ position and Q₁ value.
questions.hint: The position tells you where to look. Position 3.75 is three-quarters of the way from the third value to the fourth.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Q₁ position = (14 + 1)/4 = 3.75; a position has no centimetre unit.
  2. Q₁ value = 8 + 0.75(12 − 8) = 11.00 cm.

questions.title: One extreme wait changes
questions.promptHtml:
The ordered waits are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 minutes. The last wait is corrected from 9 to 29 minutes.

Find the new mean, median, range and IQR. Use quartile positions 0.25(n + 1) and 0.75(n + 1), with interpolation. Keep intermediate values unrounded.
questions.hint: Only the maximum changes. Check whether either quartile position uses that maximum.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The total rises from 44 to 64; mean = 64/8 = 8.00 minutes.
  2. The middle two values are still 5 and 6; median = 5.50 minutes.
  3. Range = 29 − 2 = 27.00 minutes.
  4. Q₁ at position 2.25 is 3.25; Q₃ at position 6.75 is 7.75. IQR = 4.50 minutes.
  5. Here the mean and range increase; the median and IQR remain unchanged.

questions.title: Can deleting an extreme value change the median?
questions.promptHtml:
The ordered observations are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 40. The observation 40 is excluded because it was outside the study period.

Calculate the original and revised medians, then assess the claim: “Deleting an extreme observation can never change the median.”
questions.hint: Deleting an observation changes the number of values and can change the middle position.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Original median = (3 + 4)/2 = 3.50.
  2. After deletion there are five observations; the median is the third value, 3.00.
  3. The claim is false. A median is resistant to extreme magnitudes, but it is not guaranteed to stay unchanged when observations are removed.

options.label: True: the median can never change
False: changing the number of observations can change the median

questions.title: CV is not a defect percentage
questions.promptHtml:
A sample of bottle fills has mean 250 mL and SD 5 mL. A trainee calculates CV = 2% and says: “Therefore, 2% of the bottles are defective.”

Which interpretation is correct?
questions.hint: CV compares SD with the mean. A defect rate needs an acceptance rule and counts of bottles outside that rule.
questions.solutionHtml: The SD is 2% of the mean fill. CV = 5/250 × 100 = 2%. This does not tell us the percentage of defective bottles; we need the permitted fill limits and relevant observations for that.

options.label: The SD is 2% of the mean fill
The next bottle has a 2% probability of being empty

questions.title: When is a CV comparison meaningful?
questions.promptHtml: You want to compare variation relative to the mean. Which situation is best suited to CV?
questions.hint: CV is most useful for positive ratio-scale measurements: zero represents absence of the measured quantity, and the mean is away from zero.
questions.solutionHtml: Positive bottle-fill volumes in mL have a meaningful zero and can support a relative-spread comparison. Celsius temperatures have an arbitrary zero; satisfaction codes are ordered categories; and division by a mean of zero is undefined.

options.label: Positive bottle-fill volumes in mL, with means well above zero
Signed changes whose mean is exactly zero

questions.title: Absolute and relative variation can disagree
questions.promptHtml:
Two positive output measures have these summaries: A: mean 10 units, SD 1 unit; B: mean 100 units, SD 5 units.

Calculate both CVs. Then identify the lower absolute SD and the lower relative variation.
questions.hint: Compare SDs for absolute variation. Compare SD/mean for relative variation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. CV(A) = 1/10 × 100 = 10.00%.
  2. CV(B) = 5/100 × 100 = 5.00%.
  3. A has the lower absolute SD (1 versus 5 units), but B has the lower relative variation (5% versus 10%). The two comparisons answer different questions.

questions.title: Routine deliveries: average speed and consistency
questions.promptHtml:
A print shop tests two equally priced paper suppliers. Six trial delivery times, in hours, are:

A: 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60
B: 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 52

These trials are samples used to estimate wider performance. Calculate each mean and sample SD (2 d.p.). For routine orders, the shop can order earlier and gives priority to lower variation in delivery time. Which supplier better meets this stated priority in the trial evidence?
questions.hint: Compare the average and spread separately. Use n − 1 = 5 for each sample variance.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Mean(A) = 270/6 = 45.00 hours; mean(B) = 282/6 = 47.00 hours.
  2. A: squared-deviation total 630; s = √(630/5) = 11.22 hours.
  3. B: squared-deviation total 70; s = √(70/5) = 3.74 hours.
  4. B better meets the priority of lower variation. It is two hours slower on average but has a much smaller sample SD. These small trials provide evidence, not a future guarantee.

extension.promptHtml: Optional written practice: give a two-sentence recommendation for routine orders, with numerical evidence and one limitation.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: I recommend B when lower variation is the priority: its sample SD is 3.74 hours compared with A’s 11.22 hours. B is slower on average (47 versus 45 hours), and six trials cannot guarantee future deliveries, so the shop should allow a time buffer.
rubric: States a recommendation linked to the given priority.
Compares both mean delivery times and both SDs with units.
Acknowledges the speed-versus-consistency trade-off.
States that a small set of trials does not guarantee future performance.

questions.title: An urgent order: the deadline changes the comparison
questions.promptHtml:
Six trial delivery times (hours) are A: 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60 and B: 42, 44, 46, 48, 50, 52.

For this question, compare suppliers using their observed on-time percentage. On time means arrival at or before the deadline. Calculate percentages for a 42-hour deadline and then a 54-hour deadline (2 d.p.). Choose which supplier has the higher observed percentage at each deadline.
questions.hint: Count times less than or equal to the deadline, divide by 6, and multiply by 100. Include a delivery exactly at the deadline.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. At 42 hours, A has 3/6 = 50.00% on time; B has 1/6 = 16.67%. A has the higher observed rate.
  2. At 54 hours, A has 5/6 = 83.33%; B has 6/6 = 100.00%. B has the higher observed rate.
  3. The comparison changes with the deadline. B’s six on-time trials at 54 hours do not guarantee the next delivery will be on time.

fields.label: Does B’s 100% trial rate guarantee the next arrival by 54 hours?

options.label: Yes: every future delivery is guaranteed
No: it describes these six trials only

questions.title: Do not average group means equally
questions.promptHtml:
One ward treats 4 patients with mean wait 10 minutes. Another treats 12 patients with mean wait 18 minutes. A report says the combined mean is (10 + 18)/2 = 14 minutes.

Calculate the correct combined mean and identify the error.
questions.hint: Recover each total with count × mean. Then divide the combined total by the combined number of patients.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total wait = 4 × 10 + 12 × 18 = 40 + 216 = 256 minutes.
  2. Combined count = 16; combined mean = 256/16 = 16.00 minutes.
  3. The report gives equal weight to groups of different sizes. Each patient should have equal weight, not each ward.

options.label: It weights two unequal-sized groups equally
It should report the sum 28 as the mean
Means can only be combined using the median

questions.title: Work backwards from the mean and sample SD
questions.promptHtml:
Six observations have mean 10 and sample SD 2. Four values are 9, 10, 10 and 11; two are missing.

Find the smaller and larger missing values. Use both the mean and SD conditions.
questions.hint: The missing values sum to 20. The total squared deviation is (6 − 1) × 2² = 20; the known values contribute 2.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The total is 6 × 10 = 60. The known values sum to 40, so the missing values sum to 20.
  2. The total squared deviation is 5 × 4 = 20. The known squared deviations sum to 1 + 0 + 0 + 1 = 2, leaving 18.
  3. The missing deviations sum to zero, so write them as −d and +d. Then 2d² = 18, so d = 3.
  4. The missing values are 7 and 13. Their mean is 10 with the known values, and s = √(20/5) = 2.

questions.title: Use the number of deliveries as the weight
questions.promptHtml:
A laboratory groups ten delivery delays by their recorded length. Calculate the mean delay and identify the mode.

Delay (minutes)Number of deliveries
02
55
153

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Each delay contributes once for every delivery in its row. The mean denominator is the number of deliveries, not the number of rows.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. There are 2 + 5 + 3 = 10 deliveries. Their total delay is 0 × 2 + 5 × 5 + 15 × 3 = 70 minutes.
  2. Mean = 70/10 = 7.00 minutes. The most frequent delay is 5 minutes, occurring five times.

questions.title: Order signed measurement errors
questions.promptHtml:
Six thermometer errors, in °C, are 0.7, −1.4, 0.2, −0.6, 0.7, −0.2. Find the median and range.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Put the negative and positive errors in numerical order before finding the two central values.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Ordered errors: −1.4, −0.6, −0.2, 0.2, 0.7, 0.7.
  2. Median = (−0.2 + 0.2)/2 = 0.00 °C.
  3. Range = 0.7 − (−1.4) = 2.10 °C; subtracting a negative adds its magnitude.

questions.title: A tied mode in a transport survey
questions.promptHtml: Patients report their travel method: bus, walk, rail, bus, walk, taxi. A report claims that the data have no mode because two categories are tied. Which correction is appropriate?
questions.hint: A dataset can have more than one category tied for the greatest frequency.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Bus and walk each occur twice; rail and taxi each occur once.
  2. The data have two modes: bus and walk. A tie for the highest frequency does not automatically mean there is no mode.

options.label: Bus and walk are both modes
Only bus is the mode because it is listed first
A mode is impossible for categorical data
Rail is the mode because it is least common

questions.title: Recover an unreported group mean
questions.promptHtml:
A hospital has two clinics. Together they see 20 patients with a mean consultation length of 14.2 minutes. Clinic A sees 12 patients with mean 15.4 minutes. Find Clinic B’s mean for its eight patients.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Use count × mean to recover the combined total and Clinic A total. Subtract before dividing by Clinic B’s count.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Combined total = 20 × 14.2 = 284 minutes. Clinic A total = 12 × 15.4 = 184.8 minutes.
  2. Clinic B total = 284 − 184.8 = 99.2 minutes.
  3. Clinic B mean = 99.2/8 = 12.40 minutes.

questions.title: Can a median give the total?
questions.promptHtml: A shop has 15 recorded sales. Their median value is ¥80. A trainee calculates total revenue as 15 × ¥80 = ¥1,200. Is that total determined by the information given?
questions.hint: The median locates the middle sale; it does not give the sum of all sales.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The total cannot be determined from the count and median alone.
  2. Different sets of 15 sales can share a median of ¥80 but have different totals. Count × mean, not count × median, recovers a known total.

options.label: The total is not determined by the median and count
The total must be zero because no mean was given
The total must equal the median, ¥80

questions.title: Remove an ineligible observation
questions.promptHtml:
Nine eligible-looking calls originally had a mean duration of 18.4 minutes. One call lasting 30.4 minutes was later found to fall outside the study period and is removed. Find the mean of the remaining eight calls.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Remove the excluded call from the total and also reduce the count by one.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Original total = 9 × 18.4 = 165.6 minutes.
  2. Revised total = 165.6 − 30.4 = 135.2 minutes; revised count = 8.
  3. New mean = 135.2/8 = 16.90 minutes.

questions.title: Repair a unit mismatch in the mean
questions.promptHtml:
Ten repair durations were entered in minutes, giving a reported mean of 24.6 minutes. One repair actually took 1.8 hours, but the spreadsheet entry was 1.8 minutes. Correct this entry and calculate the corrected mean.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Convert the mistaken observation to minutes, then replace its contribution to the total.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Reported total = 10 × 24.6 = 246 minutes.
  2. The correct entry is 1.8 × 60 = 108 minutes, so the corrected total is 246 − 1.8 + 108 = 352.2 minutes.
  3. Corrected mean = 352.2/10 = 35.22 minutes.

questions.title: Summaries after a unit conversion
questions.promptHtml:
A set of laboratory lengths has mean 2.46 cm, median 2.35 cm and range 0.82 cm. The same data are reported in millimetres (1 cm = 10 mm). Find the three summaries in mm.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Multiplying every length by 10 also multiplies the mean, median and range by 10.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Mean = 2.46 × 10 = 24.60 mm.
  2. Median = 2.35 × 10 = 23.50 mm.
  3. Range = 0.82 × 10 = 8.20 mm; both endpoints scale by 10.

questions.title: A mode need not be near the mean
questions.promptHtml:
Fault counts on eight shifts are 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 10. Calculate the mean and mode. Which statement correctly explains why they differ?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The mean uses every count. The mode uses the most frequent count.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The total is 16 across eight shifts, so mean = 2.00 faults.
  2. Zero occurs four times, so mode = 0 faults.
  3. The rare high count contributes strongly to the mean but does not make 10 the most frequent count.

options.label: The mean uses all counts; the mode identifies the most frequent count
One summary must be incorrect because they must agree
The mode must be negative when it is below the mean

questions.title: Median when the full list is not printed
questions.promptHtml:
A sorted list contains 20 blood-sample processing times. The 9th, 10th, 11th and 12th times are 12.4, 13.1, 14.7 and 15.2 minutes, respectively. Calculate the median.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: For an even count of 20, use positions 10 and 11, not 9 and 12.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The two central positions are 20/2 = 10 and 11.
  2. Median = (13.1 + 14.7)/2 = 13.90 minutes.

questions.title: Do subgroup medians combine like totals?
questions.promptHtml: Two wards each have five patients. Ward A’s median wait is 10 minutes and Ward B’s is 30 minutes. No other data are given. A report says the combined median is necessarily 20 minutes. What is the best assessment?
questions.hint: To locate the combined middle observations, you need information about how the two lists interleave.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The two subgroup medians do not determine the combined median, even with equal group sizes.
  2. For example, A = 1, 2, 10, 11, 12 and B = 20, 25, 30, 35, 40 produce a combined median of (12 + 20)/2 = 16, not 20.

options.label: There is insufficient information to determine the combined median
The combined median must equal the smaller subgroup median
The combined median must equal the larger subgroup median

questions.title: A fractional mean for a count
questions.promptHtml: Two laboratory shifts process 3 and 4 urgent samples. The mean is 3.5 samples per shift. A student says the mean must be rounded to 4 because a sample cannot be cut in half. Which response is correct?
questions.hint: A mean is a summary of multiple observations, not necessarily one possible individual observation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Mean = (3 + 4)/2 = 3.5 samples per shift.
  2. The mean of integer counts may be fractional. Keeping 3.5 describes the average accurately; it does not claim that any shift processed half a sample.

options.label: A fractional mean is valid even though each individual count is an integer
The exact mean must be 4 because counts are discrete
The exact mean must be 3 because means must be observed values
A mean cannot be calculated for counts

questions.title: Find a median from repeated counts
questions.promptHtml:
A pharmacist records the numbers of items on 12 prescriptions:

Items per prescriptionFrequency
13
24
32
53

Find the median number of items. Identify the two positions used.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Expand the position ranges mentally: three prescriptions have one item, then four have two items.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The median uses positions 6 and 7.
  2. Positions 1–3 contain 1; positions 4–7 contain 2. Both central observations are 2, so the median is 2.00 items.

questions.title: Find an unknown frequency from the mean
questions.promptHtml:
A machine was idle for 0 minutes on three days, 5 minutes on two days, and 10 minutes on an unknown number of days. Across all these days the mean idle time was 5 minutes. How many days had a 10-minute idle time?

Enter a whole number.
questions.hint: If the unknown count is k, the total is 10 + 10k and the number of days is 5 + k.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Set (10 + 10k)/(5 + k) = 5.
  2. Then 10 + 10k = 25 + 5k, so 5k = 15 and k = 3 days.
  3. Check: total 40 minutes over 8 days gives mean 5 minutes.

questions.title: The same mean can accompany different medians
questions.promptHtml:
Two wards record waiting times:

A: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 minutes
B: 1, 1, 2, 6, 20 minutes

Calculate each median. Both means are 6 minutes. Does equality of the means force equal medians?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Each ordered list has five observations, so its median is its third observation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A’s median is 6.00 minutes; B’s median is 2.00 minutes.
  2. Both totals are 30, so both means are 6. The medians still differ because the observations occupy different positions.

fields.label: Must equal means imply equal medians?

questions.title: A reversed scale changes endpoints
questions.promptHtml:
Scores x have minimum 20, maximum 80, mean 55 and median 60. A new score is defined as y = 100 − x. Find the new mean, median and range.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The transformation reverses the order. The new minimum comes from the old maximum.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. New mean = 100 − 55 = 45.00. The linear reversal also gives median = 100 − 60 = 40.00.
  2. The new minimum is 20 and maximum is 80, so new range = 60.00. A reversal does not make a range negative.

questions.title: Appending a middle value changes the median positions
questions.promptHtml:
The current sorted observations are 4, 6, 8, 12. A fifth valid observation of 7 is added. Calculate the new mean and median. A student says the old median of 7 should be averaged with the new observation to get the new median; is that a general method?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Rebuild the ordered list and use its new count. A coincidence in this example is not a general rule.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The new ordered list is 4, 6, 7, 8, 12. Its total is 37, so mean = 7.40; its middle value is 7.00.
  2. The general method is to reorder and locate the middle. Averaging an old median with an added observation is not generally valid; it happens to give 7 here.

options.label: Always average the old median and the new value
Reorder the data and identify the new middle position

questions.title: Interpolate using only the neighbouring values
questions.promptHtml:
There are ten ordered observations. Values at positions 2, 3, 8 and 9 are respectively 12.4, 15.6, 23.1 and 25.5 mm. Use Q₁ position = (n + 1)/4 and Q₃ position = 3(n + 1)/4, with linear interpolation. Find Q₁ and Q₃.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The positions are 2.75 and 8.25, so use different fractions of the two gaps.

questions.title: Positions apply after sorting
questions.promptHtml:
Eleven processing times are recorded in this order: 18, 4, 12, 6, 15, 9, 21, 5, 14, 8, 11 minutes. Find Q₁ and Q₃ using positions (n + 1)/4 and 3(n + 1)/4 in the ordered data.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: A quartile position is a rank in the sorted data, not a row in the original recording order.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sorted times: 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, 21.
  2. Positions are 3 and 9, giving Q₁ = 6.00 minutes and Q₃ = 15.00 minutes. No interpolation is needed at integer positions.

questions.title: Follow the stated quartile convention
questions.promptHtml:
Ordered data: 2, 6, 10, 14, 18, 22, 26, 30. This course question requires the n + 1 method with linear interpolation. One calculator reports Q₁ = 8 by taking the median of the lower four values. Find Q₁ under the required convention and identify the reason for the difference.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The requested Q₁ position is 0.25(8 + 1) = 2.25.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The required result is 6 + 0.25(10 − 6) = 7.00.
  2. Taking the median of 2, 6, 10, 14 gives 8, but that is a different quartile convention. Use the convention specified by the question.

options.label: The results differ only because of rounding
The two methods use different quartile conventions
The printed data are not sorted

questions.title: Do not round the position to a whole number
questions.promptHtml:
Fourteen ordered measurements have a 3rd value of 13.2 cm and a 4th value of 14.8 cm. Under the n + 1 convention, Q₁ position is 3.75. A student rounds this to position 4 and reports 14.8 cm. Find the correct interpolated Q₁.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Move 75% of the gap from the third value toward the fourth.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The gap is 14.8 − 13.2 = 1.6 cm.
  2. Q₁ = 13.2 + 0.75 × 1.6 = 14.40 cm. Rounding the rank before interpolation changes the method.

questions.title: Recover an adjacent value from a quartile
questions.promptHtml:
Eight ordered readings use the n + 1 interpolation convention. Q₁ is 10.5, and the second reading is 10. What is the third reading?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Q₁ lies one-quarter of the way from the second reading to the third.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Q₁ position = 9/4 = 2.25, so 10 + 0.25(x₃ − 10) = 10.5.
  2. Thus x₃ − 10 = 0.5/0.25 = 2, giving x₃ = 12.00.

questions.title: Recover the sample size from a position
questions.promptHtml:
A worksheet correctly gives the upper quartile position as 15.75, calculated using Q₃ position = 0.75(n + 1). How many observations are in the dataset? Does 15.75 itself tell us Q₃’s measured value?

Enter a whole number.
questions.hint: Solve the position formula for n. The actual data values are still needed to interpolate.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 0.75(n + 1) = 15.75 gives n + 1 = 21, so n = 20 observations.
  2. 15.75 is a rank between observations 15 and 16, not a measured quartile value. Their values are needed to calculate Q₃.

fields.label: Can Q₃’s measured value be determined here?

options.label: No: the neighbouring data values are needed

questions.title: Interpolation between tied observations
questions.promptHtml:
For nine ordered observations, the 2nd and 3rd values both equal 5.2; the 7th and 8th values are 11.6 and 14.8. Use positions 0.25(n + 1) and 0.75(n + 1), with interpolation. Find Q₁ and Q₃.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: A fractional position between two equal values still produces that same value.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Q₁ position = 2.5, so Q₁ = 5.2 + 0.5(5.2 − 5.2) = 5.20.
  2. Q₃ position = 7.5, so Q₃ = 11.6 + 0.5(14.8 − 11.6) = 13.20.

questions.title: Quartile ranks survive a unit conversion
questions.promptHtml:
Eight ordered masses have sixth and seventh values 2.46 kg and 2.74 kg. Calculate Q₃ using the n + 1 interpolation method, then report it in grams. State its position after converting every observation to grams.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Converting kg to g multiplies values by 1,000 but does not change their order or count.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Q₃ position = 0.75 × 9 = 6.75, before and after conversion.
  2. Q₃ = 2.46 + 0.75(2.74 − 2.46) = 2.67 kg = 2670.00 g.

questions.title: Use the correct fraction of the upper gap
questions.promptHtml:
