Eighteen ordered measurements have 14th and 15th values 21.6 and 30.4. Under the n + 1 method, Q₃ position is 14.25. A student uses 75% of the gap because it is the upper quartile. Find the correct Q₃.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The fractional part of the position, 0.25, determines how far to move within this particular gap.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Q₃ = 21.6 + 0.25(30.4 − 21.6) = 21.6 + 2.2 = 23.80.
  2. The 75% in the quartile-position formula does not mean that every Q₃ interpolation uses 75% of a gap.

questions.title: An interpolated quartile is not an exact observation count
questions.promptHtml:
Ordered data: 1, 3, 8, 12, 14, 20. Calculate Q₁ using position 0.25(n + 1) and interpolation. Then count how many observed values are strictly below it. Does the method require exactly 25% of the six observations to lie strictly below Q₁?

Give Q₁ to 2 decimal places and enter the observation count as a whole number.
questions.hint: First locate position 1.75. Then count actual observations; an interpolated rank and an integer count are different.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Q₁ = 1 + 0.75(3 − 1) = 2.50.
  2. Only the observation 1 lies below 2.50, so the count is 1.
  3. The method estimates a quartile location. In a small dataset it does not require an exact 25% of observations strictly below it; 25% of six is not an integer count.

fields.label: Must exactly 25% lie strictly below this interpolated value?

questions.title: Adding an extreme observation changes the count
questions.promptHtml:
Recorded waits are 1, 2, 4, 6, 7 minutes. A sixth valid wait of 70 minutes is added. Calculate the new mean and median, then identify which increased more in minutes.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Adding the wait changes both the total and the number of observations. Compare with the original mean and median of 4.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The new total is 90 and the count is 6, so the mean is 15.00 minutes.
  2. The new median is (4 + 6)/2 = 5.00 minutes.
  3. The mean rises by 11 minutes and the median by 1 minute. The mean changes more, but the median is not completely unchanged.

questions.title: An inconvenient extreme value is still evidence
questions.promptHtml:
Six repair durations are 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 85 minutes. The 85-minute repair is confirmed accurate and belongs to the study. Calculate the mean with all six records and the mean after deleting 85. Is “it makes the mean look bad” a sound reason to delete it?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Check both means, then distinguish an accurate extreme observation from an error or ineligible record.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. With all records, total = 120 and mean = 20.00 minutes.
  2. Deleting 85 leaves total 35 over five repairs, giving 7.00 minutes.
  3. Deleting a valid record only to improve the result is not justified. Report the extreme and, if useful, a resistant summary alongside the full-data mean.

fields.label: Is the stated deletion reason sound?

options.label: Yes: any extreme should be deleted
No: it is a valid record, and its effect should be explained

questions.title: A pay rise at the top of the ordered list
questions.promptHtml:
A company has 14 employees. Only the highest monthly salary rises, by ¥4,200. The employee remains the highest paid. What is the increase in the mean salary, and what happens to the median salary?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The total rises by ¥4,200 while the count stays 14. The 7th and 8th salaries do not change.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Increase in mean = 4200/14 = ¥300.00.
  2. The median depends on the 7th and 8th salaries, so it is unchanged. The top salary changes the mean even though the central salaries are unaffected.

questions.title: Reverse a measurement scale
questions.promptHtml:
A machine reports a quality score x. Most scores are near 20, with a few scores extending towards 90: the score distribution has a long right tail. A new display reports y = 100 − x for every item.

Which direction will the long tail have on the new display?
questions.hint: Try transforming one common value and one value in the old tail. Subtraction from 100 reverses the order.
questions.solutionHtml: A common score 20 becomes 80, while a tail score 90 becomes 10. The high-end tail is reflected to the low end. The new distribution therefore has a long left tail. This does not mean the observations themselves changed; the measurement scale was reversed.

fields.label: Direction of the new long tail

options.label: Right: transformations cannot alter tail direction
Left: large original values become small new values
No tail: subtracting from 100 removes skewness
Both tails must become equally long

questions.title: Choose a summary for budgeting
questions.promptHtml:
A hospital treated 100 patients last month. Treatment costs were strongly right-skewed because a few patients needed expensive care. The finance office wants the total cost for those 100 patients.

Which measure, multiplied by 100, gives the exact total? Then judge whether that measure must also be the best description of a typical patient’s cost.
questions.hint: Use the defining relationship between an arithmetic average, the number of values and their total. A total and a typical individual answer different questions.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Arithmetic mean × 100 gives the exact total because mean = total ÷ 100.
  2. This does not make the mean the best summary for every purpose. With strong right skew, the median is often more representative of a typical patient. Choosing a summary depends on the purpose, not only the shape.

fields.label: Measure that recovers the exact total
Does that guarantee the best summary of a typical patient?

options.label: Yes: one measure must serve every reporting purpose
No: the total and a typical individual are different reporting purposes

questions.title: Equal mean and median do not prove symmetry
questions.promptHtml:
Five recorded values are 0, 3, 4, 4, 9. A student calculates mean = 4 and median = 4, then writes: “The distribution must be symmetric around 4.”

Check the claim using the actual values.
questions.hint: A symmetric distribution needs matching values and frequencies at equal distances on either side of its centre.
questions.solutionHtml: The student’s conclusion is not justified. The total is 20, so the mean is 4; the middle observation is also 4. But 0 is four units below 4 and there is no 8 four units above it. The distances from 4 are −4, −1, 0, 0 and 5, which are not mirror pairs. Equal mean and median alone do not prove symmetry.

options.label: Correct: equal mean and median prove symmetry
Incorrect: the observed values do not form matching pairs around 4
Incorrect only because the mean is 5
Incorrect only because the median is 3

questions.title: A centre where no observations occur
questions.promptHtml:
A delivery company has two equally common routes. Recorded journey times are 2, 2, 2, 10, 10, 10 hours. Both the mean and median are 6 hours, and the distribution is symmetric around 6.

The manager says “Most journeys take about 6 hours.” Which response best uses the data?
questions.hint: Look at where the actual observations occur, not only at the centre. Symmetric distributions can contain separated groups.
questions.solutionHtml: The claim is misleading: three journeys take 2 hours and three take 10 hours; none takes 6 hours. Report the two route groups, or show the distribution, rather than implying that 6 hours is common. Symmetry does not guarantee that a single central value describes a typical observation well.

options.label: Agree: symmetry guarantees that most journeys are near the mean
Use the median of 6 instead; it solves the problem
Describe the two route groups; 6 hours hides the two clusters
Call 6 hours the mode as well

questions.title: Choose summaries when all values matter
questions.promptHtml:
A laboratory’s measurement errors form one approximately symmetric cluster around zero, with no unusual extremes. The report needs a centre using every recorded value and a spread in the original measurement units based on deviations from that centre.

Which pair fits these stated requirements?
questions.hint: One measure averages all observations. The other is the square root of a measure based on squared deviations.
questions.solutionHtml: Mean and standard deviation meet both requirements. The mean uses every measurement. SD summarises squared deviations from the mean and is expressed in the original units. Median and IQR can also be useful summaries, but they do not meet the specific requirements given here. Approximate symmetry by itself does not prove normality.

options.label: Mean and variance in squared units

questions.title: Do not name skewness after the tallest bar
questions.promptHtml:
A histogram of battery charge levels has its tallest bars near 90%. Small bars extend gradually down to 10%, producing a long tail towards low values. A student labels it “right-skewed because the tallest bars are on the right.”

Choose the correct correction.
questions.hint: Skewness is named after the direction of the long tail, not the location of the greatest frequency.
questions.solutionHtml: The histogram is left-skewed (negatively skewed): its long tail extends towards lower charge levels. The tallest bars identify where many observations lie, not the direction used to name skewness.

options.label: Keep right-skewed: the tallest bars decide the label
Change to left-skewed: the long tail extends towards lower values
Change to symmetric: all charge levels are positive
It cannot be negatively skewed unless some charge levels are below zero

questions.title: Separate a signed deviation from its square
questions.promptHtml:
A sample has exact mean 14.2 minutes. One wait is 12.7 minutes. Find its deviation and squared deviation. Interpret the sign of the deviation.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Deviation is observation minus mean. Its square cannot be negative.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Deviation = 12.7 − 14.2 = −1.50 minutes.
  2. Squared deviation = (−1.5)² = 2.25 min².
  3. The negative deviation means this wait is below the mean; it does not mean that the wait itself is negative.

options.label: The wait is below the mean
The patient waited a negative number of minutes

questions.title: Square a negative deviation correctly
questions.promptHtml:
A deviation is −3.4 mm. In handwritten working, a student writes −(3.4²) and records a squared deviation of −11.56 mm². What should the squared deviation be, and which expression clearly represents it?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Squaring the entire negative deviation means multiplying (−3.4) by (−3.4).
questions.solutionHtml:
1. (−3.4)² = (−3.4) × (−3.4) = 11.56 mm².
  2. Use brackets around the negative deviation. A sum of squared deviations cannot include a negative square.

questions.title: A variance table must include repeated readings
questions.promptHtml:
These are all eight readings in the target population:

Reading (mm)Frequency
32
54
82

The population mean is 5.25 mm. Find the population variance and SD.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Multiply each squared deviation by its frequency before adding. Divide the resulting total by 8.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Weighted squared-deviation total = 2(3 − 5.25)² + 4(5 − 5.25)² + 2(8 − 5.25)² = 25.5 mm².
  2. Population variance = 25.5/8 = 3.1875 mm² ≈ 3.19 mm².
  3. Population SD = √3.1875 ≈ 1.79 mm. Repeated readings must all contribute.

questions.title: Complete one missing row in the variance work
questions.promptHtml:
Six sampled observations estimate a larger process. Their exact sample mean is 20.5 seconds. The squared deviations for five observations total 12.71 s². The remaining observation is 17.8 seconds.

Find its squared deviation, the complete squared-deviation total, and the sample SD.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Add the missing square before dividing by n − 1 = 5 and taking the square root.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Missing deviation = 17.8 − 20.5 = −2.7 seconds, so its square is 7.29 s².
  2. Complete total = 12.71 + 7.29 = 20.00 s².
  3. s = √(20/5) = 2.00 seconds.

questions.title: Work backwards from a sample SD
questions.promptHtml:
A random sample of 18 measurements estimates a larger population. Its sample SD is exactly 2.4 cm. Find the sum of squared deviations from the sample mean.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Undo the square root first, then undo division by n − 1.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sample variance = 2.4² = 5.76 cm².
  2. Sum of squared deviations = (18 − 1) × 5.76 = 97.92 cm².

questions.title: Recover a total from a population variance
questions.promptHtml:
The complete target population contains 12 packaged items. Its mass variance is exactly 1.44 g². Find the sum of squared deviations and population SD.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: For a population, the squared-deviation total is N times the variance.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Squared-deviation total = 12 × 1.44 = 17.28 g².
  2. Population SD = √1.44 = 1.20 g.

questions.title: Convert a divisor without rebuilding the table
questions.promptHtml:
For the same eight measurements, dividing the squared-deviation total by 8 gives 9.8 mm². Now use those eight measurements as a sample to estimate the variance of a larger production process. Find the sample variance.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Recover the unchanged squared-deviation total, then divide that total by 7.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Squared-deviation total = 8 × 9.8 = 78.4 mm².
  2. Sample variance = 78.4/(8 − 1) = 11.20 mm².
  3. The data and squared deviations are unchanged; the variance divisor changes with the stated purpose.

questions.title: A bigger squared-deviation total need not mean a bigger SD
questions.promptHtml:
Two independent samples estimate their respective larger processes. A has n = 5 and squared-deviation total 20. B has n = 21 and squared-deviation total 80. Calculate both sample SDs and identify the lower one.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Each total has its own n − 1 divisor. Comparing totals alone ignores sample size.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. s(A) = √(20/4) = √5 ≈ 2.24.
  2. s(B) = √(80/20) = 2.00.
  3. B has the smaller SD despite the larger total because it contains more observations.

questions.title: A temperature conversion changes spread and centre differently
questions.promptHtml:
A set of temperatures has mean 18.5 °C and SD 3.2 °C. Convert using F = 1.8C + 32. Find the mean in °F, SD in °F, and variance in °F².

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The +32 shifts every value and its mean equally; it does not change deviations. The 1.8 scales deviations.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. New mean = 1.8 × 18.5 + 32 = 65.30 °F.
  2. New SD = 1.8 × 3.2 = 5.76 °F.
  3. New variance = 5.76² = 33.1776 °F² ≈ 33.18 °F².

questions.title: Variance needs a squared unit conversion
questions.promptHtml: A duration dataset has variance 225 seconds². The same durations are expressed in minutes. Find the variance in minutes² and the SD in minutes. Report the variance to 4 d.p. and SD to 2 d.p..
questions.hint: Each duration divides by 60; its squared deviation divides by 60².
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Variance in minutes² = 225/3600 = 0.0625 minutes².
  2. SD = √0.0625 = 0.25 minutes. Dividing the variance by just 60 would be incorrect.

questions.title: Raw squares are not squared deviations
questions.promptHtml:
A sample from a larger process contains 3, 4 and 8 mm, with mean 5 mm. A student uses 3² + 4² + 8² = 89 as the squared-deviation total. Find the correct total and sample SD.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Subtract the mean from each reading before squaring.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Correct total = (3 − 5)² + (4 − 5)² + (8 − 5)² = 4 + 1 + 9 = 14.00 mm².
  2. s = √[14/(3 − 1)] = √7 ≈ 2.65 mm. The total 89 contains raw squares, not squared deviations.

questions.title: Negative observations do not make SD negative
questions.promptHtml:
Four calibration errors sampled from a larger process are −0.8, −0.3, 0.1, 0.2 mm. Their mean is −0.2 mm. Calculate sample variance and SD. Is the SD negative because the mean is negative?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The deviations are squared before averaging; the SD uses the nonnegative square root.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Deviations are −0.6, −0.1, 0.3 and 0.4; their squared total is 0.36 + 0.01 + 0.09 + 0.16 = 0.62 mm².
  2. s² = 0.62/3 ≈ 0.21 mm²; s = √(0.62/3) ≈ 0.45 mm.
  3. The SD is nonnegative. The sign of the mean does not change this.

questions.title: Zero variation within groups can hide variation overall
questions.promptHtml:
Two complete groups have readings A: 0, 0 and B: 10, 10. Each group has population SD zero. Treat all four readings together as the complete target population. Find the combined mean and population SD.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The combined mean lies between the two groups. Deviations from that combined mean are not zero.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The combined mean is (0 + 0 + 10 + 10)/4 = 5.00.
  2. Each reading is 5 away from this mean. The variance is (25 + 25 + 25 + 25)/4 = 25, so SD = 5.00.
  3. Averaging the two group SDs would miss the difference between their means.

questions.title: Combine squared deviations around a shared mean
questions.promptHtml:
Two complete groups have the same mean. A contains four readings with population variance 9; B contains six readings with population variance 4. The target population is all ten readings. Find its population variance and SD.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Because the means are equal, both groups already measure deviations from the combined mean. Add their squared-deviation totals.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A contributes 4 × 9 = 36; B contributes 6 × 4 = 24.
  2. Combined variance = (36 + 24)/10 = 6.00.
  3. Combined SD = √6 ≈ 2.45. The shared-mean condition is essential to this direct addition.

questions.title: Put the divisor inside the square root
questions.promptHtml:
All nine target readings have squared-deviation total 81 cm². A student reports population SD = √81/9 = 1 cm. Find the correct population SD and choose the correct expression.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Calculate variance first: divide the total by 9. Then take the square root of the whole variance.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Population variance = 81/9 = 9 cm².
  2. Population SD = √(81/9) = 3.00 cm, not (√81)/9.

questions.title: Absolute deviation and SD are different measures
questions.promptHtml:
The complete target population is 7, 10, 13 minutes, with mean 10. A student averages the absolute deviations and calls the result 2 minutes “the standard deviation.” Calculate the actual population SD.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The 2-minute result uses absolute values. SD instead squares the deviations, averages the squares, and takes a root.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Absolute-deviation average = (3 + 0 + 3)/3 = 2, a different spread measure.
  2. Population variance = (9 + 0 + 9)/3 = 6 min²; SD = √6 ≈ 2.45 minutes.

questions.title: Taking a square root is not dividing by two
questions.promptHtml:
A sample variance is correctly reported as 36 mm². A student divides it by two and writes SD = 18 mm. Correct the SD and identify the operation needed.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The SD is the value whose square equals the variance.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. √36 = 6.00 mm because 6² = 36.
  2. Take a square root, not half of the variance.

questions.title: Small variance must not be rounded away too early
questions.promptHtml: A sample of four positive concentrations from a larger process has squared-deviation total 0.0067 (mg/L)². A trainee rounds the variance to 0.00 before taking its square root and reports zero SD. Find sample variance to 6 d.p. and sample SD to 3 d.p..
questions.hint: Keep 0.0067/3 in the calculator when finding the square root.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Sample variance = 0.0067/(4 − 1) = 0.002233333… ≈ 0.002233 (mg/L)².
  2. Sample SD = √(0.0067/3) = 0.047258… ≈ 0.047 mg/L.
  3. Rounding the intermediate variance to zero destroys the recorded variation.

questions.title: Spread of a complete two-item population
questions.promptHtml:
The target population consists of just two packaged masses: 23.4 and 28.2 g. Their mean is 25.8 g. Calculate population variance and SD.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Both values are 2.4 g from the mean. Average their two squared deviations.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Squared deviations are both (2.4)² = 5.76 g².
  2. Population variance = (5.76 + 5.76)/2 = 5.76 g²; SD = 2.40 g.

questions.title: A squared deviation has two possible directions
questions.promptHtml:
A delivery has squared deviation 9 hours² from the mean delivery time of 12.5 hours. Its time is known to be above the mean. Find the delivery time. Why is the direction information needed?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: A square of 9 can come from a deviation of +3 or −3.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The deviation’s magnitude is √9 = 3 hours. Above the mean selects +3.
  2. Delivery time = 12.5 + 3 = 15.50 hours.
  3. Without the direction, 12.5 − 3 = 9.5 hours would also have the same squared deviation.

options.label: The square alone loses the sign of the deviation
The square alone has no units
The mean must always be smaller than every observation

questions.title: The same range can hide a different concentration
questions.promptHtml:
Two complete target populations of waits are A: 4, 8, 8, 8, 12 and B: 4, 4, 8, 12, 12 minutes. Both have mean 8 and range 8. Find both population SDs and identify which dataset is more concentrated around the mean.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Count how many observations lie at the centre and how many lie four minutes away.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. A has squared-deviation total 16 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 16 = 32; σ(A) = √(32/5) ≈ 2.53 minutes.
  2. B has total 16 + 16 + 0 + 16 + 16 = 64; σ(B) = √(64/5) ≈ 3.58 minutes.
  3. A is more concentrated around the mean. Equal ranges do not force equal SDs.

questions.title: Repeating every value leaves population spread unchanged
questions.promptHtml:
A complete population has values 2, 4, 6. A second complete population repeats each value twice: 2, 2, 4, 4, 6, 6. Find each population variance. Why are they equal?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The mean remains 4. Repeating every observation doubles both the squared-deviation total and the population size.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Original population: squared total 4 + 0 + 4 = 8; variance = 8/3 ≈ 2.67.
  2. Repeated population: squared total 16; variance = 16/6 ≈ 2.67.
  3. The numerator and denominator double together, so the population variance and SD are unchanged.

options.label: Squared-deviation total and population size both double
The population divisor must become n − 1

questions.title: A missing reading was incorrectly entered as zero
questions.promptHtml:
A sample spreadsheet lists six readings with total 30 and sum of raw squares 190. One row is actually a missing reading incorrectly entered as zero. Remove that row: the five remaining measurements are the valid sample from a larger process.

Use Σ(x − x̄)² = Σx² − n(x̄)². Find the corrected sample mean and variance.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Removing an entered zero changes the count, but not either supplied total.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The valid count is 5. Corrected mean = 30/5 = 6.00.
  2. Corrected squared-deviation total = 190 − 5 × 6² = 10.
  3. Corrected sample variance = 10/(5 − 1) = 2.50. Missing data should not be silently treated as measured zeros.

questions.title: A negative multiplier reflects the data but keeps SD nonnegative
questions.promptHtml:
Readings x have mean 6 and SD 1.5. A new scale is y = 12 − 2x. Find the new mean, SD and variance.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Multiplication by −2 reverses signs of deviations and doubles their magnitudes. Squaring removes the negative sign.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Mean(y) = 12 − 2 × 6 = 0.00.
  2. SD(y) = |−2| × 1.5 = 3.00.
  3. Variance(y) = 3² = 9.00. A reflected dataset does not have negative SD.

questions.title: Centre the deviations on the mean
questions.promptHtml:
All three target readings are 7, 8, 12 cm. A student subtracts the first reading, 7, and squares the differences to get 0 + 1 + 25 = 26. Find the correct population variance and SD.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: For variance, deviations must be measured from the mean, which is 9 cm, not from the first observation.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The mean is (7 + 8 + 12)/3 = 9 cm.
  2. Squared deviations from the mean are 4, 1, 9, totaling 14.
  3. Population variance = 14/3 ≈ 4.67 cm²; SD = √(14/3) ≈ 2.16 cm.

questions.title: A survey can contain all replies but not all people
questions.promptHtml:
A course has 50 students. Everyone is invited to report their weekly study hours, but only 40 reply. The teacher has every reply.

Choose the variance divisor when describing only those 40 respondents, and when treating their replies as a sample to estimate variance among all 50 students. Also evaluate whether changing the divisor fixes possible nonresponse bias.
questions.hint: Every reply is the whole respondent group, but the respondent group is not the whole class. A formula adjustment cannot recover the missing students’ information.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. For the complete group of 40 respondents, use population divisor 40.
  2. When using those replies as a sample to estimate class variance, the usual sample formula uses 40 − 1 = 39.
  3. Using 39 does not fix nonresponse bias. If students who did not reply have systematically different study habits, the estimate may still be misleading.

fields.label: Divisor: use replies as a sample for the whole class
Does the sample divisor remove nonresponse bias?

options.label: Yes: subtracting one compensates for every missing student
No: possible differences between respondents and nonrespondents remain

questions.title: A selected department becomes the target group
questions.promptHtml:
A university randomly selects one department and records salaries for all 18 employees in that department.

Report A describes salary variation only within this selected department. Report B treats the department’s employees as a sample to estimate variation among all university employees, while discussing the limitations of selecting just one department separately.

Select the standard variance formula for each report.
questions.hint: The way the department was chosen does not make its own complete employee list incomplete. Re-read the target group of each report.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Report A observes everyone in its target department, so use population variance: divide by 18.
  2. Report B has only part of the university workforce, so the usual sample variance formula divides by 17.
  3. A single department may be unrepresentative of the university. Selecting the sample formula does not solve that sampling-design limitation.

questions.title: A large fraction can still be a sample
questions.promptHtml:
An inspector measures 95 randomly selected items from a shipment of 100. She wants to estimate the shipment’s variance using the usual sample variance formula. Another inspector measures all 6 items in a separate shipment and wants to describe only those 6 items.

A trainee claims that the first inspector must use population variance because 95 is a large number, while the second must use sample variance because 6 is small.

Choose the appropriate divisor for each inspector.
questions.hint: Sample size does not decide whether the whole target group was observed. Use n − 1 for the stated sample formula, and N for a complete target population.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The 95 items are still a sample of the 100-item shipment. The stated sample variance formula uses 95 − 1 = 94.
  2. All 6 items in the second target shipment were measured. Its population variance uses 6.
  3. The trainee confused the size of a dataset with whether it covers the entire target population.

fields.label: Divisor for the complete shipment of 6

questions.title: Random order does not turn a census into a sample
questions.promptHtml:
An engineer measures the output of all 8 machines currently installed in one workshop. A random-number generator determines the order in which the machines are measured. The report describes variation among those 8 installed machines only.

A colleague says that using random numbers means sample SD must be used. Which procedure is appropriate?
questions.hint: Randomising the measurement order is different from selecting only some machines. Identify whether any member of the target group is missing.
questions.solutionHtml: Use population SD: find squared deviations from the mean, divide their sum by 8, then take the square root. Every machine in the stated target group was measured. Random order changes neither the target group nor the number of its members observed.

options.label: Divide squared deviations by 7, because any use of random numbers implies sampling
Divide squared deviations by 8 and take the square root, because the whole target group is observed
Use the variance of the random measurement-order numbers
Neither formula applies when measurement order is random

questions.title: Recover SD from a reported CV
questions.promptHtml:
A positive bottle-fill volume has mean 312.5 mL and CV 1.6%. Zero mL means no liquid. Find its SD in mL.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: CV = SD/mean × 100, so SD = mean × CV/100.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. SD = 312.5 × 1.6/100 = 5.00 mL.
  2. A CV of 1.6% means the SD is 1.6% of the mean volume.

questions.title: Recover the mean from SD and CV
questions.promptHtml:
Positive package masses have SD 7.8 g and CV 6.5%. The mean is well above zero. Find the mean mass.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Rearrange CV = SD/mean × 100 to make the mean the subject.

questions.title: CV survives conversion from kilograms to grams
questions.promptHtml:
Positive package masses have mean 2.4 kg and SD 0.18 kg. The same values become mean 2400 g and SD 180 g. Calculate CV in each unit and explain the comparison.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: A multiplicative unit conversion changes the numerator and denominator by the same factor.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. In kg: CV = 0.18/2.4 × 100 = 7.50%.
  2. In g: CV = 180/2400 × 100 = 7.50%.
  3. The conversion cancels in the ratio. The physical relative spread has not changed.

options.label: The gram CV is 1,000 times larger
The gram CV is 1,000 times smaller

questions.title: An arbitrary temperature zero makes a CV misleading
questions.promptHtml: A student calculates a “CV” from temperatures with mean 20 °C and SD 2 °C, obtaining 10%. The same temperatures have mean 68 °F and SD 3.6 °F, giving about 5.29%. The student claims the physical temperature pattern is more consistent when written in °F. Identify the problem.
questions.hint: CV needs a meaningful ratio-scale zero. Celsius and Fahrenheit use different arbitrary origins.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The Celsius and Fahrenheit values describe the same physical measurements.
  2. Their arbitrary zeros cause SD/mean to change under this conversion. These percentages should not be used to claim a change in relative physical consistency.
  3. For routine CV comparisons, use positive ratio-scale measurements with a meaningful zero and a mean away from zero.

options.label: The scales have arbitrary zeros, so this CV comparison is inappropriate
The SD must be the same numeric value in every unit
The temperatures must all be negative
Writing °F genuinely makes the measurements less variable

questions.title: Equal relative variation with unequal absolute SDs
questions.promptHtml:
Two sizes of positive liquid fills have summaries: small: mean 80 mL, SD 4 mL; large: mean 320 mL, SD 16 mL. Calculate each CV. A manager says the large fills have four times as much relative variation. Assess the claim.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Both the mean and SD are four times larger for the large fills.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Small CV = 4/80 × 100 = 5.00%.
  2. Large CV = 16/320 × 100 = 5.00%.
  3. The absolute SD is four times larger, but relative variation is equal because the mean also increases by a factor of four.

options.label: Four times as large for the large size
One-quarter as large for the large size

questions.title: Low variation does not guarantee the correct target
questions.promptHtml:
A machine should fill an average of 500 mL. Two positive-fill datasets have summaries: A: mean 490 mL, SD 2 mL; B: mean 500 mL, SD 4 mL. Find both CVs. Which dataset has its mean closer to the target?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Consistency and closeness to the target are different questions. Calculate CV, then compare means with 500.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. CV(A) = 2/490 × 100 ≈ 0.41%; CV(B) = 4/500 × 100 = 0.80%.
  2. A has less relative variation but its mean is 10 mL below target.
  3. B’s mean equals 500 mL, so B is closer to the average-fill target. Lower CV alone does not establish better target accuracy.

questions.title: Start with variance before comparing CVs
questions.promptHtml:
Three processes measure positive fill volume in mL, with meaningful zero:

ProcessMean (mL)Variance (mL²)
A20025
B500100
C1009

Calculate each CV and choose the smallest relative variation.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: CV uses SD, not variance. First take the square root of each variance.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The SDs are √25 = 5 mL, √100 = 10 mL and √9 = 3 mL.
  2. CV(A) = 5/200 × 100 = 2.50%; CV(B) = 10/500 × 100 = 2.00%; CV(C) = 3/100 × 100 = 3.00%.
  3. B has the smallest relative variation.

questions.title: The numerator and denominator were reversed
questions.promptHtml:
Positive fill masses have mean 68 g and SD 1.7 g. A student calculates CV as 68/1.7 × 100 = 4000%. Find the correct CV and identify the error.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: CV expresses the SD as a percentage of the mean, not the mean as a percentage of the SD.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. CV = 1.7/68 × 100 = 2.50%.
  2. The student inverted the ratio. The numerator must be SD and the denominator must be the mean.

options.label: Mean and SD were put in the wrong positions
The numerator should be variance instead of SD

questions.title: Keep the original SD when calculating CV
questions.promptHtml:
Positive measured liquid volumes have mean 0.240 L and SD 0.018 L. A trainee first rounds the SD to 0.02 L and reports CV = 8.33%. Calculate CV from the supplied unrounded summaries.

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Use all supplied significant digits in the ratio. Round only the final percentage.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. CV = 0.018/0.240 × 100 = 7.50%.
  2. The early rounding changed the numerator by more than 11%, producing an avoidable difference in CV.

questions.title: Combining groups changes the relevant mean and spread
questions.promptHtml:
Two complete groups of positive volumes are A: 9, 10, 11 mL and B: 99, 100, 101 mL. The target population is now all six volumes together. Its population variance is 2025⅔ mL².

Calculate the combined mean, population SD and CV. Is averaging the two separate group CVs a valid shortcut here?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The combined variation includes the large separation between the group means.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Combined mean = (9 + 10 + 11 + 99 + 100 + 101)/6 = 55.00 mL.
  2. Population SD = √(2025 + 2/3) ≈ 45.01 mL.
  3. Combined CV = √(2025 + 2/3)/55 × 100 ≈ 81.83%.
  4. Averaging group CVs ignores the separation of the means and is not a valid shortcut for the combined CV.

fields.label: Can you obtain this combined CV by averaging the two group CVs?

questions.title: Translate a CV limit into an SD limit
questions.promptHtml:
A positive-fill process has mean 425 mL. Its quality target requires CV ≤ 3%. Find the largest SD allowed by this target. The observed SD is 14.1 mL; does it satisfy the target?

Keep full precision while working. Give numerical answers to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Rearrange the limiting equation SD/425 × 100 = 3, then compare the observed SD with the limit.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Largest allowed SD = 425 × 3/100 = 12.75 mL.
  2. The observed 14.1 mL exceeds 12.75 mL, so it does not meet the target. Its CV is about 3.32%.

fields.label: Does observed SD 14.1 mL meet the target?

questions.title: Reconcile two kurtosis conventions
questions.promptHtml:
Two software packages analyse the same distribution. Package A reports Pearson kurtosis = 2.4, with a normal benchmark of 3. Package B reports excess kurtosis = −0.6, with a normal benchmark of 0.

Do the reports agree, and how is the distribution classified relative to the normal benchmark?
questions.hint: Excess kurtosis equals Pearson kurtosis minus 3. Compare values only after aligning their conventions.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Package A’s excess value is 2.4 − 3 = −0.6, so the reports agree.
  2. The value is below the normal benchmark, so the distribution is platykurtic.
  3. A negative excess kurtosis is possible; it does not mean a negative variance or SD.

options.label: No: kurtosis must have the same numerical value under every convention
No: a negative excess kurtosis is impossible

questions.title: Separate SD from kurtosis
questions.promptHtml:
Two production processes have the same mean and the same population SD of 4 units. Their supplied Pearson kurtosis values are A = 2 and B = 7 (normal benchmark = 3).

A manager says the kurtosis values must also be equal because the SDs are equal. Evaluate this statement.
questions.hint: SD summarises average squared deviations. Kurtosis contains additional information about extreme deviations relative to spread.
questions.solutionHtml: The manager is incorrect. Equal SDs do not require equal distribution shapes or equal kurtosis. Process B has the higher supplied kurtosis, reflecting greater influence of extreme standardized deviations. The SDs can still be equal. These summaries alone do not tell us the exact probability of exceeding any chosen production limit.

options.label: Correct: equal SDs force equal kurtosis
Incorrect: equal SDs can coexist with different shapes and kurtosis
Incorrect only because process A must have negative variance
The figures prove process B exceeds every possible limit more often

questions.title: Kurtosis does not identify a skew direction
questions.promptHtml:
A report gives a distribution’s Pearson kurtosis as 6.2, compared with the normal benchmark 3. No histogram or skewness measure is provided.

Which description is supported, and can the direction of skewness be determined from this number alone?
questions.hint: Kurtosis compares extreme standardized deviations with a reference. Skewness concerns an imbalance between the two sides.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. 6.2 exceeds 3, so the distribution is leptokurtic relative to the normal benchmark.
  2. Skew direction is not determined by kurtosis alone. A distribution with this kurtosis could be symmetric or asymmetric; a positive kurtosis value does not mean positive skewness.

fields.label: What can be concluded about skewness?

options.label: It must be positively skewed because 6.2 is positive
It must be negatively skewed because extreme values exist
It must be symmetric because kurtosis is supplied
The direction cannot be determined from kurtosis alone

questions.title: A normal benchmark is not a proof of normality
questions.promptHtml:
A distribution has supplied excess kurtosis = 0, using the convention in which a normal distribution has excess kurtosis 0.

A student writes: “This proves that the distribution is normal and contains no extreme observations.” Which correction is best?
questions.hint: Matching one summary measure with a reference distribution does not establish every feature of its shape.
questions.solutionHtml: The justified description is mesokurtic under the stated convention. Zero excess kurtosis matches the normal benchmark, but it does not prove normality or the absence of extreme observations. Kurtosis is one summary of shape, not a complete description of a distribution.

options.label: No correction: both conclusions necessarily follow
It matches the normal kurtosis benchmark, but neither conclusion is guaranteed
It proves the distribution is uniform instead
It proves SD is zero because excess kurtosis is zero

questions.title: Do not classify kurtosis from peak height alone
questions.promptHtml:
Two histograms use the same measurement units. Histogram A has a taller central bar. A separate calculation supplies Pearson kurtosis A = 2.1 and B = 4.8, with a normal benchmark of 3.

A student calls A leptokurtic solely because its central bar is taller. Which distribution has the higher supplied kurtosis, and what is wrong with the student’s method?
questions.hint: Use the stated numerical convention. A histogram’s central bar alone does not describe the extreme deviations that influence kurtosis.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. B has the higher supplied kurtosis because 4.8 > 2.1. Relative to 3, B is leptokurtic and A is platykurtic.
  2. Central peak height alone is insufficient. Kurtosis concerns the influence of extreme deviations relative to overall spread. A tall central bar cannot override the supplied kurtosis values.

options.label: Equal because the measurement units match
Peak height alone does not determine kurtosis
Kurtosis values must equal the measurement units
A Pearson kurtosis below 3 is impossible
The tallest bar always determines tail direction and kurtosis

questions.title: Organise lunch orders
questions.promptHtml:
A café records these 12 lunch orders:

Rice, Noodles, Rice, Salad, Soup, Noodles, Rice, Salad, Rice, Soup, Noodles, Rice

Complete the frequency count for each category. Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: Count how many times each category appears. The four frequencies should add to 12.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Rice appears 5 times; Noodles appears 3 times.
  2. Salad appears 2 times; Soup appears 2 times.
  3. Check: 5 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 12 orders.

questions.title: Compare commuting methods
questions.promptHtml:
How 60 students travel to campus
MethodFrequency
Cycling12
Walking18
Bus30

Find the relative frequency for Walking as a decimal to 2 decimal places. Then express it as a percentage to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: Relative frequency = category frequency ÷ total. Multiply that decimal by 100 for the percentage.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total students = 12 + 18 + 30 = 60.
  2. Walking relative frequency = 18 ÷ 60 = 0.30.
  3. Percentage frequency = 0.30 × 100 = 30.0%. Thus 30% of the surveyed students walk to campus.

fields.label: Relative frequency as a decimal (2 d.p.)

questions.title: Count low and high daily totals
questions.promptHtml:
Number of support tickets per day over 20 days
Tickets in a dayFrequency (days)
0–94
10–197
20–296
30–393

How many days had fewer than 30 tickets? How many days had at least 20 tickets? Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: For fewer than 30, add the first three frequencies. For at least 20, add the last two.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Cumulative frequency below 30 = 4 + 7 + 6 = 17 days.
  2. Frequency at or above 20 = 6 + 3 = 9 days.
  3. Check the overall total: 4 + 7 + 6 + 3 = 20 days.

questions.title: Interpret an interval
questions.promptHtml:
Waiting times are measured to the nearest whole minute. One class interval is labelled 10–19 minutes, and the next is 20–29 minutes.

Find the midpoint, the lower continuous class boundary and the class width. Give all answers to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: The midpoint is the average of the class limits. For whole-minute measurements, the continuous boundaries lie half a minute outside the limits.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Midpoint = (10 + 19) ÷ 2 = 14.5 minutes.
  2. The continuous boundaries are 9.5 and 19.5, so the lower boundary is 9.5 minutes.
  3. Class width = 19.5 − 9.5 = 10.0 minutes, not 19 − 10.

questions.title: Draw a survey category
questions.promptHtml:
In a survey of 80 students, 24 choose the library as their preferred study location.

Calculate the percentage of students and the angle for the Library sector in a pie chart. Give whole-number answers.
questions.hint: Use 24 ÷ 80 as the fraction of the circle. A complete circle contains 360 degrees.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Library proportion = 24 ÷ 80 = 0.30.
  2. Percentage = 0.30 × 100 = 30%.
  3. Sector angle = 0.30 × 360° = 108°.

questions.title: Read grouped delivery times
questions.promptHtml:
The histogram represents 20 deliveries. Every interval includes its lower boundary and excludes its upper boundary; for example, 5 to under 10 minutes.

Select the interval with the highest frequency, then enter the number of deliveries that took less than 10 minutes.
questions.hint: All class widths are equal, so compare bar heights directly. For less than 10 minutes, add the first two bars.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The tallest bar has frequency 8 and represents 5 to under 10 minutes. This is the modal class.
  2. Deliveries below 10 minutes = 4 + 8 = 12 deliveries.
  3. The total frequency is 4 + 8 + 6 + 2 = 20, matching the number of deliveries.

questions.title: Read a frequency polygon
questions.promptHtml:
This frequency polygon groups whole-minute waiting times into classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39 and 40–49 minutes. The two extra zero points only close the line.

For the 20–29 minute class, give the horizontal coordinate and its frequency. Then give the total number of patients. Use 1 decimal place for the coordinate and whole numbers for the counts.
questions.hint: Frequency polygons plot class midpoints on the horizontal axis. Sum the four nonzero class frequencies for the total.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. The 20–29 midpoint is (20 + 29) ÷ 2 = 24.5 minutes.
  2. At x = 24.5, the frequency is 7 patients.
  3. Total frequency = 3 + 7 + 5 + 1 = 16 patients. The closing zero points add no observations.

questions.title: Read cumulative waiting times
questions.promptHtml:
This ogive shows the cumulative number of patients with waits below each time boundary.

How many waited less than 30 minutes? How many waited from 20 up to, but not including, 30 minutes? What percentage waited less than 20 minutes? Enter whole numbers.
questions.hint: An ogive gives cumulative totals. Subtract two cumulative totals to find the frequency between their boundaries.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. At 30 minutes, the cumulative count is 18 patients.
  2. Count from 20 to under 30 minutes = cumulative below 30 − cumulative below 20 = 18 − 10 = 8 patients.
  3. The total is 20 patients. Percentage below 20 minutes = (10 ÷ 20) × 100 = 50%.

questions.title: Summarise category Vegetarian
questions.promptHtml:
CategoryFrequency
Vegetarian6
Chicken12
Fish8
Noodles14

Find the total frequency, relative frequency of Vegetarian, and percentage frequency of Vegetarian. Give relative frequency to 3 decimal places.
questions.hint: Relative frequency is a proportion; percentage frequency is that proportion multiplied by 100.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total = 40.
  2. Relative frequency = 6/40 = 0.150; percentage = 15.00%.

questions.title: Summarise category Walk
questions.promptHtml:
CategoryFrequency
Bus18
Walk9
Cycle6
Rail12

Find the total frequency, relative frequency of Walk, and percentage frequency of Walk. Give relative frequency to 3 decimal places.
questions.hint: Relative frequency is a proportion; percentage frequency is that proportion multiplied by 100.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total = 45.
  2. Relative frequency = 9/45 = 0.200; percentage = 20.00%.

questions.title: Summarise category AB
questions.promptHtml:
CategoryFrequency
A12
B8
AB4
O16

Find the total frequency, relative frequency of AB, and percentage frequency of AB. Give relative frequency to 3 decimal places.
questions.hint: Relative frequency is a proportion; percentage frequency is that proportion multiplied by 100.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total = 40.
  2. Relative frequency = 4/40 = 0.100; percentage = 10.00%.

questions.title: Summarise category Morning
questions.promptHtml:
CategoryFrequency
Morning15
Afternoon21
Evening24

Find the total frequency, relative frequency of Morning, and percentage frequency of Morning. Give relative frequency to 3 decimal places.
questions.hint: Relative frequency is a proportion; percentage frequency is that proportion multiplied by 100.
questions.solutionHtml:
1. Total = 60.
  2. Relative frequency = 15/60 = 0.250; percentage = 25.00%.

questions.title: Summarise category Phone
questions.promptHtml:
CategoryFrequency
Online28
Phone12
In person10

Find the total frequency, relative frequency of Phone, and percentage frequency of Phone. Give relative frequency to 3 decimal places.
questions.hint: Relative frequency is a proportion; percentage frequency is that proportion multiplied by 100.

extension.modelAnswerHtml: The box runs from 10.5 to 25 minutes, with the median line at 17. Whiskers extend to 8 and 30 minutes. IQR = 14.5 minutes.
rubric: An even numerical scale and minutes are shown.
The box starts at Q₁ = 10.5 and ends at Q₃ = 25.
The median is at 17; min-to-max whiskers end at 8 and 30.

questions.title: Read equal medians and different spreads
questions.promptHtml:
The whiskers below show the minimum and maximum. Exact summaries are A: 5, 15, 20, 25, 40; B: 10, 17, 20, 23, 30 minutes.

Which comparison is supported?
questions.hint: Compare the median lines, then the widths of the boxes on the same scale.
questions.solutionHtml: Both medians are 20 minutes. A has IQR 25 − 15 = 10; B has IQR 23 − 17 = 6. Thus B has the smaller IQR. Matching medians do not imply identical distributions.

fields.label: Best comparison
fields.answer: Both medians are 20; B has the smaller IQR

options.value: A has the smaller median and IQR

questions.title: A lower median does not mean every value is lower
questions.promptHtml: Delivery service A has a median of 18 minutes and range 8–36 minutes. Service B has a median of 22 minutes and range 12–30 minutes. A student concludes: “Every A delivery was quicker than every B delivery.” Is that conclusion justified?
questions.hint: A median describes the middle, not every observation. Compare A’s maximum with B’s minimum.
questions.solutionHtml: No. A includes a delivery taking 36 minutes, while B includes one taking 12 minutes. A’s lower median indicates a lower central delivery time, not universal superiority.

fields.label: Best evaluation
fields.answer: No; the overlapping ranges include some A times above some B times

questions.topic: What grouped data can tell us
questions.title: Explain why a grouped mean is an estimate
questions.promptHtml: A researcher replaces every observation in each interval by that interval’s midpoint, then calculates Σ(fm)/Σf. Why may this differ from the exact mean?
questions.hint: Think about which individual values remain unknown once only interval frequencies are stored.
questions.solutionHtml: The original observations need not equal their class midpoints. The calculation treats each class as if all its values occurred at the midpoint. The estimate may be above, below or equal to the exact mean.

fields.label: Reason
fields.answer: The original observations need not equal their class midpoints

options.value: A mean can never use frequencies
options.label: A mean can never use frequencies

questions.topic: What grouped data can tell us
questions.title: A threshold inside a class is uncertain
questions.promptHtml:
Leftover mass x (g)Meals
0 ≤ x < 209
20 ≤ x < 4012
40 ≤ x < 607

Only this grouped table is available. How many meals had less than 30 g of leftovers? Give the smallest and largest possible counts; do not assume values are evenly spread inside a class.
questions.hint: The first nine meals are definitely below 30 g. Any number from zero to all twelve in the middle class might also be below 30 g.
questions.solutionHtml: The exact count is unknown. The smallest possible count is 9 if all middle-class values are at least 30 g. The largest is 9 + 12 = 21 if all are below 30 g.

questions.topic: What grouped data can tell us
questions.title: Same grouped table, different exact means
questions.promptHtml:
Dataset A is 11, 12, 21, 22. Dataset B is 18, 19, 28, 29. Both give two values in 10 ≤ x < 20 and two in 20 ≤ x < 30.

Find the midpoint-based estimated mean for either grouped table. Which statement about the original datasets is correct?
questions.hint: The shared midpoints are 15 and 25. Compare what grouping retains with what it loses.
questions.solutionHtml: The grouped estimate is (2×15 + 2×25)/4 = 20. Exact means are 66/4 = 16.5 for A and 94/4 = 23.5 for B. Thus identical grouped tables can hide different exact means.

fields.label: Exact means
fields.answer: The exact means differ even though the grouped estimates match

options.label: A grouped table preserves every original observation

questions.promptHtml:

questions.hint: At 50%, the required rise from 20% is 30 percentage points out of the interval’s full rise of 40 percentage points.
questions.solutionHtml: The median lies in 10–20 minutes. Estimated median = 10 + [(50 − 20)/(60 − 20)]×10 = 17.5 minutes. Straight-line interpolation assumes an even spread within that interval; the original individual times are unknown.

questions.title: Changing histogram intervals changes detail
questions.promptHtml: The same 60 waiting times are graphed using intervals of width 5 minutes, then using intervals of width 10 minutes over the same overall range. What should remain the same, and what may change?
questions.hint: Regrouping changes the display, not the original observations.
questions.solutionHtml: The total remains 60. Wider intervals combine neighbouring values and can hide gaps, clusters or differences in shape. They do not change the raw times.

fields.label: Best statement
fields.answer: The total frequency remains 60, but wider intervals can hide detail

options.value: The total frequency remains 60, but wider intervals can hide detail

questions.title: Count a lower-inclusive Excel interval
questions.promptHtml: As in the café workbook, column F contains leftover mass in grams. In a small practice sheet, F2:F7 contains 20, 39.9, 40, 55, 59.9, 60. Select the formula for 40 ≤ x < 60, then give its result.
questions.hint: COUNTIFS requires both conditions to be true for the same cell. Include 40 and exclude 60.
questions.solutionHtml: =COUNTIFS(F2:F7,">=40",F2:F7,"<60") counts 40, 55 and 59.9: 3 meals.

questions.title: Count meal identifiers, not numeric cells
questions.promptHtml: The workbook’s Data sheet has a text header in A1 and 300 nonblank text meal IDs in A2:A301, with no blank IDs. A student enters =COUNT(A2:A301) and gets 0. Which formula counts the meals correctly?
questions.hint: COUNT counts numeric cells. COUNTA counts nonblank cells, including text. Exclude the header.
questions.solutionHtml: =COUNTA(A2:A301) returns 300. COUNT ignores the text IDs. Including A1 would incorrectly count the header as an extra meal.

questions.title: Apply fixed references to category shares
questions.promptHtml:
A practice sheet follows the workbook layout: H11:H14 lists four meal types, I11:I14 contains frequencies 9, 6, 3, 2, and I15 contains their total. A student enters =I11/$I$15 in J11 and copies it to J12.

Choose the copied formula and calculate the percentage displayed in J12 to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: The numerator row moves down by one. Dollar signs keep both the total’s column and row fixed.
questions.solutionHtml: The copied formula is =I12/$I$15. The total is 9 + 6 + 3 + 2 = 20, so the second category share is 6/20 = 0.30, displayed as 30.0%.

questions.title: Repair a misleading bar-chart baseline
questions.promptHtml: A bar chart compares 48 tea orders with 52 coffee orders. Its vertical axis starts at 45, making the coffee bar look more than twice as tall. What is the best repair for a fair comparison of counts?
questions.hint: Bar lengths represent magnitudes. A common zero baseline allows their lengths to be compared fairly.
questions.solutionHtml: Start the frequency axis at zero and use an even scale. Coffee has only 4 more orders than tea. Truncating the baseline makes the small difference appear much larger.

fields.label: Best repair
fields.answer: Start the frequency axis at zero and use an even scale

options.value: Start the frequency axis at zero and use an even scale
options.label: Start the frequency axis at zero and use an even scale

options.value: Use a different vertical scale for each category
options.label: Use a different vertical scale for each category

options.value: Relabel the orders as percentages without changing the bars
options.label: Relabel the orders as percentages without changing the bars

questions.title: Clinic case: build, summarise and choose a graph
questions.promptHtml:
A clinic records these 12 waiting times in minutes:

3, 4, 5, 8, 9, 11, 13, 14, 17, 18, 22, 27

Group them into 0 ≤ t < 10, 10 ≤ t < 20 and 20 ≤ t < 30. Find the frequency in the middle interval, calculate the midpoint-based estimated mean to 2 decimal places, and choose a graph to show the grouped distribution.
questions.hint: Count each observation exactly once. The midpoints are 5, 15 and 25 minutes. Divide the weighted midpoint total by 12.
questions.solutionHtml: Frequencies are 5, 5, 2. The estimate is (5×5 + 5×15 + 2×25)/12 = 12.50 minutes. A histogram displays the grouped numerical distribution. The exact raw mean is 151/12 ≈ 12.58 minutes, illustrating the small information loss from grouping.

options.value: Scatterplot of each time against itself
options.label: Scatterplot of each time against itself

options.value: A single total with no intervals
options.label: A single total with no intervals

extension.promptHtml: Draw the histogram in Excel or on paper. Use the stated intervals and label both axes. This practical extension is self-checked, not automatically marked.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: Use touching equal-width bars over 0–10, 10–20 and 20–30 with heights 5, 5 and 2. Title: Clinic waiting times. Horizontal axis: Waiting time (minutes). Vertical axis: Number of patients. The vertical scale begins at zero.
rubric: All 12 patients are included once; frequencies are 5, 5, 2.
The intervals are adjacent and bars touch; the scale is even.
Both axes and their units/count meanings are labelled.
The chart has a clear title and the frequency axis starts at zero.

questions.title: Café case: evidence for a portion trial
questions.promptHtml:
These simulated teaching data represent eight café meals. Each row belongs to one meal.

Portion (g)Leftovers (g)

Find the percentage of meals with less than 40 g left over. Then choose the supported interpretation and a sensible way to investigate a smaller-portion option.
questions.hint: Four rows are below 40 g. Look for an overall pattern while allowing exceptions. A recommendation should collect both waste and satisfaction evidence fairly.
questions.solutionHtml: Four of eight meals are below 40 g: 4/8 × 100 = 50.0%. There is an overall positive association, with exceptions; it does not prove a single cause. A small comparison measuring both leftovers and satisfaction is defensible. Use the same neutral satisfaction question with randomly selected customers from each option, rather than selecting only favourable replies.

extension.promptHtml: Enter the eight paired rows in Excel and create a scatterplot. Then write a short recommendation using one numerical fact and one limitation, and explain how you would check satisfaction fairly across the two portion options. This practical extension is self-checked, not automatically marked.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: Use portion mass (g) on the horizontal axis and leftovers (g) on the vertical axis; plot all eight original pairs without independently sorting columns. Example: “Four of eight meals left under 40 g, and larger portions generally had more leftovers. Trial an optional smaller portion, because these eight observational meals do not prove that portion size caused the differences. Measure satisfaction by asking a randomly selected set of customers from each portion option the same neutral question.”
rubric: All eight pairs remain matched and both axes show grams.
The chart is an XY scatterplot with a clear title.
The recommendation includes a correct numerical fact and an appropriate action.
The limitation avoids a causal guarantee and recognises the small observational dataset.
The satisfaction check uses neutral wording and fair selection across both options.

questions.title: Audit a library service tally
questions.promptHtml:
A library records one main reason for each visit: Borrow, Return, Study, Borrow, Study, Study, Return, Borrow, Study, Return, Borrow, Study.

Find the Study frequency and the total number of visits.
questions.hint: Tally every listed visit once, including repeated reasons.
questions.solutionHtml: Study occurs 5 times. The full list contains 12 visits. The category frequencies are Borrow 4, Return 3 and Study 5.

questions.title: Recover the survey size from a share
questions.promptHtml: In a survey with one main commuting method per person, 18 people cycle. This is exactly 15% of all respondents. How many people responded?
questions.hint: The cycling frequency is 0.15 times the total.
questions.solutionHtml: 0.15n = 18, so n = 18/0.15 = 120 respondents.

questions.title: Complete a relative-frequency table
questions.promptHtml:
Appointment typeRelative frequency
Routine0.48
Follow-up0.27
Urgent?

All 200 appointments belong to exactly one listed type. Find the missing relative frequency and the number of urgent appointments.
questions.hint: The relative frequencies sum to 1. Multiply the missing share by 200.
questions.solutionHtml: Urgent share = 1 − 0.48 − 0.27 = 0.25. Urgent appointments = 200×0.25 = 50.

questions.title: Use recorded responses as the denominator
questions.promptHtml: A help desk sent 100 feedback invitations. There were 80 replies: 52 Good, 20 Fair and 8 Poor. Calculate the percentage of respondents who selected Good.
questions.hint: The requested group is the people who replied, so the denominator is 80.
questions.solutionHtml: 52/80×100 = 65.0%. Say 65% of respondents; the result does not describe all invited people.

questions.title: Decide whether a pie chart fits a survey
questions.promptHtml: Forty staff could choose every training topic they wanted. Twenty-five selected Excel, 22 selected writing and 13 selected presentation skills. Is a pie chart with one slice per topic suitable for showing percentages of staff?

fields.label: Best answer
fields.answer: No; the categories overlap and do not divide staff into exclusive parts

options.value: Yes; every survey should use a pie chart
options.label: Yes; every survey should use a pie chart

options.value: No; the categories overlap and do not divide staff into exclusive parts
options.label: No; the categories overlap and do not divide staff into exclusive parts

options.value: No; pie charts cannot display percentages
options.label: No; pie charts cannot display percentages

questions.hint: A pie represents one whole divided into nonoverlapping categories. Here one person can contribute to several counts.
questions.solutionHtml: The topic counts total 60 for only 40 staff, because responses overlap. A bar chart can show the separate topic counts; a pie of percentages of staff would misleadingly imply exclusive parts of one whole.

questions.title: Read a support-request bar chart
questions.promptHtml:
The bars show the main issue for each of 50 support requests.

How many more Login than Print requests were recorded? What percentage were Other?
questions.hint: Read the bar heights and use the stated total of 50.
questions.solutionHtml: The difference is 18 − 10 = 8 requests. Other = 8/50×100 = 16.0%.

questions.title: Read a labelled booking pie chart
questions.promptHtml:
The chart represents 150 clinic bookings. Each booking has one type.

How many were Review bookings, and what sector angle represents New bookings?
questions.hint: Convert 30% of the total to a count; convert 20% of a full 360° turn to an angle.
questions.solutionHtml: Review count = 0.30×150 = 45. New sector angle = 0.20×360° = 72.0°.

questions.title: Compare shares when survey sizes differ
questions.promptHtml:
CampusBus usersRespondents
North3660
South48100

Which campus has the larger bus-user percentage? By how many percentage points?
questions.hint: Calculate a percentage for each campus before comparing them.
questions.solutionHtml: North: 36/60 = 60%. South: 48/100 = 48%. North has the higher share by 12.0 percentage points, although South has more bus users in absolute numbers.

questions.title: Check a rounded percentage total
questions.promptHtml: Three equally common categories each contain 1 of 3 observations. A table displays each percentage to one decimal place as 33.3%, so the displayed total is 99.9%. What is the best explanation?

fields.label: Explanation
fields.answer: Rounding each percentage can make the displayed total differ slightly from 100%

options.label: Rounding each percentage can make the displayed total differ slightly from 100%

options.label: Each category should instead be displayed as 30%

questions.hint: Distinguish the exact fraction 1/3 from its rounded percentage.
questions.solutionHtml: The exact shares sum to 1, or 100%. Rounding each 33.333…% to 33.3% gives a displayed total of 99.9%. This small discrepancy is a rounding effect, not evidence of a missing observation.

questions.title: Recover a percentage from a pie sector
questions.promptHtml: A report shows a category as a 126° sector of a pie chart. The survey has 80 respondents, each in exactly one category. Find the category percentage and count.
questions.hint: The sector is 126/360 of the whole.
questions.solutionHtml: Share = 126/360 = 0.35 = 35.0%. Count = 80×0.35 = 28.

questions.title: Avoid counting the total row twice
questions.promptHtml:
ResultFrequency

A student adds all three displayed rows and uses 48 as the denominator for the Pass percentage. What percentage should be reported?

questions.title: Represent a zero-frequency category honestly
questions.promptHtml: A form offers Bus, Walk, Cycle and Car. No respondent chooses Cycle. The teacher wants the chart to show all four available options. How should Cycle appear?

fields.label: Chart treatment

questions.title: Order satisfaction bars meaningfully
questions.promptHtml: Satisfaction categories are Poor, Fair, Good and Excellent. Which order makes their natural progression clearest in a bar chart?
questions.hint: These categories have an order in their meaning, even though they are not numerical measurements.
questions.solutionHtml: Poor, Fair, Good, Excellent preserves the ordinal progression. Alphabetical or random ordering would hide that structure.

questions.title: Make missing responses visible in a table
questions.promptHtml: A survey file contains 50 people. Meal preference is recorded as Rice for 20 and Noodles for 25; five people left the item blank. You want a table of all 50 people. What should the final row be?

options.label: Ignore the blanks but label the table as all 50 people

questions.title: Compare counts without confusing sample size
questions.promptHtml: A chart shows that Clinic A received 30 Good ratings and Clinic B received 45. The clinics surveyed 40 and 90 patients respectively. Which statement is correct?

questions.title: Label a horizontal bar chart
questions.promptHtml: A horizontal bar chart shows how many patients attend each clinic department. Department names are on the vertical axis. What should the horizontal axis label say?
questions.hint: In a horizontal bar chart, the bar length runs horizontally and represents the measured frequency.
questions.solutionHtml: The horizontal axis should be Number of patients. Department names label the categories on the vertical axis.

questions.title: Diagnose a sector-angle mistake

options.label: A pie chart must always contain 100 sectors

questions.solutionHtml: The share is 12/48 = 0.25. Sector angle = 0.25×360° = 90.0°. The number 25 is the percentage, not the angle.

questions.title: Combine categories before drawing the pie
questions.promptHtml: A training survey has 80 responses: Introductory 18, Intermediate 22 and Advanced 40. A report combines the first two categories into Foundation training. Find its percentage and pie-chart angle.
questions.hint: Combine the two frequencies first, using the same total of 80.
questions.solutionHtml: Foundation frequency = 18 + 22 = 40. Its share is 40/80 = 50.0%, so its sector is 180.0°.

extension.promptHtml: Optional drawing practice — self-check, not automatically marked. Draw the pie chart after combining Introductory and Intermediate into Foundation training. Include a title, the total number of responses, and category labels with percentages.

A clear title explains what the pie chart represents.

questions.title: Identify the denominator in a two-way table

questions.title: Separate percentage points from percent change
questions.promptHtml: In one cohort, 40% choose a bus pass; in the next cohort, 50% do. A chart labels the difference as “10 percentage points.” Is that label correct?

fields.label: Evaluation
fields.answer: Yes; the difference between the two percentages is 10 percentage points

questions.title: Check a catering claim against the table
questions.promptHtml:

The caterer says, “More than two thirds of these 50 orders were Rice or Noodles.” Calculate their combined percentage and evaluate the claim.

questions.solutionHtml: (18 + 16)/50×100 = 68.0%. Two thirds is about 66.67%, so the claim is supported for these recorded orders.

questions.title: Allocate decimal boundary measurements
questions.promptHtml: Temperatures are 22.8, 23.5, 24.1, 24.5, 24.49, 25.5 °C. Count the measurements in 23.5 ≤ t < 24.5, then calculate that interval’s midpoint.
questions.hint: Include the lower endpoint but exclude the upper endpoint.
questions.solutionHtml: The interval contains 23.5, 24.1 and 24.49: 3 measurements. Its midpoint is (23.5 + 24.5)/2 = 24.00°C.

questions.title: Group temperatures below zero
questions.promptHtml: Freezer temperatures are −12, −10, −9, −5, −1, 0 °C. The intervals are −15 ≤ t < −10, −10 ≤ t < −5 and −5 ≤ t < 5. How many values belong in the middle interval?
questions.hint: The lower endpoint −10 is included. The upper endpoint −5 goes in the next interval.
questions.solutionHtml: Only −10 and −9 belong in the middle interval, so the frequency is 2.

questions.title: Repair overlapping numerical classes
questions.promptHtml: A table uses 0 ≤ x ≤ 10, 10 ≤ x ≤ 20 and 20 ≤ x ≤ 30. The raw data include x = 10 and x = 20. What repair gives every value from 0 up to, but not including, 30 exactly one class?

options.value: Remove every observation equal to a boundary
options.label: Remove every observation equal to a boundary

questions.hint: Adjacent intervals must not overlap or leave gaps at shared boundaries.
questions.solutionHtml: Use lower-inclusive, upper-exclusive intervals. Then 10 belongs only to the second class and 20 only to the third. The stated covered range excludes 30.

questions.title: Choose the minimum equal-width coverage
questions.promptHtml: Observed lengths range from 2.4 cm to 32.0 cm. Use width-10 intervals, starting at 0, with lower-inclusive upper-exclusive boundaries. What is the minimum number of classes needed, and the midpoint of the last class?
questions.hint: Three classes starting at 0 end at 30 and would miss the largest observation.
questions.solutionHtml: Use [0,10), [10,20), [20,30), [30,40): 4 classes. The final midpoint is (30 + 40)/2 = 35.0 cm.

questions.title: Find boundaries for readings rounded to tenths
questions.promptHtml: Mass readings are rounded to the nearest 0.1 g. A class is labelled 10.0–10.9 g. Give its continuous lower and upper boundaries and its midpoint, each to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The half-unit rounding adjustment is 0.05 g because readings are rounded to 0.1 g.
questions.solutionHtml: Boundaries are 10.0 − 0.05 = 9.95 g and 10.9 + 0.05 = 10.95 g. Midpoint = (9.95 + 10.95)/2 = 10.45 g.

questions.title: Recognise an open-ended class
questions.promptHtml: A delivery table ends with the class 80 minutes or more. No upper limit is given. Can its midpoint be calculated from that label alone?

fields.label: Best answer
fields.answer: No; an upper boundary or an additional assumption is needed

options.value: No; an upper boundary or an additional assumption is needed
options.label: No; an upper boundary or an additional assumption is needed

options.value: No; all numerical intervals lack midpoints
options.label: No; all numerical intervals lack midpoints

questions.hint: The midpoint calculation needs both the lower and upper boundaries.
questions.solutionHtml: No. The label provides a lower boundary of 80 but no upper boundary. A midpoint cannot be justified without more information or an explicitly stated assumption.

questions.title: Weight the midpoints by their frequencies
questions.promptHtml:
Waiting time t (minutes)Frequency
0 ≤ t < 102
10 ≤ t < 206
20 ≤ t < 3012

Estimate the mean from class midpoints. Give your answer to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Multiply each midpoint by its class frequency before adding.
questions.solutionHtml: Midpoints are 5, 15 and 25. Estimated mean = (2×5 + 6×15 + 12×25)/20 = 400/20 = 20.00 minutes. An unweighted average of the three midpoints would incorrectly give 15.

questions.title: Compare a grouped estimate with raw observations
questions.promptHtml: Exact times are 2, 3, 8, 12, 14, 18 minutes. Group them as 0 ≤ t < 10 and 10 ≤ t < 20. Calculate the exact mean and the midpoint-based estimated mean, both to 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: The two classes have equal frequencies, but their actual observations need not average to their midpoints.
questions.solutionHtml: The exact sum is 57, so the raw mean is 57/6 = 9.50 minutes. Group frequencies are 3 and 3; estimated mean = (3×5 + 3×15)/6 = 10.00 minutes.

questions.title: Do not invent a midpoint for the final class
questions.promptHtml:

4 ≤ d < 810

options.value: Midpoints can never be used for grouped means
options.label: Midpoints can never be used for grouped means

options.value: The final midpoint of 10 assumes an upper boundary that was not supplied
options.label: The final midpoint of 10 assumes an upper boundary that was not supplied

questions.hint: A class ending “or more” is open-ended.
questions.solutionHtml: Using 10 implies an assumed upper boundary of 12 for the last class. The table does not justify that assumption, so a single midpoint-based estimate cannot be obtained from these labels alone.

questions.promptHtml:

questions.hint: Estimate in seconds first, then divide by 60.
questions.solutionHtml: Estimated mean = (4×30 + 8×90 + 4×150)/16 = 90 seconds. This is 90/60 = 1.50 minutes.

questions.promptHtml:

Find the estimated mean duration for all 30 visits together, using class midpoints. Give 2 decimal places.
questions.hint: Combine corresponding class frequencies, then divide the combined weighted midpoint sum by the total count.
questions.solutionHtml: Combined frequencies are 8, 11 and 11. Estimated mean = (8×5 + 11×15 + 11×25)/30 = 480/30 = 16.00 minutes. Do not take an unweighted average of two means from unequal sample sizes.

questions.title: Recover a frequency from the estimated mean
questions.promptHtml:
Time t (minutes)Frequency

The midpoint-based estimated mean is exactly 13 minutes. Find k.
questions.hint: The weighted midpoint total is 4×5 + 15k + 2×25, and the number of observations is 6 + k.
questions.solutionHtml: (70 + 15k)/(6 + k) = 13. Therefore 70 + 15k = 78 + 13k, giving 2k = 8 and k = 4.

questions.topic: What grouped data can tell us
questions.title: Know when regrouping leaves the estimate unchanged
questions.promptHtml: A record is corrected from 21 to 29 minutes. Both values are in the same class, 20 ≤ t < 30. The class boundaries and all class frequencies remain unchanged. What happens to the midpoint-based estimated mean?

fields.label: Effect on grouped estimate
fields.answer: It stays unchanged, even though the exact raw-data mean increases

options.value: It stays unchanged, even though the exact raw-data mean increases
options.label: It stays unchanged, even though the exact raw-data mean increases

questions.hint: The grouped calculation uses only midpoints and frequencies, both unchanged here.
questions.solutionHtml: The grouped estimate stays unchanged. It still represents that observation by the same midpoint, 25. The raw-data sum rises by 8, so the exact mean rises by 8/n.

questions.title: Find a mode and range from leaves
questions.promptHtml:
Key: 3 | 2 = 32 minutes.

StemLeaves

Find the mode and range of these seven times.
questions.hint: Repeated leaves represent repeated values. Read the smallest and largest full values using the key.
questions.solutionHtml: The values are 18, 21, 25, 25, 29, 32 and 37. Mode = 25 minutes. Range = 37 − 18 = 19 minutes.

questions.promptHtml:
