questions.hint: Include both repeated 4.2 g observations and all greater values.
questions.solutionHtml: The qualifying masses are 4.2, 4.2, 4.7 and 5.1 g: 4 of 7. Percentage = 4/7×100 ≈ 57.1%.

questions.title: Identify what a missing key prevents
questions.promptHtml: A stem-and-leaf plot includes the entry 12 | 4, but its key and measurement unit have been omitted. Which statement is safest?

fields.label: Best interpretation

options.value: The entry cannot be interpreted uniquely until the key and unit are known

questions.hint: The digits alone do not tell you which place values or measurement units were intended.
questions.solutionHtml: A key specifies the place values, and the unit specifies the meaning. 12 | 4 could represent 124, 12.4 or another scale, so do not guess.

Which ordered dataset matches this plot exactly?
questions.hint: An empty stem adds no observation. Repeated leaves must remain repeated in the reconstructed list.
questions.solutionHtml: The plot represents 10, 15, 15, 32. Stem 2 is empty, so there is no observation in the twenties and no invented value of 20.

extension.promptHtml: Optional drawing practice — self-check, not automatically marked. Starting from the reconstructed values, write a complete ordered stem-and-leaf plot on paper. Include the empty stem, preserve repeated observations and supply a key with the time unit.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: Use stems 1, 2 and 3 in order. Stem 1 has leaves 0, 5, 5; stem 2 has no leaves; stem 3 has leaf 2. Key: 1 | 5 = 15 minutes. There are four leaves in total, representing 10, 15, 15 and 32 minutes.
rubric: Stems 1, 2 and 3 appear in ascending order, including empty stem 2.

questions.title: Choose a display that preserves exact readings

questions.solutionHtml: A stem-and-leaf plot with a key retains every individual reading while also showing the distribution. A grouped histogram does not reveal exact positions inside its intervals.

questions.title: Read a hospital waiting-time histogram
questions.promptHtml:
The bars show 30 waiting times. All intervals include the lower boundary and exclude the upper boundary.

Find the count below 10 minutes and the percentage who waited at least 15 minutes.
questions.hint: Add the first two bars for the first count. The last bar gives waits of at least 15 minutes.
questions.solutionHtml: Below 10 minutes: 3 + 9 = 12 patients. At least 15: 6/30×100 = 20.0%.

questions.title: Build histogram frequencies from decimal data
questions.promptHtml: Masses in grams are 0.8, 1.0, 1.9, 2.0, 2.0, 2.4, 2.9, 3.1. Use intervals 0 ≤ m < 1, 1 ≤ m < 2, 2 ≤ m < 3 and 3 ≤ m < 4. Give the four bar heights, in order.
questions.hint: Use the same lower-inclusive upper-exclusive rule at every boundary. Keep both observations equal to 2.0.
questions.solutionHtml: The four frequencies are 1, 2, 4, 1. They total 8. Boundary observations 1.0 and 2.0 enter the interval beginning at that value.

extension.promptHtml: Optional drawing practice — self-check, not automatically marked. Draw the histogram on paper or in a spreadsheet using the four stated intervals. Label both axes and add a clear title. Show the numerical class boundaries.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: Title: Distribution of measured masses. Horizontal axis: Mass (g), with boundaries 0, 1, 2, 3, 4. Vertical axis: Number of readings, starting at zero. Draw touching bars over [0,1), [1,2), [2,3), [3,4) with heights 1, 2, 4, 1 respectively. The frequencies total eight.
rubric: The four bases align with boundaries 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 g on an even numerical scale.
Bar heights are 1, 2, 4 and 1 and total eight readings.
Adjacent bars touch because the intervals are contiguous.
Both axes, the mass unit and a clear title are provided.

questions.promptHtml:
Two samples use intervals 0–10, 10–20 and 20–30 minutes, with lower-inclusive upper-exclusive boundaries. Polygon A is solid red; B is dashed blue. Each midpoint gives its interval’s percentage.

Which sample has the larger percentage below 10 minutes, and by how many percentage points?
questions.hint: For the first interval, compare the two points at midpoint 5.
questions.solutionHtml: At midpoint 5, A has 20% and B has 40%. Thus B has the larger percentage below 10 minutes by 20.0 percentage points.

questions.title: Interpret the closing points of a polygon
questions.promptHtml: A frequency polygon has actual class midpoints 15, 25 and 35, with frequencies 4, 9 and 7. It is closed using extra points (5, 0) and (45, 0). How many observations are represented, and do the closing points add observations?

questions.title: Read a cumulative-percentage graph as a count
questions.promptHtml:
The ogive summarises 50 laboratory processing times using lower-inclusive upper-exclusive classes.

How many times were below 30 minutes? How many were at least 30 minutes?
questions.hint: Read 80% at the boundary 30, convert it to a count, then use the complement.
questions.solutionHtml: Below 30 minutes: 0.80×50 = 40. At least 30 minutes: 50 − 40 = 10.

questions.title: Distinguish a known boundary count from an estimate
questions.promptHtml: A grouped table says 12 waits are below 10 minutes and 28 are below 20 minutes. The ogive joins these boundary points with a straight line. Which claim is justified?

fields.answer: The count below 20 is known; a count read at 15 is an estimate

options.label: The count below 20 is known; a count read at 15 is an estimate

questions.title: Fix a histogram that double-counts a boundary
questions.promptHtml: Raw values are 6, 10, 10, 14 and 18. A histogram uses 0 ≤ x < 10 and 10 ≤ x < 20. The student puts the two values of 10 in both bars, producing heights 3 and 4. What should the heights be?
questions.hint: A value equal to 10 belongs only in the interval beginning at 10.
questions.solutionHtml: The first bar contains only 6, so its height is 1. The second contains 10, 10, 14 and 18, so its height is 4. Total frequency is correctly 5.

questions.title: Start an ogive at the real lower boundary
questions.promptHtml: The first class of a length table is 50 ≤ x < 60 cm, followed by 60 ≤ x < 70 and 70 ≤ x < 80. No observation is below 50 cm. Which point starts the less-than ogive before adding the first class frequency?
questions.hint: At the first lower boundary, none of the observations has yet been accumulated.
questions.solutionHtml: Start at (50, 0): the cumulative count below 50 cm is zero. The first nonzero point belongs at the upper boundary 60.

questions.title: Check the final cumulative total
questions.promptHtml: A complete frequency table contains 36 observations. A student’s less-than ogive ends at cumulative frequency 41 after the final class. What does this indicate?

fields.label: Diagnosis

options.value: A valid result because cumulative values are always larger than n
options.label: A valid result because cumulative values are always larger than n

options.label: The vertical axis must show class midpoints

questions.hint: Each observation must be counted once in the complete cumulative total.
questions.solutionHtml: The final cumulative frequency must be 36. A value of 41 signals an error in the table, accumulation or plotting.

questions.title: Name both axes of a frequency histogram
questions.promptHtml: A hospital draws an equal-width frequency histogram for patient waiting times. Which pair of labels correctly distinguishes the measured variable from its frequency?

options.label: Horizontal: waiting time (minutes); vertical: number of patients

options.label: Horizontal: number of patients; vertical: class midpoint

questions.hint: The horizontal axis gives intervals of the numerical measurement; the vertical axis gives how many observations fall inside them.
questions.solutionHtml: Use waiting time (minutes) horizontally and number of patients vertically. This is a frequency histogram with equal-width classes.

questions.title: Choose the right adjacency for interval bars
questions.promptHtml: A graph displays masses in adjacent intervals 0–5, 5–10 and 10–15 g, each lower-inclusive and upper-exclusive. Which construction matches a histogram of this grouped variable?

options.label: Three dots with no numerical horizontal scale

options.label: A separate vertical scale for every bar

questions.solutionHtml: Histogram bars touch and their bases follow the numerical boundaries 0, 5, 10 and 15 g. Categorical bar charts use separated bars instead.

questions.title: Merge adjacent histogram intervals
questions.promptHtml:
The histogram uses 5-minute intervals and lower-inclusive upper-exclusive classes.

Redraw it with intervals 0 ≤ t < 10 and 10 ≤ t < 20. Give the new bar heights.
questions.hint: Combine neighbouring frequencies; the total number of observations stays the same.
questions.solutionHtml: The new heights are 2 + 5 = 7 and 7 + 6 = 13. Both displays represent 20 observations.

questions.title: Use the complement at a class boundary
questions.promptHtml: In a group of 64 processing times, a less-than cumulative table records 46 times below 30 seconds. How many are at least 30 seconds, and what percentage of all times is this?
questions.hint: “At least 30” is the complement of “below 30,” including any value exactly 30.
questions.solutionHtml: Count = 64 − 46 = 18. Percentage = 18/64×100 = 28.13% to 2 decimal places.

questions.title: Avoid claiming an exact mode from a histogram
questions.promptHtml: The tallest bar in an equal-width histogram is the interval 20 ≤ x < 30. A student says, “The mode must be exactly 25.” What is the best response?

fields.label: Best response
fields.answer: 20 ≤ x < 30 is the modal class; the exact mode cannot be identified from these grouped counts

options.value: The exact mode is always the midpoint of the tallest bar
options.label: The exact mode is always the midpoint of the tallest bar

options.value: 20 ≤ x < 30 is the modal class; the exact mode cannot be identified from these grouped counts
options.label: 20 ≤ x < 30 is the modal class; the exact mode cannot be identified from these grouped counts

options.value: A modal class must have frequency zero
options.label: A modal class must have frequency zero

questions.hint: A class frequency does not reveal which individual values occurred most often within it.
questions.solutionHtml: The histogram identifies a modal class, not necessarily an exact mode. The midpoint 25 is a convenient representative value, not evidence that 25 was the most frequent observation.

questions.title: Read a frequency polygon before calculating a share
questions.promptHtml:
The polygon uses class midpoints 5, 15, 25 and 35 for equal-width classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30 and 30–40. Boundaries are lower-inclusive and upper-exclusive.

What percentage of observations are in 20 ≤ t < 30?
questions.hint: Read the frequency at midpoint 25, then divide it by the sum of all four frequencies.
questions.solutionHtml: The interval’s frequency is 9. Total = 6 + 12 + 9 + 3 = 30. Share = 9/30×100 = 30.0%.

questions.title: Interpolate the 50% crossing on an ogive

Estimate the median waiting time to 2 decimal places.

questions.solutionHtml: Estimated median = 20 + [(50 − 40)/(80 − 40)]×10 = 22.50 minutes. This is an estimate because the individual positions within 20–30 minutes are unknown.

questions.promptHtml: An ogive has cumulative percentages 20% at 10 minutes, 60% at 20 minutes and 100% at 30 minutes. A student reads at 75% to find the median. Which percentage should be used, and what median does linear interpolation give to 2 decimal places?
questions.hint: The median is the 50th percentile, so read at 50%, between the first two points.

questions.hint: An unusual point is a reason to check the record and context; it is not automatically an error.
questions.solutionHtml: D, at (5, 29), is unusually high compared with the pattern of A, B, C, E and F. First check the score, reported study time and relevant context. Keep a valid observation; do not delete it merely because it weakens a preferred pattern.

questions.title: Repair one incorrectly plotted observation
questions.promptHtml:
The source records are A (1, 4), B (2, 7), C (3, 9), D (4, 10). Inspection time is x and faults found is y. One point in this draft scatterplot is wrong.

Identify it and enter the correct y-coordinate. Keep the correct x-coordinate unchanged.
questions.hint: Match each labelled point to the same labelled source record.
questions.solutionHtml: C should be at (3, 9), but is drawn at (3, 6). Move it vertically to y = 9 faults, leaving x = 3 minutes.

questions.title: Recover a prediction from two points on a fitted line
questions.promptHtml:
The two labelled points lie exactly on the fitted line. They are (2 km, 14 minutes) and (6 km, 26 minutes). The line was fitted using journeys from 1 to 8 km.

Find the slope, then predict the time for a 5 km journey.
questions.hint: Slope = change in predicted time ÷ change in distance. Start from either labelled point to make the 5 km prediction.
questions.solutionHtml: Slope = (26 − 14)/(6 − 2) = 3 minutes per km. At 5 km, prediction = 14 + 3(5 − 2) = 23 minutes. Equivalently, ŷ = 8 + 3x. This is within the observed range.

questions.title: Work backwards from a predicted response
questions.promptHtml: For outdoor temperatures from 16°C to 24°C, a fitted line predicts daily heating use as ŷ = 92 − 3x, where x is outdoor temperature (°C) and ŷ is heating use (kWh). According to this model, what outdoor temperature gives a predicted heating use of 29 kWh? Then check whether your answer lies within the stated input range.
questions.hint: Set 29 = 92 − 3x and solve for x. Compare the resulting temperature with 16–24°C.
questions.solutionHtml: 29 = 92 − 3x, so 3x = 63 and x = 21°C. This lies within 16–24°C. It is a model-based calculation; it is not a guarantee that every day at 21°C uses exactly 29 kWh.

questions.title: Compare the model prediction with an actual result
questions.promptHtml:
A line predicts packaging time as ŷ = 4.5 + 0.8x, with x the number of parcels and ŷ the time in minutes. The data used to fit the line included batches of 5–30 parcels. A batch of 15 parcels actually took 19 minutes.

Calculate the predicted time and the actual minus predicted difference. Then interpret the sign.
questions.hint: First use x = 15. For the requested difference, subtract the prediction from the actual 19 minutes.
questions.solutionHtml: Prediction = 4.5 + 0.8(15) = 16.5 minutes. Actual − predicted = 19 − 16.5 = +2.5 minutes. This batch took 2.5 minutes longer than predicted, so the line underpredicted its time.

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.answer: The model underpredicted this batch’s time

questions.title: Compare two straight-line cost models
questions.promptHtml:
For printing jobs from 0 to 500 copies, the quoted total prices are:

Printer A: y = 18 + 0.06x
Printer B: y = 6 + 0.10x

x is the number of copies and y is the total price in pounds. Calculate both prices for 250 copies, then find the whole number of copies at which the two prices are equal.
questions.hint: Substitute x = 250 into each model. For the equal-price quantity, set 18 + 0.06x = 6 + 0.10x.
questions.solutionHtml: At 250 copies, A costs 18 + 0.06(250) = £33.00; B costs 6 + 0.10(250) = £31.00. For equality, 12 = 0.04x, giving 300 copies. Both then cost £36.00. All these quantities lie in the stated range.

fields.label: Number of copies giving equal prices

questions.title: A narrow box can have long whiskers
questions.promptHtml:
Two groups take the same test. Whiskers show the minimum and maximum. The exact summaries are A: 2, 18, 20, 22, 38 and B: 10, 14, 20, 26, 30 minutes.

Calculate A’s IQR and range. Then choose the comparison that correctly distinguishes the middle-half spread from the full spread.
questions.hint: The box width is Q₃ − Q₁; the full spread is maximum − minimum. These can lead to different rankings.
questions.solutionHtml: A: IQR = 22 − 18 = 4 minutes; range = 38 − 2 = 36 minutes. B: IQR = 26 − 14 = 12; range = 30 − 10 = 20. Thus A has the smaller IQR but the larger range. The word “spread” needs the measure to be stated.

fields.label: Correct comparison
fields.answer: A has the smaller IQR but the larger range

questions.title: Repair a boxplot’s middle line
questions.promptHtml:
Ordered processing times are 2, 3, 5, 6, 6, 8, 9, 11, 14 minutes. Use quartile positions (n + 1) × 0.25 and (n + 1) × 0.75, with linear interpolation between neighbouring values. The draft uses min-to-max whiskers.

The plotted positions are 2, 4, 8, 10 and 14 minutes. Which feature is misplaced, and what should its correct value be?
questions.hint: There are nine observations. Locate the middle observation, then check the quartiles at positions 2.5 and 7.5.
questions.solutionHtml: The median is the fifth ordered value, 6 minutes, so the median line must move from 8 to 6. Q₁ = (3 + 5)/2 = 4 and Q₃ = (9 + 11)/2 = 10 are correct. The minimum 2 and maximum 14 are also correct.

extension.promptHtml: Optional drawing practice — self-check, not automatically marked. Redraw the corrected min-to-max boxplot on paper. Use an even numerical scale, label the five-number summary and include the time unit.
extension.modelAnswerHtml: The correct five-number summary is 2, 4, 6, 10, 14 minutes. Draw the box from Q₁ = 4 to Q₃ = 10, with its median line at 6. Whiskers run to the minimum 2 and maximum 14. Label the horizontal axis Processing time (minutes). The median line is not required to be halfway across the box.
rubric: The scale is numerical, even and labelled in minutes.
The box begins at 4 and ends at 10.
The median line is at 6, correcting the draft value of 8.
The min-to-max whiskers end at 2 and 14, and all five values are identifiable.

questions.title: Know what an ordinary boxplot leaves out
questions.promptHtml:
Two departments have ordinary min-to-max boxplots with the same five-number summary: 10, 15, 20, 25, 40 minutes. The box widths are fixed for display; they do not represent sample size. No individual observations or sample sizes are given. A report says: “The departments must have the same mean and the same number of observations.”

Which evaluation is correct?
questions.hint: A five-number summary records selected positions, not every value or the number of observations.
questions.solutionHtml: Neither claim follows. The shared summary establishes the same minimum, quartiles, median and maximum. Different observations between these positions can give different means, and ordinary fixed-width boxplots do not encode sample size.

fields.label: Evaluation of the report
fields.answer: Neither the same mean nor the same sample size is established

questions.title: Equal-looking boxes on different numerical scales
questions.promptHtml:
These two charts use different numerical scales. Both show result turnaround times in hours, with min-to-max whiskers. The exact summaries are Lab A: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 and Lab B: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30.

A student says: “The boxes look equally wide, so the IQRs are equal.” Calculate the two IQRs and evaluate the statement.
questions.hint: Read the numerical values on each axis. The same distance on the screen need not represent the same number of hours.
questions.solutionHtml: Lab A: IQR = 8 − 4 = 4 hours. Lab B: IQR = 24 − 12 = 12 hours. The statement is wrong: Lab B’s IQR is three times Lab A’s. Physical widths are comparable only when the numerical scales match. A shared scale would make this comparison clearer.

fields.label: Correct evaluation
fields.answer: Lab B’s IQR is three times Lab A’s
